Another year has passed, and again the .Representatives of our Fraternity
have assembled in Annual Communication to consult in reference to our noble
Order. The pa.st year has been one of prosperity to our common country, and
our own beloved Sta.te has aha.red in the blessings of a. beneficent Providence.
I congratulate you, my brethren, a.nd assure you that Masonry ha.a felt
the vivifying touch, a.nd this Grand Jurisdiction is in a. peaceable and prosperous condition.
The two Lodges to which charters were granted at our last Annual Communication, were duly constituted and their officers installed by special
deputies appointed for that purpose.
While we a.re assured of our Ma.sonic and National prosperity, let us pause
and pay due respect to our " Fra.terna.l Dead."
On Sunday la.st I convened this Gra.nd Lodge to pay the la.st sa.d tribute to
Past Grand Master Bro. .ALvAH RussELL CONKLIN, who died in this city on
October 6th. Bro. CoNXLIN wa.s elected Grand Master in 1890. He served
one year. As a soldier he lea.med obedience to constituted authority, the
necessity of promptness, the value a.nd power of organized effort ; as a lawyer
he was taught a. forceful style of reasoning, which constituted the charm of
his public utterances ; a.s a. judge he wa.s charged with the function of protecting the rights of property ; and no ma.n ever met these respollllibilities more
bravely.
As Grand M!lllter he rose to the full requirements of the exalted office. In
the crucible of every human career, there should rema.in a.t last, refined and
prepared for external use, a.n immortal soul.

On May lst, 1897, Pa.st Grand Master CLAY WEBSTER TAYLOR, after a long
and painful illness, quietly passed awa.y. On Ma.y 6th I convened the Grand
J..odge in Special Communication in the City of San Francisco, and, under the
solemn ritual of our Order, la.id him quietly away. To the older members
of this Grand Body, he wa.s a. familiar figure. He was elected R. ·• W. ••
Senior Grand Wardeii in October, 1879; R. ·• W. ·.· Deputy Grand Master in
1880; and Most Worshipful Grand Master in October, 1881a.nd1882-aerving
two terms.
Brother TAYLOR was a man noted for his intellectual attainments and
brilliant mind, an enthusiastic Mason, an upright citizen, and an honorable
man. Living, he had the respect and confidence of his countrymen; and dying,
left a na.me for integrity and manhood.
While I would not dry one tear that is shed for him ; while I would not
suppress one moan that breathes out the sorrow of those who mourn for him,

yet I take heart in the glad thought that in those things which made our
brother beloved, in those things which made him a leader among men, in all
these things he is not dead a.nd cannot die.
On July 12th, 1897, at his beautiful home in Sacramento, surrounded by
those who were near and dear to him, suddenly-almost instantaneously-our
venerable and beloved Past Grand Master N ATRANIEL GREENE CURTIS silently
passed to the Great Beyond. On July the fifteenth I convened the Grand
Lodge in Sacramento, and, under the impressive ceremonies of our Craftthe Craft he loved so well-laid all that was mortal of Past Grand Master
NATHANIEL GREENE CURTIS in the beautiful cemetery at Sacramento.
Brother CURTIS was a. member of this Grand Lodge for forty-five years,
serving as Grand Master for four years, and as a. member of the Committee
on Jurisprudence sixteen years, being its chairman at the time of his death.
The life of such a man is a sermon, a psalm, a.n inspiration. The death of
such a man is a. bereavement to society and to the State. Hnma.nity cannot
suppress its moan in the presence of death; a.round it there is an impenetrable
mystery-beside the bier the only remembrance of the great change.
Of his life and labors I do not wish to speak, but will leave that to others
more a.ble a.nd competent. I recommend that a. committee be appointed to
draft suitable memoria.ls to the memory of Pa.st Grand Masters.

During the past year I have issued six dispensations for the formation of
new Lodges. I granted several applica.tions for special dispensations, which
in my judgment the exigencies of the circumstances fully warranted me in so
doing.
I have a.pproved amendments to the By-Laws of several Lodges, that were
not in conflict with our Constitution and the Uniform Code of By-Laws.

When applications have been made to reduce the monthly dues, ' I have
carefully inquired into the financial condition of the Lodges; and where, in
my opinion, the proposed amendments sought to reduce the dues to an amount
that would destroy the usefulness of the Lodge, I have sedulously withheld
my approval. For a full and complete account of these acts, I refer yon to
the report of the Grand Secretary.
SPECIAL COMMUNICAT,IONS OF THE GRAND LODGE.
At the request of the Boa.rd of Supervisors of the county of Kings, on
October 30th, 1896, I convened the Grand Lodge in the city of Hanford, and
laid the corner-stone of-the new court-house in that prosperous community.
Brother EDWARDS, the Grand Lecturer, was witb me, and he devoted his
time while we were there to instruction. The brethren of the Lodge held a
special meeting and conferred the Third Degree in a creditable manner.
At the invitation of the Mayor and Board of Supervisors of the City
and County of San Francisco, on December 19th, 1896, I called a Special Communication of the Grand Lodge a.nd conducted the ceremonies of laying the
corner-stone of ·t he Hall of Justice. There was an immense outpouring of
the Fraternity. All elective, and ma.n y of the appointed officers of the Grand
Lodge, were present. The Grand Lodge, escorted by the mounted police,
Knights Templar, Ma.sonic Veterans' Associat\on, the Grand _Consistory
A. & A. Scottish Rite, marched from the Temple to the site of the proposed
building, and, amidst an immense concourse of people, with the formalities of
our Craft, laid the corner-stone of the Hall of Justice.
Accepti.iig a cordial invitation from the brethren of Los Angeles, on the eve·
ning of December 28th, 1896, I dedicated their commodious and beautiful
Temple. After our exercises we were entertained at a snmptnons banquet.
Brother l!:DwARDS, the Grand Lecturer, was there holding Lodges of Instruction. From the attendance and close attention given, I am satisfied that
Masonry in Los Angeles is progressing.
At the request of the Board of Regents of the State University, ·on March
20th, 1897, I conducted the ceremonies of laying the corner-stone of the
Affiliated Colleges. The day was nnpropitiona, but nevertheless there was
quite an audience. Our ceremonies harmoniously blended with the other ex·
ercises as a. fitting incident to the foundation of a. great University.
At the request of MiMion Lodge, No. 169, on April 24th, 1897, I laid the
comer-stone of the new Temple that the brethren a.re erecting in the western
part of this great city. There was a large number of the Craft present. The
day wa.s beautiful, and all nature seemed smilin~ as if to ~eer the brethren
of Miasivn Lodge to a speedy consummation of their hopes.
At the kind invitation of the bret~ren of Salinas City, on June 10th, 1897,
I laid the corner-stone of a new Masonic Temple. The brethren of Salinas are
erecting a beautiful home for themselves, and when completed it will sta.nd
as a living monument of their untiring industry. In the evening, Salinas
Lodge, No. 204, held a special meeting and conferred the Third Degree. Bro.
F. W. LucAs, the Inspector, wa.s present, with many visiting brethren.
After work we were invited to a repa.st, prepared by the Sisters of the O. E.
s., which demonstrated that the sisters had not neglected the cook book by
becoming a.doptive Masons.

On December the 5th, 1896, I received a letter from Brother M. J. SAVAGE,
. M. of Occidental Lodge, requesting that the Lodge be allowed to decorate
its altar with the American Flag. Without giving the matter serious thought,
and being in a patriotic mood, I granted the request. Since then, having
seriously considered the question, I am compelled to confess that I am of the
opinion that I erred in so doing. I believe that the best interests of Masonry
will be subserved by not allowing s.uch permission.
On January lat, 1897, I received a request from Enterprise Lodge, No. 70,
to allow that Lodge to receive and act upon the petition of LEROY JOHNSTON
CoPR, of Yuba CitY, he having lost three fingers of the left hand. I authorized
the Lodge to receive the petition, which was done. Later I learned that
almost the entire left hand had been lost ; also that Brothel" Past Grand Mastel"
PRESTON had refused Enterprise Lodge the same request. I am of the opinion
that I erred in allowing the Lodge to receive the petition.
I might say here, brethren, that .it appears to me that our regulations with
reference to physical qualifications are too exclusive, when we come .to compare
them with those of other and older jurisdictions. Is he a sound man! Can
he receive and impart the knowledge of the Craft! The internal soundness

The following is a brief statement of my decisions and rulings, which I
submit for your co~sideration :
DECISIONS.

Orland Lodge, No. 265, elected an applicant on November 16th, 1888. He
received the first two degrees of Masonry in that Lodge. A brother Mason, a
member of a neighboring Lodge, objected to his being raised to the sublime
degree of a Master Mason. A committee was appointed to investigate the
objection. The committee brought in an unfavorable report and the candidate
was denied advancement.
In the meantime the candidate removed to the jurisdiction of Olay Lodge,
No. 101, at Dutch Flat. After having resided there several years, Olay Lodge
requested Orkind Lodge to grant it the privilege to confer the remaining
degree.
Being governed by a ruling made by Past Grand Master BELCHER in 1865,
and the report of the Committee on Jurisprudence in regard to that ruling
made in 1868, I decided that two courses. were open for the disposal of the
case.
First-Let Orland Lodge receive the pebition, with the fee for the degree.
Let the petition take the usual course. If the petitioner were elected, Orl,and
Lodge could then confer the degree, or request Clay Lodge to confer for
Orland Lodge.
Second-Let the applicant request Orland Lodge to grant Clay Lodge the
privilege to receive and act on the petition, which, if granted, Olay Lodge
could receive, and it would have to go through the usual course of petitions
for the degrees.
The second alternative was acted upon-and the candidate was, by CT,ay
Lodge, rejected .
OT,ay Lodge desired to be informed to wha.t Lodge did the candidate owe
allegiance as a Fellow Craft Mason. I ruled that he was a Fellow Craft
Mason under the jurisdiction of Clay Lodge.
A complaint was made against one of the Lodges in San Francisco on account of a printed folder that is sent to the members of the Lodge prior t
each.stated meeting. The folder contained an epitome of the business tha
would be brought before the Lodge, together with the names, residence an
occupation of the candidates for whom the Lodge would ballot. The objectio
was, tha\ the Lodge was publishing to the profane tha.t which should be kep
within its tiled precincts. Upon a thorough investigation, I learned tha
most of the Lodges in San Francisco were doing this ; also that it was a cus
tom among the English Lodges ; Section 6, ArticlP. II, Part III, of the Con
stitution requires Lodges having concurrent jurisdiction to send this informa
tion to the other Lodges.
I decided that, in sending out the folder, no Masonic precedent was]
violated, and allowed the Lodges to continue the use of the printed folder.
There was an appeal to me to use my power to compel a Lodge to render
assistance to the widow of a deceased brother Mason. I declined to do so.

12

Procwlings of the

[Oct. 12,

1897.]

A~ there was no evidence

that the lady was unable to support herself, I did
not consider that the Lodge was under any moral or Masonic obligation to
render her financial assistance.
An Entered Apprentice, nor a Fellow Craft Mason, is not, as a right,
entitled to relief from the funds of a Lodge.
·
The funds of a Lodge cannot be used to defray the expenses of the accused
in a Masonic trial, nor to repay money expended for attorney's fees.
A Lodge has no authority to use its funds ·to pay assessments on a life
insurance policy, even though made out in favor of the Lodge, especially where
there were grave doubts that the amount of the policy would he paid to the
Lodge in case of the death· of the insured.
Where there was no evidence of a legal marriage, a woman claiming to be
the widow of a deceased brother Mason should not be recognized as such, and
is not an object of a Loilge's charity.
A rejected applicant for affiliation is not a special charge for charity on the
Lodge that rejected him.
MISCELLANEOUS.
There were many questions propounded to me during the year, which I
answered, that require no detailed report, as they were such as could be
answered by referring the writer to our Constitution and General Regulations,
or to the plain interpretation of the law as promulgated by this Grand Lodge.
On March 20th, 1897, I found the daughter of Past Grand Master ISAAC
SuTVENE TITUS in distreBS and need. She had just lost a child and was dependent upon the charity of friends. I drew a warrant to the amount of fifty
dollars in her favor, on the general. fund of the Grand Lodge. Since then I
received from her a letter of thanks, in which she states th'at she is now in
more comfortable circumstances.
I have had some correspondence with foreign jurisdictions, endeavoring to
have money refunded that our Boards of Relief and Lodges had expended for
the benefit of indigent members.
Fi.rat-With the Grand Master of Maine, with reference t~ charity
furnished a member of a Lodge in that jurisdiction by the Masonic Board of
Relief of San Diego. The Grand Master absolutely refused to do anything in
the matter.
In my correspondence with the Grand Master of Oregon, with reference to
a claim of Durant Lodge against a Lodge in that Grand Jurisdiction, I re·
ceived a courteous reply, and the Grand Master, PHILll' METSCHAN, in hie
Annual .Address, recommends that the Lodge settle the indebtedness, or, if
unable to do so, that the Grand Lodge of Oregon pay the amount. From correspondence on file in the office of our Grand Secretary, I am of the opinion
there will be a speedy settlement of the matter.
I wrote the Grand Master of Nebraska with reference to charity furnished
members of Masonic Lodges from that Grand Jurisdiction by the Stockton
and Oakland Boards of Relief. An acknowledgment of the receipt of my let·
ter is all that has been done as yet in the matter.
I have written the Grand Masters of Texas and Michigan in regard to
claims of Phmnix Lodge, No. 178, against Lodges in their respective jurisdictions. Sufficient time has not yet elapsed for a reply.

July 16th, 1897, I visited our venerable Past Grand Master JOHN A. TUTT.
He is now eighty.four years of age. He sent hie fraternal greetings to the
brethren. I recommend that this Grand Body continue the appropriation heretofore made to Bro. TuTT.
The reports of the several Boards of Relief will be presen~ for your
consideration. To them I direct your special attention, and recommend that
Grand Lodge make such provision for them as the needs of the several Boards
seem to require.
Not having received reports from the Inspector in all of the several
Masonic Districts, I cannot speak in detail of the condition of the subordinate
Lodges. The Grand Lecturer, in hie report, will specifically give you all of
the information desired.

Charges were preferred by members of Yo8emite Lodge, No. 133, against
the W :irshipful Master, for the reason that he had not entertained charges preferred against a member of the Lodge. After a thorough investigation I was
satisfied that the Master was doing his duty. When I wrote for information,
the Worshipful Master had already convened the Lodge, and elected trial comrmss10ners. When the case came on for trial, the accuser had nothing but
newspaper clippings and heal'l!ay evidence. This the Master properly ruled out.
There being no evidence, the accused was cleared. As no appeal has been
taken in the case, it is 8ettled so far as this Grand Body is concerned.
Wmows' AND ORPHANS' HOME.
There has not been much done this la.et year with reference to the Widows'
and Orphans' Home. A detailed statement of its affairs will be given you.
You have a capable and working Board of Trustees, and I hope that this
Grand Lodge will give that board its enthusi38tic and loyal support.
We, as a Grand Lodge, a.re approaching our half century mark. This
Grand Lodge was organized on the 19th day of April, 1850. In my opinion it
is proper that we take some preliminary steps looking forward to celebrating
the fiftieth annivel'l!ary of the organization of the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of California., the Pioneer of Masonry, the Mother Grand Lodge of the
Pacific Slope. I therefore recommend that a permanent committee be appointed to take the matter in hand, so that we may pay due tribute to "those
who builded better than they knew."
In this connection, I feel like directing your attention to "Fifty Years of
Masonry in California," edited by our venerable and scholarly brother, EDWIN
A. SHERMAN. It is a work replete with information and entertaining to the
reader.
For information with reference to our foreign brethren, and the general condition of Freemasonry throughout the world, I refer you to the erudite report of the Committee on Correspondence.
I wish to commend the universal courtesy of the officers of the Grand
Lodge, and the promptness with which they obeyed all invitations to attend
special communications, when in their power so to do. I especially thank the
Grand Secretary for his assistance and his counsel; courteous, without being
officious, he has lightened my labors and divided my burdens.
My brethren, here ends all that I think necessary for me to report to you.
I am not unmindful of the high honor which you have bestowed on me. 1 return to you the power which you vested in me, and from a sincere heart thank
you one and all for the universal consideration shown me throughout the
jurisdiction; not as an individual, but for the time being, the representati\•e
of the grandest association known of men.
We now are ready to proceed with the business of .this. Communication, and may our .deliberations be governed by "Temperance, Fortitude,
Prudence and Justice."
WILLIAM THOMAS LUC.AS,
Grand Master.

in detail the traneactions of his office since the last Annual Communication,
and presenting all such matters appertaining to tha.t office as may require
action by this Grand Body, or may, in any way, be of iuteriost to its officers
and members.
As soon as possible after the close of the last Annual Communication, two
thousand two hundred and fifty copies of the proceedings thereof were printed
a.nd distributed, or reserved for future binding, in the customary manner, viz.:
one copy to ea.ch of the present Grand Officers ; one copy to ea.ch of the elective
Past Grand Officers ; four copies to each of tl;ie Grand :Bodies, American and

In accordande with a standing direction of the Grand Lodge, three hundred

the uniform style adopted from the commencement ; the two years' transactions
form the twenty-second volume of the series which constitutes the history of
the Grand Lodge of California.
The proceedings of all the Grand Lodges of the United States, for the year
since last report, have been received and placed in the hands of the Chairman
of the Committee on Correspondence, with the exception of Georgia and New
Hamplhire, as have also those of Canada, England, Ireland, New South
Wales, New Zealand, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, South
Australia and Victoria.

Proposed amendments to the By-Laws, relative to the reduction of dues of
members, from Lodges Nos. 194, 203 and 291, were disapproved by the Grand
Master, for the reason that the rate proposed was thought to be too low for
the Lodges to maintain a healthy and useful existence.
A proposed amendment to the By-Laws of Lodge No. 127, relative to the
collection of dues, was disapproved by the Grand Master, as not coming
within the category of amendments provided for in Art. XIII of the Uniform
Code.
The approval of the Grand Master being but a temporary authorization,
the foregoing amendments, as required by our law, have been placed in the
·hands of the Chairman of the Committee on By-Laws of Lodges, and will be
submitted to the Grand Lodge for final action, as have the books of By-Laws
of the six Lodges now working under dispensation.

. Your Special Committee, to which was referred that portion of the Address
of Grand Master PRESTON, devoted to "The Ritual," and appearing on pages
575 and 576 of the proceedings of the forty-seventh Annual Communication,
A. L. 5896, respectfully report as follows :
1. We recommend the passage of a resolution for the creation of a permanent Committee on Ritual, the members of which shall be the custodians and
censors of the text of the work.
2. Whether the work, as now taught, is strictly the work as adopted by
this Grand Lodge, is al.most impossible to determine ; but your committee do
not believe it is, and certainly, whether htlretofore adopted or not, it stands
in need of some slight corrections.
The population of this jurisdiction is eminently cosmopolitan, being made
p of people from all parts of the habitable earth, and comprising Masons from
almost every known jurisdiction. It is no matter of wonder that amon~ such
. a people the peculiarities which have intruded themselves into other jurisdictions should assert themselves here, nor that some d~partures from the ancient
text and some crudities and inconsistencies should have had birth on our soil.
All Masons desire the preservation of the ancient work, and bear loyal adherence to those ceremonials and forms of teaching and impressing the grand
moral lessons of Masonry which were inspired by }Qfty wisdom, and which
have been sanctified by centuries.
Innovat~on and modern invention· have at all times been unpopular in the
Masonic Lodge, and your committee, in its review of the work, has not assumed to lay unkind hands upon a single fragment of the honored structure,
but wherever we have discovered a palpable innovation we have, for the pur·
poses of this report, condemned it and thrown it out.
Especially in the first and third degrees, as l;he work is now done, there
are some inconsistencies, and we may say some absurdities, the elimination of
which we earnestly recommend.
Take no fright at this language, and be not apprehensi~e that we are about
to put a coat of paint upon the old Marble Mansion; we merely propose to
brush off the dust and cobwebs and leave the ancient structure as our honored
progenit.ors builded it.
Each change in the work as recommended is but slight in its extent; it
will subject the officers of Lodges to little if any extra labor to conform to the
work as restored, and we trust and beµeve the members of this august Body
will approve what we have done.
The committee convened in full session on the da.y succeeding 'their ap·
pointment and proceeded to adopt measures for the successful prosecution of
the work intrusted to their hands. This work was given to a sub-committee
of three, consisting of Past Grand Master EDMUND CLEMENT ATKIN!ION,

Grand Lecturer ·WILLIAM HARVEY EDWARDS and FREDERICK WILLIAM LucAB,
Inspector of the Twenty-eighth :Pistrict, with instructions to report to the
General Committee on completion of their labors. This sub-committee have
worked diligently·anJ faithfully, giving much of their time during the past
year to the work entrusted to them. They have carefully revised and corrected the work of the three degrees and changed the phraseology so far as it
relates to the grammatical construction of sentences and the proper use of
terms. They have made extended research into the work of the second section
of the third degree as taught and practiced in eastern jurisdictions, and have
adopted so much thereof as will make the work of this jurisdiction conform
thereto. They have sncceeded in preparing a ritualistic work which your
commitee believe will be most pleasing and satisfactory to this Grand Body,
and which, intelligently rendered, will impreBS in a forcible manner upon the
candidate the beautiful teachings of Freemasonry.
It is gratifying to this committee to observe that so muoh of the work of
this jurisdiction has been preserved in this section of the third degree, and
that so few changes have been made in the inauguration of the new features.
It is the opinion of this committee that the work which will be presented for
the consideration of this Grand Body will be recoguized as being especially
consistent with the ancient traditions upon which were founded the scenes
represented in this degree. The commiti6e designated for this work have prepared for the exemplification of the new Ritual by selecting and instructing a
sufficient number of accomplished brethren, who will, it is believed, present
the proposed work in a very pleasing and acceptable manner. And, in order
that members of this Grand Body may witness the exemplification, your committee recommend that authorization he given for the conferring of the several
degrees in accordance With a resolution herewith presented.
In conclusion, your committee cannot too strongly emphasize the neceBSity
of selecting permanent custodians of the work adopted, in order that a uniformity of the same may he preserved and promulgated throughout the jurisdiction.
All which is respectfully submitted..
SAMUEL CRAWFORD DENSON, }
JACOB HART NEFF,
EDMUND CLEMENT ATKINSON, . Committee.
FREDERICK WILLIAM LUCAS,

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge oj'Oalifornia :In compliance with the usual methods of the Grand Lecturer, I beg leave
to submit the followini;p; report, and, by way of preface, desire to say that it
is much easier to do the work of the Grand Lecturer in the field than to summarize the result of his labors at the close of the year.
I have devoted as much time as was possible to the discharge of my duties,
and feel that with all that has been done much more would have been desirable.

..

October 24th to 25th I visited Arcturus Lodge, No. 180, at Petaluma, and
witnessed the conferring of the second degree by the Worshipful Master, F. K.·
LIPPITT, and the officers of his Lodge. They conferred the degree in a manner
worthy of the enthusiasm which seemed to pervade the Lodge.
October 29th to November lat I spent in holding Lodges of instruction at
Santa Rosa. There was a good attendance by the officers of the different Lodges
in the District. I found that they were all up to their work and enthusiastic.
Bro. PERKINS, the Inspector of this District, was present one evening during
the meeting and assured me that all the Lodges of his District, save two, were
in splendid working condition. There are several Past Mastera at Santa Rosa
who a.re thoroughly competent to impart instruction to the officers of their
Lodges, and the result of their labors, as well as those of the Inspector of the
District, is plainly visible.
November 5th to November 8th visited Hanford Lodge, No. 214 on the occasion of the laying of the corner-stone ef the new court house, where our
M.-. W. ·.Grand Master, W. T. LUCAS, presided in a manner that reflected great
credit upon the Grand Lodge and upon himself. .I spent several hours in imparting instruction to the Inspector of the District and the officers of the
Lodge in attendance, and in this was greatly assisted by the M.-. W.-. Grand
Master. •
November 20th to 22d, held a Lodge of instruction at Stockton, at which
all the Lodges of the District were represented. There were many Past
Mastera present, and great interest was manifested in the work. Each degree
was thoroughly gone over and practiced, and the meeting appeared to be of
great benefit to those in attendance.
November 25th. to 29th held Lodges of instruction at Fresno. Nearly all
the Lodges in the District were represented at the meeting. Past Grand
Lecturer JAMES WR!GHT ANDERSON was in attendance part of the time and
rendered valuable assistance in giving the work and commending that which
was given.
December 19th to January 3d was devoted to Lodges of instruction held
in San Diego, ,LQa Angilea and Colton. Under the auspices, and with the
assistance, of our able Bro. JAMES WELLl:I, Inspector of that District, the
meeting at Sa'1 Diego was much enjoyed by myself and all who were present.
The officers of the various Lodges in the District seemed to be vecy desirous
of getting the work letter-perfect. Past Mastera R. C. CHAPMAN of Fallbrook
Lodge, No. 317, and J. K. BLACKMER, San Diego Lodge, No. 35, were present
at evecy session of the Lodges of instruction, and rendered great assistance to

38

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 12,

myself and the Inspector in imparting the work to the various officers of the
District.
December 24th to 31st held Lodges of instruction at Los Angeles, which
were the most satisfactory of any held in the State during the year. All the

June 18th started from San Francisco to Susanville, arriving there on the
21st. Held Lodges of instruction in Susanville Jnne 22d, 23d and a part of
the 24th. The Lodges were well attended. Bro. WILLIAM BROCKMAN, that
venerable Mason and prince of good fellows, was unceasing in his efforts to
make my visit a pleasant one. Myself and wife enjoyed the hospitality of his
home and the genial companionship of his family. His carriage and horses
were at oi;ir disposal as long as we remained in his county. He drove with us
to the grave of our deceased brother, PETER LASSEN. As we stood by his
grave in the shade of a giant tree, which stands over it like a sentinel, we
read the inscription upon the monument of our departed brother, and regretted
that the Masons of California were patiently standing by and permitting this
pioneer of our craft to sleep on in that ''sleep that knows no waking " with
so unpretentious a resting place. Even the monument is chipping off and falling away, piece by piece, and ere long will crumble and fall, leaving the grave
of our honored brother unmarked and unknown.
Bro. BROCKMAN sent his son with a carriage to mt>et me on my arrive.! at
Amidee and to bring myself and wife to his home. When I had finished my
labors at SuBllllvill!', instead of permitting me to stage it back to Amidee and
thence to Alturas, in Modoc county, he again kindly took us in his carriage
across the country to Madeline, a distance of fifty miles, thereby saving us a
most fatiguing and uncomfortable stage ride, and also saving us the hardship
of traveling in the night. Long live such Masons as Bro. ''BILLY" BROCKMAN.

Grand Lodge of California.

And from the answers received from the Inspectors throughout the jurisdiction, I gleaned that the Fraternity is in a more prosperous condition than
it has been for several years prior to this. That the Inspectors have generally
visited the respective Lodges of their Districts at least once during the year,
and have spent considerable time in instructing the same. That the work '
throughout the jurisdiction is generally fairly well done by the different
Lodges; that the increase in membership bas been satisfactory, and in some
cases phenomenal, particularly with some of the Lodges iri San Francisco,
Mission Lodge having conferred during the year more degrees than any Lodge
has ever done in the same length of time before. That the fina.ncial coudition
of the Lodges throughout the juri~diction is fair, many Lodges owning considerable property and having a cash balance on the right side of the ledger.
That the books of the various Lodges are kept in accordance with the require·
ments of the Grand Lodge. That the Lodges in the Districts where the Grand
Lecturer has held District Lodges of instruction were well represented. That
the various Lodges throughout the jurisdiction have endeavored to conform to
the instructions given by the Grand Lecturer, and that there is an earnest desire to render the work in the most acceptable manner.
The Insp~ctors have pfodged themselves to issue no certificates of qualification to Masters-elect at the end of this year who are not thoroughly qualified,
both by their knowledge of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge and by their
acquaintance with the ritual of our Frater.n ity, to fill .completely the requirements of the Grand Lodge. .
RECOMMENDATIONS.
My experience as Grand Lecturer Juring the year has convinced me that
the jurisdiction of California is too large a field for one man to cover. It is
impoasible for the Grand Lecturer to visit more than one-half of the Districts
in the State during bis term of office. It requires from three days to one week'
to render such assistance to the Lodges as will enable them to do the work
correctly. And while it is true that by holding District Lodges of instruction
at which all ~be Lodges of the District may receive instruction simultaueonsly, ·
yet if we devoted the necessary time at such meetings, working day and night,
it is impossible for the Grand ·Lecturer to visit all the Districts. It seems to
me that the correct policy would be to appoint at least three Deputy Grand
. Lecturers, for which purpose the State should be divided into at least four
1
Districts, and a Deputy Grand Lecturer should be appointed for three oftheae

/

Pro~edirtgB of the

Districts which are most remote from San Francisco, leaving the San Francisco
District without a Deputy Grand Lecturer, and to be looked after by the
Grand Lecturer in person. I would suggest that one Deputy Grand Lecture~
should be appointed for that portion of the State lying south of Tehachapi
Pass, and that his headquarters should be at the City of Los ~~eles, from
whence he could radiate in all directions and do the work which is now sup·
posed to be done by the Grand Lecturer. I would suggest that another Deputy
Grand Lecturer be assigned to that portion lying north of Red Bluff, and t~at
his headquarters should be at Redding or Red Blnff, which would enable him
to embrace in his instructions all the northern part of the State. And that
the third Deputy Grand Lecturer be appointed for that portion of the State
including and lying north and east from Sacramento with headquarters at
Sacramento.
This would leave the Grand Lecturer that portion of the State not included
in the Districts suggested for the Deputy Grand Lecturers.
With such a corps of assistants the work of this Grand Ju~sdicti~ii ~ou.ld
be so systematized as would render it poBBible for every Lodge in ~he JUrl~dic­
tion to receive a fair share of attention and to perfect themselves in the ntual
and floor work of the several degrees, and wonld inspire greater zeal among
the Fraternity at large. These Deputy Grand Lecturers should be pai~ the'.r
traveling expenses and a fair remuneration for their time. And I believe it
would be a most profitable investment for the Grand Lodge. It wo~ld be a
most radical remedy for eliminating the errors which have crept mto our
ritual by the infnsio.n into it of patches of the work of other juriedictions
through the election of officers who have been Masters or.Ward~n~ of. L?'1~es
in other jurisdictions, and who have brought with them into this JUnsdict1on
fragments of their "first love."

Sandwiched between the journal and the Report on Correspondence we find a
portrait of the firdt Grand Secretary, Bro. EPHRAIM KIRBY, with a most interesting biographical sketch of hid life. Bro. KIRBY was one of the delegates who
assembled in 1783, and again in 1789, to formulate a plan for the formation of the
Grand Lodge of Connecticut. Bro. KIRBY was the Secretary of the Convention
and one of the committee who relJorted, .substantially, the present Grand Lodge
Oonstitution. He held the positions of Junior Grand Deacon and of Junior and
of Senior Grand Wardens. At tbs organization of the General Grand Chapter in
1798, he was "found worthy to be chosen by the voice of his companions to the
office of General Grand High Priest." Like many another valiant soldier of the
Revolution be was an enthusiastic Mason. Peace to his memory.

We have great confidence in their experience in Masonic matters; but it is
human nature, pure aud simple, for man to murp, when he thinka he can do so,

there is an effort to get entire control of the Gra.nd Lodges by those old stagers,
and thus make our Institution an oligarchy. Masonry, &a a whole, in any one
Grand Jurisdiction, is more in the form of a republic. Our representatives of the
separate Lodges constitute our legislature; the Grand Master iR the Governor or
presiding officer; his powers are defined, generally, by the "Old Regulations of
1721," and by the Constitution of hie own Grand Lodge. He cannot go one step
beyond these without usurping authority. He is governed by law as every other
Mason U.. His prerogatives are laid down clearly and distinctly in the " Old
Regulations " and in hie own local Constitution, and he is amenable to any new
law that may be made, should occasion require, for hitherto, thanks to the good
sense manifested by all Grand Masters, no occasion baa required that new law.J. and
woe be to that man who may so far forget hiil obligations as to require it. There
was one Judas ! Jet us hope that in Masonry there may nevl'r be one.

A Special Session of the Grand Lodge of Idaho was held on the 6th of January,
1896, in Boise, for the purpose of paying the last sad tribute of respect and affection to the remains of their late Grand Tyler, W. ·. AUGUSTINE HAAB, who died
on the 3d instant. The ceremonies were performed in accordance with ancient
usage; the body was conveved to the cemetery and buried; the procession returned to the hall, and Grand Lodge closed.

Among his visitations, Grand Master recalls this pleasant historical incident.
After acknowledging the fraternal and courteous receptions which met him in
every Lodge jurisdiction, he says :-

The most vl\lued jewel of the Grand Lodge of Idaho is its Orphan Fund,
amountinl!' now to $27,000. It was created and nourished by an assessment levied
by Grand Lodge twenty.seven years ago of one dollar for each Mason borne upon
the rolls of constituent Lodges. The fund proper is "irreducible;" the interest is
placed in the "Interest Orphans'· Fund" and applied to the relief of needy orphan
children and distressed brethren.
The Grand Master said good words for the Idaho MtUOn, a Masonic journal
recently established for the growth of the Order of the Eastern Star, and closed by
presenting to Grand Lodge, on behalf of Place:r Lodge, No. 3, the original set of
'' Tin J euela" used by that Lodge in its work of days gone by.

:Under District of Columbia, in reviewing the work of tbe eminent veteran,
SINGLETON, he says, speaking of tbe Grand Lodge:An amendment to permit all Past Masters to sit and vote in Grand Lodge,

Very well for Idaho, Bro. STEVENSON, in her present condition, hut a dangerous
. policy for California or any other State having large cities with a.corresponding
Masonic population. To illustrate: in San Francisco we have sixteen Lodges, who
carry upon their rolls three hundred Past Masters; Oakland, across the bay,
another hundred; Santa Clara, distant only two hours, another hundred. Give
the five hundred brethren each a vote, and while the country Lodges would be
taken care of it might not be always to their taste. That same amendment divided
the Grand Lodge of New York fifty years ago, and, after years of bitter recrimination, was healed in 1850. We were present at the wedding festivities. We think
our present law giving the Past Masterd, collectively, of each Lodge one vote, is
the only safe method in the matter o~ the ballot.

The question of jurisdiction over rejected mate1·ial still continues to attract
more attention than any other, fresh instances of deadlock between soverei11n jurisdictions differing in their law of Mas0nry, serving to keep it continually to the

clearly seen ·that a necessary .condition pr&eedent to any agreement must be a recognition by both sides of the fact that Masonry, not the candidate, is the chief
factor in the problem; in other words, it must be agreed that the Masonic acts of
a lawfully constituted Lodge, working in conformity to the Regulations of the
Grand Lodge, which i~ eonceded to be for thoae of its obedience the authorized
interpreter of Masonic: law, mlll!t be given full faith and credit. Under the irritation caused by the unwarrantable trespass, it took us a good while to see that the
maJdng of material belonging to us by Lodge11 of a different obedience must be
confessed to have given the material so made a lawful Masonic sta.tu•, beeause they
were lawful Lodges lawfully at labor in conformity with the regulations imposed

of making by a Lodge thus at labor .is without Masonic virtue, null, fJOiLl, and of
no elfeet.
On the question of non-affiliation, he says :There a.re increasmg and qualifying signs of returning reasfln in the consideration of the rights and wrongs of non-affiltates apparent not only in the discussions

followed by prayer and the declaration that the Lodge is opened. Of course, all openings and closings are similar.

The Gran Dieta Symbolica was organized in Mexico in the year 1890,·and is now
the governing Body over the three degrees of Symbolic Masonry. In its Constitution,, originally, it required Lodires to use upon their altars the "Ancient
Constitutions," and made no provisions as to ·the use of the Bible on the altar,
and in practice it was not used in Mexican Lodges, except such Lodges as were
comprised principally of American residents.
Shortly after its organiz..tion, the Gran Dieta authorized the conferring of the
dej!T6!ls in its Lodges upon women, and organized by charter three Lodges com·
pnsed of women, and some of the Lodges conferred degrees upon women.
R. ·. W. ·. Grand Secretary PARVIN traveled extensively through the Republic
of Mexico two years ago, and visited Grand and subordinate Lodges and President

6

..
82

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 13,

1897.]

DIAZ, the Grand Master of the Gran Dieta, and other Grand Officers, and protested against the practice of conferring the degrees upon women and of not
requiring the use of the Bible upon the altar in Lodges, and urged them to eliminate these objectionable features from their laws and practice. His urgent request
was received with favor, and in the summer of 1895 the Gran Dieta, by edict,
forbade the making of women Masons, excluded th ose i>lready ma<le from visiting
its Lodges, and revoked the charters granted to the three Lodges of women, and in
August of the Harne year promulgated a new "Constitution and Code of Statutes,"
embracing the provisions of its previous edict, and further, requiring the use of
the Bible upon its altars. There bas been considerable olposition in Mexico t;>
those provisionl!I of the Constitution and Code, and some o the Lodges refused to
Ull6 the Bible upon their altars and withdrew from the Gran Dieta; others objected
because of the exclusion of women and the recalling of their charters.
Since the promulgation of the new Constitution and Code of Statutes, the Gran
Dieta has been endeavoring to enforce these provisions, and in this respect to comply with the requirements of American Masonry. There are three American
Lodges in the city of Mexico, with a membership of over four hundred, and there
are several other American Lodges in the Republic of Mexico. They hold their
charters from the Gran Dieta. and are loy"l to it, and support it in its endeavors to
uphold these Masonic principles. The great wealth and vast resources of our sister
Republic, that have for centuries la.in dormant, are now attracting hundreds and
thousands of American• to assist in their development, and from this time on the
number of American citizens and American Masons visiting and taking up their
residence in Mexico will greatly increase, and on their account and in their behalf
the Gra.nd Lodge of Iowa should, in my judgment, P.xtend fraternal recognition to
the Gran Dieta of Mexico. Several of the Grand Lodges of the United States
have already done so.
Believing that the fraternal recognition by this Grand Lodge of the Gran Dieta
would have a beneficial effect upon Masonry on the American Continent, I recommend that this subject be referred to a special committee to investigate and report
their conclusion at this session of the Grand Lodge.
This recommendation was approved' by the Committee on the Address of the
Grand Master, who reported as follows. Said report was concurred in by Grand
Lodge and the accompa.nying resolutions adopted :To the M. •• W. •• GTand Lodge of I<YUJa :Your special committee, to whom was referred the question of the recognition
of the Gran Dieta Symbolica of Mexico, discussed in the Address of the Grand
Master, and also more fully in the report on Moxican Masonry by Grand Se~retary
PARVIN, have fully considered the subject embraced in these papers, and in view
of the facts set forth can see no reason why the Grand Lodge of Iowa should not
follow the usual custom of extending the right band of fellowship to this Grand
Body of our sister Republic, and we recommend the adoption of the following resolut1on :lluolvea, That the Grand Lodge of Iowa hereby recognizes the "Gran Dieta
Symbolica of Mexico" as an independent, sovereign Grand M&.11onic Body, exer·
cising sole jurisdiction over the three degrees of Ancient Craft Masonry in Mexico,
and will excba.nge fraternal courtesies therewith; a.nd,
.Further, That a.ll Masons in Mexico bailing from Lodges or Grand Lodges not
in affiliation with said Gran Dieta Symbolica, be denied admiBBion to our Lodges.
Fraternally submitted.
MATT. P ABBOTT,
J. N. MoCLA.NAHAN,

Past Grand Master and Cbe.irmao Bro. W1LLiill W. CLARU, who bas written in
the Kentucky journal of proceedings convincingly and forcibly upon the heresy of

Io bis cooclosion be treats as to a third paper devoted to a farther examination
of 'be fooodation for the erroneous doctrine be bas so thoroughly analysed in
former arguments. We dislike to disturb the thread of bis reasoning by a mutilation of bis cooclosloos and woold give the paper entire, but for the space demanded;
however, we will quote what appears to us the unanswerable points in the premises.
We quote:No Grand Lodge has the right or possesses the aothority to qoestion the acts of,
or the laws promulgat~d by, another Grand Lodge, except where socb other Grand
Lodge bas sanctioned acts or promulgated laws contrary to the universal and uorepealable laws or customs of Masonry. This proposition can not be questioned.
That sovereignties are e?,ual in rights it! a universally accepted maxim of international law. When one Urand Lodge refuses recognition of the acts and laws of
another it devolves opon it to show that .the act or law, recognition of wh ich is
refused, falls within the exception stated, otherwise eqoallty is destrol.ed, and the
Grand ·Lodge refusing recognition at once becomes paramount, while toe other
sinks into a condition of subordination.
Is perpetual jurisdiction an onrepealable law of Masonry! If so, it most be
oniversal ; bot the fact that it is approved only by a minority of the Grand Lodges
of America, and by no foreign Grand Lodge,. absolotely negatives the assumption.
We can not imagine a law of a universal society to be oorepealable If it be not
universal ; nor can we imagine a law- of a society to be onrepealable If we know
that lo a single instance, to say nothing of a majority or the governing bodies of
society, that le.w is not recognized.
This argument bas proceeded for a while on the assumption that the doctrine of
perpetual jorisdiotioo was at one time a law , bot in many places bas been repealed,
bot it is irresistibly intensified when it Is shown that by a majority of Grand LodKes
it bas never been recognized, and therefore coold never have been a part of the
oorepealable law of the Order, and, as a corullary thereto, those Grand Lodges
which adhere to it, and thereby refuse to recognize the acts of other Grand Lodges
which repodiate it, are arrogating to themselves powers supreme to other Grand
Lodges lo derogation of the maxim quoted, aupra.
A custom presupposes an antecedent law, bot the record of which, from long
lapse of time, bas been lost; bot, to raise this presumption, the costom must have
existed from "the time whereof the memory of man roooetb not tu the contrary."
Is this predicable of the doctrine nuder examination! The Grand Lodge of England
repudiates It; it finds no favor by any Grand Lodge outside the United Ste.tee, and
is recognized by a pitiable minority of those within the United States. Theo the
precedent law can not be presumed, nor can it be alleged that it has existed time
oat of mind. Bot, further, Mr. Justice Blackstone observes that a custom must be
co11tinoous. Any diecootiooance would be fatal, from the fact that a resumption of
the custom would give it a new beginning, which could not be from the time
whereof the memory of man ronoetb not to the contrary. Not only, therefore,
does the rejection of the doctrine by so many and so large a majority of Grand
Lodges work a discontinuance of tbe custom, at least as to them, bot every Qraod

The usage in England is appealed to in both reports. Thia provides that after
opening and the giving of necessary directions and iostrnctions the Lodge is " ad·
journed," and on its return Is "closed."
The majority, as we think, may properly hold that "adjourn" can mean no lees
than " calling olI." It would naturally imply even more.
Bro. SCHULTZ maintains that it means no more than passing from the place of
meeting to the procession-au interpretation very much forced and nnoatnral. Bro.
SoHULTZ argues that noless the Lodge has been open it could not be closed direotly
after returning. The brevity of the record evidently omits to say, as we have
always been accustomed to seeing done, that the Lodge was called on and generally
transacted some business before it was closed. Bro. BcHULTZ says if a Lodge is not
open, why most the Tyler head the procession, the brethren be clothed, and the
officers have their jewels, working tools, etc.! We might answer in detail that the
Tyler, in a pnblio procession, is not discharging the nsual functions of his office, and
it is not usual to take along an altar, etc., bot we are arguing the question upon
"authority," and not npon the inherent reason and propriety of the case. And
when the oldest and most reliable authority speaks of " adjourning" for the pnr·
pose of appeatiog in publio, we 11.re at a loss to comprehend bow an open Lodge
can at th~ same time be adjonrned. We readily concede that a Lodge, Grand or

thereafter close.
Though Bro. SCJIULTZ says he can conceive or but three conditions in which a
Lodge may be at any time either open, closed or at refreshment, yet he himsE!lf
provides a fourth condition, i. e., boing at "exoteric" work, during part of whioh
time, at least, the Craft is in charge of a Marshal. The term "caillng off" seems
the most appropriate term to apply in paBBing from "esoteric to exoteric work.
Unless langnage has become an instrument to conceal, rather than reveal ideas,
adjonrn co·mes nearer 'calling off' than merely going out in procession, and·
perhaps, it c.omes nearer 'clo6ing' than either of the interpretations. Certainly,
the case is not yet closed."

And now comes the gem of the journal, the Report on Correspondence,
although clouded in this instance by the sad affliction of Bro. DRUMMOND, who
has been so long associated with this work for the Grand Lodge of Maine as to be
thoroughly identified with its history and jurisprudence, and is recognized as their
most able exponent. Our heart goes out in sympathy to Bro. DRUMMOND in his
great grief. He says :-We write this report in the shadow of the sorest affiiction of our life. For the
first time death has invaded our family circle and taken away our youngest.
daughter, who for thirty years has veritably been a "light in our household."
We had always taken it for granted that our last look upon earthly things would
have rested upon her sweet face. We cannot yet realize that we shall never again
look upon it with mortal eye; but how we miss it, We now know that only those
who have had a similar experience can appreciate. If length of life is to be measured by what one does for others, hers was indeed a Ion~ life.
It may be deemed a weakness to thus obtrude our private grief upon the Craft,
but so be it-the words of sympathy, condolence and encouragement that have come
to us from all over the country, especially from the brotherhood, have greatly aided
us in this terrible trial, and we take this method of acknowledging our appreciation
of them.
Bro. DRUMMOND'S review of California is of the administration of Grand Master
PRESTON. In noticing the Grand Master's deprecation of hasty legislation, he
says:We doubt if a single law, restricting the powers or privileges of Lodges or individual Masons can be found, that was not suggested by some act that was deemed
injurious to the Institution or to the <;Jraft. Undo~l;>ted)y laws have been enacted
in consequence of such an act, when m all prohab1hty 1t would never have been
repeated, but·as a whole, experience shows that legislation has not been enacted
for the mere sake of legislating, but to prevent the continuance of evils growing out
of the tendency of which Grand Master PRESTON speaks. This is forcibly illustrated by some of his decisions, which often are what we may call judicial legislation.
He notes the case of WILLIAM .HENBY MENTOR, on review before the Grievance
Committee, whe•e the judgment of expulsion by the Lodge was reversed for irregularity, and upon recommendation of the Committee MENTOR was expelled by the
Grand Lodge from ail the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Bro. DRUMMOND commends this judgment by Grand Lodge to the attention of
Bro. M. M. MILLER, of Kansas.
We will add that it is in accordance with the practice warranted by the following provision of our Constitution:Article V, Section 1. All transcripts of trial-records, required to be transmitted
to the Grand Secretary, shall by him be forwarded to the Committee on Grievances,
who shall examine them, with such additional evidence in writing, if any, as may
be presented, and shall report thereon at the next succeeding Annual Communication; and upon such report the Grand Lodge may affirm, modify, or may reverse
the judgment of the Lodge, or may make such other order relative thereto as shall
be deemed proper.
Bro. DRUMMOND quotes the report of our Committee on Jurisprudence concerning the action of the Grand Lodge of Maine in relation to the necessity of securing
uniform legislation in the matter of rejected candidates, and expresses his disap· ·
pointment at the conclusions of the committee. The report was as follows:-

1897.]

Grand Lo<lge of California.

95

We have given the foregoing communications (the resolutions of the Grand Lodge
of Maine) careful and fraternal consideration. We have also read the able report
of Bro. J. H. DRUMMOND, Chairman of the lJommitteeof .Jurisprudence of Maine,
with great pleasure and satisfaction. It is an able and forcible statement of
'Masonic law upon the question involved. We earnestly recommend the perusal of
the said report to every member of the Fraternity in this jurisdiction, as it contains
informat10h upon the Masonic law to be found nowhere else within the knowledge
of your committee. The Grand Lodge of California in 1883 (should be 1856), made
rejection a bar for one ye_ar only, after which the Lodge having territorial jurisdiction can receive him. We believ'e that this regulation is well adapted to our local
condition and has proved satisfactory; therefore we see no reason why it should be
changed.
Bro. DRUllllllOND says:We very greatly regret that the committee did not view the matter from a
higher Masonic standpoint than the one indicate<! in the concluding sentence.
There is a vast diversity in the law of the different jurisdictions, which has already
produced discord and threatens serious difficulty in the future. He appeals for the
consideration of the question for the good of American Masonry, yielding ail local
selfish preference for the harmony of the whole Fraternity.
He says, with much feeling :The danger of discord is imminent. To avert this attempts have been made to
secure uniformity of law, very gen.,ral if not uni versa!. Each jurisdiction is asked
to yield something. While Maine had found that perpetual jurisdiction was "well
adapted to our local position and had proved satisfactory,". she modified her law,
and is ready to modify it still further to secure uniformity. It is true she will not
go so far as to endanger Masonry by opening the doors too readily, but she has
gone a great way ; and is not California willing to sacrifice, if need be, something
for the good of the Institution at large, or must she decide the q_uestion according
to h~r own interests, without caring how it may affect other•? We hope our California brethren will reconsider thi~ matter and vidw from the standpoint of the
common good rather than from that of their particular interest.
We are impressed with the belief that the importance of this question has not
been recognized. We think an unselfish consideration of the matter by representative Masons-brethren willing to yield to the will of the majority for the harmony
of the whole-would virtually establish such action as would be well adapted to the
interests of the whole Fraternity.
Bro. DRUMMOND dissents from our views referring to the Grand Master of New
Jersey, and his "by the authority in me vested " way of making Masons at sight.
He says:We can remember when the Lodges possessed the power of makin~ Masons
"at sight," and that the law taking away the power was deemed an invasion of the
power~ of Lodges under the old UHages of the Craft.

And he adds :- .
It really was, but was made necessary by abuse of those powers.
We can't controvert the statement, Bro. DBUllllllOND; we only know that the
Lodges were not located in central New York, or it was more than fifty years ago.
Bro. DRUMMOND don't like our non-affiliate regulations, and illustrates witB. a
very pointed stick; but, I suppose, we will have· to stand it until he comes West
and sees how it is himself.

The Committee on Benevolence and Charity say in their report:.....,
Your committee have had under careful consideration the proposal of the Grand
Lodge of Wisconsin in regard to reciprocal Masonic charity. They cannot advise
this Grand Lodge to fall in with those suggestions, for the following reasons:
let. The proposal suggests that this Grand Lodge be drawn opon for absolute
necessaries, but there is no definition or what absolute necessaries might be under·
stood to mean ; oo this point there might be very considerable divergement of view
between the Lodge administering the charity and tbe Lodge paying for it.

99

2d. It seems an on wise and quite on businesslike proceeding for any public body
administering what are practically trust CondR to give what would amount to a blank
check to be filled op by another body over whose action it has no sort or control.
3d. Your committee feels that with the necessarily limited resources or a Grand
Lodge, numerically so small as oors, it would be specially unwise for ns to take any
action in this direction, or in any way to connect ourselves to a scheme whose
possibilities or expense are entirely unknown to us.

The one hundred and tenth Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge was
held in the city of Baltimore, November 17, i896. All the Grand Officers and many
Past Grand Officers, with the representatives of thirty-one sister jurisdictions, were
in attendance. All the constituent Lodges were represented.

The Grand Master being advised of the opening of Grand Lodge, his entrance
was proclaimed by the Grand Marshal. The Grand Honors were given, and he
assumed the authority tendered him by the B.·. W.·. Deputy Grand Master, and
proceeded to deliver his address. He first extended a cordial welcome to the
brethren in attendance upon the one hundred and tenth Annual Communication,
and congratulated all, as a result of their labors, on the present condition of the
Fraternity in Maryland. He said;I can truly say of the Craft in oar State that it is pressing onward and forward.
Harmony prevails, good fellowship abonnds, and the Order is prosperous beyond
precedent. Notwithstanding the depression in all mercantile pnrsnits in the past
year, Masonry in Maryland has increased in numbers and enthusiasm. Our Lodges,
with scarcely an exception, have had an abundance of work, and that work has
been well done. Not a single Lodge has fallen by the wayside, and we have added
two or three to our roster.

The following bit of experience of a Past .Master of Maryland, while visiting the
Holy Land, is interesting.
Bro. JAMES T. DBNNIB, Past Master of Manolcin Lodge, No. 106, related the
following experience of a trip to the Holy Land and his visit to the Lodge at
Jerusalem:J~rusalem, while full of interest in itself, has yet for Masons a significance beyond

and above what would attract the mere ple!lsnre seeker. There, close beside the
huge foondation·stones, left as they came from the hands of the craftsmen of Solomon and the two Hirams, within a short walk of the so-called " quarries of. Solomon,'' and not many miles from the scene of Jeptha's battle and victory over the
men of Ephraim, stands to-day the modern representative of that Order founded

101

Jong ago by Israel's King. A few minutes' walk beyond the "Jaffa gate " stands
one of the two-story buildings of modern erection, which grace the ontskirts of the
aged citr, and within its sheltering walls are held the meetings of "Mother Solomon
Lodge, No. l," the Temple of Modern Masonry in the country. It was my pleasani
fortune to visit this Lodge at one of its regular Communications, as a visiting member of the Grand Lodge of Maryland-a slight tribute of fraternity from the west
to the east-from the newest to the oldest Home of our great and noble Fraternity.
The Lodge-room, while comparatively small, is tastefully arranged and carefully
adorned with the emblems of the Craft, and as the Lodge is acting nuder the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Canada, there was a similarity in the work of oar
own, which would have made one feel at home, even without the most cordial and
kindly reception I met with, from the brethren and the Worshipful Master to the
youngest Entered Apprentice.
The membership is truly Masonic-English, Germans, Hessians, Syrians-all the
nations gathered togetber oat of the Syrian region, even including the swarthy
Bedouin of Arabia, find their brethren within these walls; and nowhere else on the
three Eastern continents did I receive any warmer or more fraternal greeting than
here. The work of the Lodge iR carried ori in English, which all present, very
probably, understand, while signs, grips and tokens are identical with onr own.
It gives me great pleasure to add, that "Mother Solomon Lodge, No. 1,'' requested me to be the bearer of their fraternal greetings to the Grand Lodge of .Mary·
land, and their assurance of the "universality of Masonry, and the action of the
Grand Lodge of Maryland in its proposed 1tction regarding the Lodge at Jernsalem
is doubly pleasing to me, as having been the vehicle of communication between the
two. May the kind brethren .f.Onder be long spared to this "house, not made with
hands," and may their advancement to the Grand Lo!!ge of the Supreme Grand
Master win for them as sincere, cordial and true a welcome as was e:x;tended by them
to myself.

Having full confidence io your skill in the Royal Art, it remains for me to finish
the work. The Grand Master then gives three knocks npon the stone, saying,

to the laws of oar country, professing to fear God, and to confer benefits on mankind. We practice universal beneficence towards all. We have secrets concealed
from the eyes of men which may not he revealed to any bnt Masons; they are, however, lawful and honorable. We are assembled iu the broad face of open day, under
the canopy of Heaven, to lay the corner-stone of this Temple of Jnstice. May God
prosper oar handiwork as shall most please him. May this Tem{lle bedtime a place
wherein just and upright Judges shall preside, and dispense Justice and equity
throughout this community.

DEAR SIB AND BROTHRB :-Yon may have bee.rd that while in England, IBBt
February, I met with a.n accident which nearly cost me my life , aucl on a.cconnt of
which I am still on crotches, with little prospect of being able to walk without
them. I sustained a compound comminnted fre.ctnre of the right leg and other very
serious external and internal injuries. I we.a first attended by llr. W. J. FLEBTWOOD,
of Aintree, Liverpool, England, a brother Mason of high standing. For six months
I le.Id fiat on my bacll, not being able to tnro on my side nor to sit np once daring
that time. I we.a constantly visited during that time by Bros. S. RENNIX, 44 Clarenoe
Grove, Everton, Liverpool, and P. ABM:BTBONG, Ma.sonic Hall , Hope street, Liverpool,
and to them, possibly, I owe my life. After I we.a pronounced fit to travel, my
Injured leg we.a placed in a rigid iron frame, and lncased in a plaster cast from hip
to toe. Appllcatioa was then made for passage to four dift'erent steamship lines,
but the surgeon of each line rejected me. Finally, Dr. FLEETWOOD offered to take
me In charge, and without any hope of remuneration, he left his enormous practice
and accumpa.nied me home. For this he would take no pa.y. A large number of
bro thers accompanied us on board the ship and bade as God speed. The ship's
company charged me an extra rate for invalid passage, and this extra charge was
paid by the MaRonic Lodge of which Bro. ABM:STBONG Is W. •. M.·. Naturally enough,
I reel very grateful to these brothers. and more than ever in love with our noble
Order, and it is my wish that a vote of thanks be given by our Lodge and sent under
seal of the Lodge to these brothers. Will you kindly bring the matter before the
Lodge at the next regular, and inform me of the action taken. Wishing to be
remembered to all my brothers, I remain, truly, fraternally yours,

A. T. STA.JU:.

Your Special Committee, to whom was referred so much of the M.·. W.·. Grand
Master's address as relates to the Masonic Home, respectfully report,That the address of the M.-. W.-. Grand Master so folly sets forth the proposition for the transfer of the Masonic Home to the Masone o( Michigan that your
committee bep:s to refer to it for the information necessary for the intelligent consider.tion of the proposition.
Your committee takes occasion to add only, that the other Masonic Grand Bodies
have accepted the offer, subject to the favorable action of Grand Lodge.
The Masonic Home Association offers to the Masons this property, worth nearly
one hundred thousand dollars, unconditionally, and without a shadow of restriouon.
Grand Lodge is to assume no pecuniary obligation, only to join io the manage·
ment of the Home and to become an almoner of the charity of the fraternity.
In the opinion of that committee, Grand Lodge can do no less than to accept this
magnificent gift, and execute the trust in the same generous and Masonic spirit that
animates the donor.
Your committee, therefore, recommend that Grand Lodge. In connection with the
other Masonic Grand Bodies, on behalf of all the Masons of the State, accept said
property as recommended by the M.-. w.-. Grand Master, it being understood that
Grand Lodge, by this action, assumes no pecuniary obligation in behalf of the Home,
but confidently relies upon the voluntary contributions of the Craft for its support
and management.
·
It is farther recommended that the
W. •• Gra.nd Master appoint one Trustee,
to hold the title of said property in trust, in conneolion with like representatives of
of the other Grand Bodies, aod three members of the Board of Control to hold ofllce
for ooe, two aod three years respectively.
·

ooe represeotiog each of the Grand Bodies of Grand Lodge, Chapter, Council aod
Oommaodery.
The Board of Oootrol consists of fifteen, three chosen by each of the above·
named bodies aod three by the Gaod Obapter of the Eastern Star.
God bless the Michigan Home.

have felt in no small degree the universal depression of the business of the State,

Question 7. Is one who travels for a wholesale grocery house, and who in addition to soliciting orders for groceries also solicits orders for wines and liquors, eligible
for initiation!

M.·. W:·. Bro. PAXTON reviews tne subject, and concludes that whatever doubt
formerly existed was cleared op by the legislation of 1896, when the construction of
the rule was adopted .by Grand Lodge absolutely prohibiting wholesale and ret.ail

I stand as squarely as my a:1Bociates against the admission or retention of those
who peddle out bell by the glass, which, in my judgment, is what is meant by selling
intoxicating liquor as a beverage. There Is no telling the use the liquor sold by this
aJ>plicant is to be put to; it may be to core a mule of the colic, to preserve peaches,
or in the communion In a church. The regulations were not Intended to cover all
uses to which the liquor might be put, bot was limited to the Ringle condition thRt it
was to be used as a beverage, and limited to this. The regulation and rule met with
my hearty approbation, and cannot be too stringently enforced; but I am impressed
with the thought that there is such a thing as carrying a reform too far , and tbat It
is now but one single step from the Lodge to the Total Abstinence Society's ball; to
cross the line bnt one more deciRlon is necessary. If some one has not the percep1ion to see the direction in which we are rnshing, and the co11rage to cry out a warning, that step will be taken. Thinking that I see it, I reluctantly raise my voice, and,
without abating one jot or tittle from the position I have held for many years, that
the business of making men drink is not compatible with Freemasonry, I think we
have gone just as far as it is safe to go, unless we are bent upon making Masonry
somethinir else than what it bas been from the beginning, a temperance society, bot
not a total abstinence club. I believe that, consistently with the written law of tliis
Grand Lodge, though, perhaps, not with the sentimental, this candidate is eligible.

MONTANA..
A Special Communication of the Grand Lodge of Montana was held in Dillon,
April 9, 1896, for the purpose of placing the corner-stone of the State Normal
School Building.
Grand Lodge was opened in Due Form, the R. •• W. ·. E. P. DUNGAN acting as
Grand Master, R. ·. W. ·• T. M. O'CONNOR as Grand Secretary.
The Grand Master stated the purpose of the Communication. A procession
was formed, and, in charge of the Grand Marshal, proceeded to tbe site of tbe
intended building, where, after an eloquent prayer by the Grand Chaplain, the
corner-stone was laid in accordance with the ancient ceremonies of tbe Craft.
A large number of citizens, with the children of the public schools and their
teachers, were in attendance.
Grand Lodge returned to the Temple and closed.

~e also, as Chairman of Correspondence, submitted the following special
report, which was adopted :The auestion of the recognition of the Gran Dieta Simbolica of Mexico has
for some time been pendin!f before the Grand Lodges of this country. So far as
we have heard at this writmg, only the Grand Lodges of Texas, New York and
Kansa.s have voted recognition. Many more have investigated the case, and have
stated their objections. We have carefully read all the reasons urged both for
and against recognition, and have become satisfied that all substantial objections
have been removed; that the body which asks recognition confine• its jurisdiction
to the three symbolic degrees, but over these is supreme, acting through Grand
Lodges in eech separate State. These State Grand Lodges have existed for many
yea.re, and several of them formerly secured recognition from some of our Grand
Lodges. It simplifies matters greatly to deal with one general body like the Gran
Dieta rather than with so many Reparate States.
We submit for your adoption the following:.--

From the Grand Master's report of his official acts the jurisdiction would
seem to be fairly prosperous. He had visited a majority of the Lodgea, which, for
a oonstituency as widely scattered as the territory of New Mexico, speaks loud in
praise of his exertions to discharge fully the responsibilities assumed at his installation. He reports no decisions, as he says the many questions asked were confined
to the construction of existing rules and regulations. There is, howe•er, abundant
evidence in the address of the Grand Master's dissati•faction with the "moral
tone" of the Craft in the jurisdiction. He says :Our annual gatherings have heretofore been content with meeting euch caaual
matters as have come up from time to time, together with the personal enjoyment
of the attending members of Grand Lodge. Let us from now on become what we
really shoul? be-;-the la.w-making and law pr~rvi.ng center of the jurisdiction.
Let us begm this session. Let us not contmue m our old course and give our
Lodges the opportunity to feel that the Grand Lodge is aside and by itself. Let
us, on ~e 0th.er hand, show that .we owe a .duty to thoae Lodges; that we are interested In their welfare; that thell' depreBBJOn should be the object of our sohcitude, and have them feel as they should feel-that the entire Fraternity is with
them praising their successes and regretting their reverses.
In ·con~lueion, it is. clearly my duty. to call the. attention .of this Grand Lodge
to the rapid an.d extensive growth of a disease that 1s threatemng the very existence
of the Fratermty-that is, the frequency with which the Masonic obligations to
protect the reputation, person and well being of a brother Mason are constantly
disregarded in this jurisdiction.
I will not attempt to indulge in high flown generalities, but will endeavor to
speak of the subject in straightforward words of soberness and truth.
" If our ~olemn obliga.tion.s, entered into at the altar of Freemas?nry, ~re merely
as eoundmg brass or tmklmg cymbals," we had better cease administenng_ them
for it seems from what we read in the public press that in New Mexioo the Masoni~
obligations are "more honored in the breach than in the observance."

Brethren, at our last Annual Meetinl' I addreeeed a few words to you upon the
state of the Craft. I tohi you then that we commenced the year 1894 and 1895
with a membership of 8112, that we had initiated 700 members during the year,
and that 140 brethren had joined our various Lod~s. Owing, however, to the
absence of the necessary returns, I was unable to show what our l8sses had been.
When those returns came in, they disclosed the fact that our losses had been
greater, so far as mere numbers were concerned, than our gains. While by initiations and affiliations we had gained 840 members, we had lost .from :roll sources
1254, leaving a net loss of 414. The year 1895-96, which closes to-mght, commenced therefore with a membership of 7698. During the year we have initiated
about 685 brethren, and admitted by affiliation about 100, making a total membership during the year of about 8428, from which our losses by death, resignation and
other causes will, when they are ascertained, have to be deducted to show our present state of membership.

We note also by the Superintendent's report tha~ this asylum is a beneficiary of
Mr. JAMES A. BRADLEY, who died in Oakland, in December, 1894-, and who; while in
his last sickness, deeded certain lots owned by him in t~e city of Minneapolis to the
• Oxford Orphan Asylum, Davidson College and Union Theological Seminary at
Hampton, Sidney, Virginia, two lots to each beneficiary. The conveyance to the
Oxford Asylum was mailed December 5th, arrived at its destination, Oxford, North
Carolina, in doe time, and was carelessly permitted to remain in the postoffice unde·
livered several days. As soon as received and examined it was at once seen thl\t
the deed was defective, as the asylum was not an incorporated institution, and it
was returned to have Grand Lodge of' North Carolina F. and A. M. inserted in lien
of Oxford Asylum, as Mr. BBADLBY's instructions were to make the conveyance in
such shape as would best carry out his purposes. Mr. RICHABDBON, Bradley's agent,
acting under these instructions, erased the name of Oxford Orphan Asylum and in·
serted Grand Lodge of North Carolina F. and A, M. This was after December 19th,
and as evAnts proved, snbseqoent to the death of Mr. BBADLEY.
These facts led to a contest by the heirs, and a final compromise by which the
Oxford Orphan Asylum receives a portion of the property described, from which it
receives an annnal rental of about six hundred dollars. It is not often that the
purpose of a person is defeated by such a succession of blunders.

as vou are doubtless aware, a believer in the Christian reiiipon, but I am com•
palled, for the reasons above given, to decline granting a dispensation to your

By Nelson Williams.

For forty long successive years,
Upon our Grand Lodge roll,
Your name has had an honored place,
And honored well the scroll.
For forty l_ears, almost tbe length
Of Life s uncertain span,
No name ha.a been more honored
Than the ~me of Cunningham.
'Twas in the balmy spring of life
When you first entered here,
When formed those friendships which have grown
In strength from year to year ;
And as the tender sapling grows
Into the mighty tree,
So God has let thy years increase,
And added strength to thee.
You labored faithfully and well
At morning, noon, and ·night ;
Your hand was ever at the wheel,
To guide our Craft aright ;
When storms arose and mutinv
Was seen on every hand,
You proved your loyal Masonry
To all our Mystic band.
You climbed the ladder step by step,
And reached the topmost round ;
Since then your labors win for you
A lasting true renown.
You knew that one lllllSt ever toil
If he wish to succeed ;
You did as Masons e'er should do
And reaped our golden meed.
Your whitened hairs the story tell
Of Life's advancing years;
The sun is sinking toward the west,
The evening light appears ;
A little while and you must go
To that Grand Lodl{e above,
Whose Tvler, Death, stands sentry at
The gofden gates of love.
.
When this unwelcome hour shall come,
And you are laid to rest,
No need for thee a stately shaft,
From costly granite dressed.
The service you have rendered here,
The good will you have shown,
Will be for thee a monument
More la.sting than of stone.
