Before closing his Address under the head of "Miscellaneous " the Grand
Master completes the record of a Ma.sonic impostor who forced himself upon the
attention of the Fraternity in California. We quote it for the benefit of the Craft
and in vindication of the action of our Grand Chapter:On January 13, 1896, Goodale Lodge, No. 372, F. and A. M., of Columbus,
completed the struggle of several years' dur1Ltion to purify their Lodge membership and rid the Order of defiant Masonic offenders, by the expulsion of JAMES C. ·
KBOESEN, CLINTON D. FBIEBTONE, WILLIAM A. HERBHISEB, RoBEBT W. LINEN,
IBA40 B. POTTS, CHABLES H. SIMMEB and IsAAO C. A!>HTON, all of Columbus.
Later in the vear, MOSES P. SMITH and .JOSEPH H. OUTHWAITE were expelled
by the same Lodj!e. This was the culmination of the litigation alluded to in another part of this Address, in which the final decision of the court was, that a
:Masonic Lodge " is a society, not for profit but for Masonic purposes, and that it
has power to expel one or more of its members for unmasonic conduct and to determine wherein unmasonic conduct consists, and that this court has no jurisdiction
to Festrain the Lodge from proceeding to expel a member or members for an
alleged irregularity by the Lodge, or its proper officers in the exercise of its
powers of expulsion."
The other case was the expulsion from all the rights and benefits of the Order
of GRANVILLE A. FBAMBES, formerly of Columbus, by Lafayette Lodge, No. 81,
F. and A. M., of Cincinnati. The charge was gross unma.sonic conduct, in at·
tempting to organize, within the State of Ohio, bodies of men into Masonic Lodges,
so-called, without authority so to do from the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of Ohio. This fellow cam·e within the penal jurisdiction of Lafayette
Lodge, to practice his scheme upon the unwary, and was promptly handled.
FBAMBKS is a notorious peddler of clandestine degrees, and has been expelled from
Lodge, Chapter, Commandery and Scottish Rite in·turn.
He was for a time affiliated with Wigton Lodge, in Hart, Michigan, but took a
dim it in ]'ebruary last. He claimed to be a regular Mason and, as such, was taken
in by Lafayette Lodge, and stamped "Counterfeit." FBAMBES ha.a visited Newark, Coshocton, Cincinnati, Columbus and other points, trying to make spurious
Masons, and the Lodges in Ohio are warned to be on the lookout for him and warn
the credulous against his irregular and clandestine work.
The Report on Correspondence is a veritable book, a volumne of 350 pages,
wherein our M. '. W. ". Bro. PBl!t Grand M~ter CUNNINGHAM reviews the doing&
of seventy-three Masonic Legislatures, including eleven non-English speakin!i'
Grand Lodges.
His review of Mexican Masonry, now so prominently before the Masonic public by the recognition of La Gran DUta by the Grand Lodge of Texas, New York
and Kansas, is a valuable paper, containing a compilation of the most important
information bearing upon the legitimacy and worthiness of Masonry in our
neighboring republic. Its preparation by Bro. CUNNINGHAM is timely and will be
effective in cleaning up many of the unfounded fears of doubting brethren, while
turning the light of truth upon a subject of vital importance to the Masons of the
next generation and most welcome to the believers in the great moral influence of
the principles of Freemasonry upon the rise and progress of the nations of the
earth.

The reports of the Grand Lodge officers speak in no uncertain tone of the
prosperity that generallv prevails, and of the harmony and good feeling that exists
among the brethren. It is pleasant to note the testimony of Grand Lodge officers
to the honor and obedience paid to them in their official capacity, and to the warm .
welcome and hospitality extended to them on a.II occasions when brought into intercourse with the Lodges. With rare exceptions, they are able to compliment
the Lodges in possessing competent officers, conducting the work in an impressive
manner, and keeping books and records in a business-like way.

In the days of the seignioria.l tenure of lands in the province of Quebec, the
Seignior, or lord of the manor, po88essed a number of very remarkable rights, llimilar to those exercised a century ago iu France. These included the Devil de gambage or Preltibation, and to borrow an expression of my literary friend, Sir James ·
M . Le Moine, "as I do not care to be too explicit in deecribiilg it, " it will suffice
to say that it bad for its object, as many pretended, to confer on the Lord of the
Manor the same rights which some royal Lotharios iq France claimed in those
marriage contracts, mi l£ Roi a trigne." That this right-high prerogative if you
prefer-which might have suited old King Solomon, appears in charters and
grants, there can be no doubt. There is no record that the right was ever exercised here .in Canada, but it is related that jealousy for the maintenance of the
Prerogative led some Canadian seigniors, in years gone by, to enter the bridal
chamber and touch the nuptial couch with the seigniorial knee. What sticklers
they would have made a11 Masone for the prerogatives of Grand Masters!

We shall hereafter always a88ociate the Grand Master's prerogative of makin11;
a Mason at sight, with Bro. E. T. D. CHAMBERS and his little story.

tlosb. We see no inconsistency in giving the remains of a brother, after cremation, a

The report of Grand Secretary REED is such a paper as one might expect from
a Mason of hi• ripe experience. He had evidently had much trouble and vexation
of spirit in his efforts to enlighten the Lodges as to the correct procedure under the
law touching delinqllent members, and in the present report he tells them that the.
intent and object of the existing law is not only to lighten the burden upon
Lodges who have been paying annually to Grand Lodge for members who have
contributed nothing for their support, but to restore to the Fraternity that just
and equitable theory in Masonic government, inalienable in the right of every
Freemason, that all may know and understand th!lt Lodge privileges and Masonic
privileges, per 11e, are separate and distinct ; that failure to contribute to the means
necessary to claim enjoyment of the former, does not necessarily exclude him from
the privileges of the latter, so long as the latter ar11 not abused through those channels pointed out by the landmarks of the Fraternity.

That the Craft in California may be fully advised as to the much abused Wisconsin proposition, a.s weli as for its vigorous style and earnestness, we excerpt it
here:W e re-state the proposition :
It is the duty of each J;odge to take care of its own members in dilltress, wherewr they
be: In CIJ:Be of its inability BO to do, this duty devolves upon the Grand Lodge from
which it holds its chmrter. It being understood that in no case iB the Lodge furnishing
1·elief and asking reimbursement, to go be11ond actual necesBitieB, tDithout ezpress
author·l ty from the reimbursing Body.
Now, as to the meaning of this prop0sition:
We do not propose to relieve any Mason from his duty of charity, which is
broader than merely giving relief.
\Ve do not propose to relieve any brother from his duty of individual relief.
We do not propose any innovation, or new departure in Masonry.
We do propose to relieve our Frnternity from .confusion worse confounded, by
subetituting method for entire lack of method.
.
We do propose that a worthy brother in distress shall have relief, when absolutely necessary to him, and which he is not at all sure of, under present lack of
method.
~t. is !ll~inly because we recognize the fact that many subordinate Lodges, and
their mdividual members as well, are unable either to relieve their own members,
or to care for the •tranger within their gates. that our proposition becomes necessary, and because of that fact we made it. All Grand Lodges should have, and
?early all ~o have, ~elief funds. And our propositi?n simply asks Grand Lodges,
ID case their 1mbo~.Jmates are ah!e but unwilling, as is freqoently the case, to see
that the;!' do their duty, and ID case they are unable, to come to their relief, as
Wisconsm has always done. The effect of this would be to remove all controversies on this subject between Lodges.

It is very seldom that a member of a Wisconsin Lodll'e is relieved abroad without the bill being promptly sent to bis home Lodge. It is very frequently the case
that the distressed br0ther cannot get relief unless his home Lodge first guarantees
the expense. This in itself shows that there is a prevalent idea that it is the duty
of the Lodge to look after its own members.
Let us look at this duty of individual relief for which ·our eminent brethren
contend. The writer of this circular claims to have done his full share in this
line, but he does not knO'IJJ that he has ever given one dollar to a wrn-thv applicant
for relief. He does know that in every case where he has had a subsequent chance
for investigation he has found that he has been imposed upon. In cities of the
aize of Milwaukee no day passes without appj!als for assistance. '.l'he writer has
aometimes had three or four in one day. Under such circumstances what is my
duty? To give without investiiration? That encoura1res fraud, and does not rtllieve the worthy. To investi1rate? That takes more time than a busy man has at
his disposal. To turn away the applicant with a refusal? I may h1we rejected a
worthy brother in his distrePs. 'l'he only other recourse is to sivid the applicant to
a committee, whose dutv it is to investigate such cases. This seems to us to
effectually dispose of the "individual relief" theory. It applied in early days
when the country was sparsely settled. It applies now when the applicant and
bis circumstances are known; but for the relief of ·the transient., unknown brother,
it is utterly inefficient and impracticable. And it is to these transient distressed
brethren that our proposition is intended to apply.
.
There is another feature of the objection to our proposition. In our tiret
circular we called attention to existing evils, and suggested it as a remedy. nut
we expressly stati;d that it was our suggestion of 11 remedy, and, in making it, we
asked for sugge•tions from others. But those who have opposed it have devoted
themselves entirely to attacking our proposition, and have not given one word or
thought to the consideration of the evils they must admit to exist. We are notso
infatuated with the proposition that we can •ee no room for improvement, and we
ask, as we a.eked in our first circular, those who oppose it to su1tgest something
better.

We cannot conceive how so distinguished a brother can gravely cast such an aspersion upon the Masonic Fraternity. No man in active business but has, at·
times, to trust those with whom he deals to as great an extent, and certainly our
own brethren are to be trusted to that extent, or we had better disband. In all
legislation, civil or Masonic, the principle is recognized that laws may be adopted
containing certain provisions subject to restrictions.
We have put the question plainly. What is to be done with cases, constantly
occurring, where a sick or destitute brother is stranded in the jurisdiction of a
weak Lodge unable to ·Care for him? We have never been able to obtain but one
answer. Bro. DrU1Dmond, when asked point blank, says that when we have done
what we can, there is the end. In other words the brother must go to the poor
house. We have a hopeleRS'iy sick brother from Iowa, with a family, whom we·
have been supporting several years. We should drop him and let the town take
care of him. We are now supportin!f the widowed dau!fhter oi a former Grand
High Priest of Ohio. Shall we send her to the poor house?
We again ask you to consider this question in all its bearings, with full confidence that you will see the necessity, if not of our proposition, of some relief
from existing confusion. ·
In closing, Bro. SwAIN says: "We are pieased to report that our proposition
is ll!'ining ground, though slowly, &c., &c., &c.
On motion of Bro. W. c. SWAIN, Grand Lodge re-affirmed its condemnation of
the unmasonic practice of soliciting profanes, or even hin~inlt' to such person that
his membership in the Fraternity was desirable.
As per order of business, Past Grand Master W. W. l'EBBY was called to the
East and presented with the jewel of a Past Grand Master, as evidence of the appreciation of the service rend9red by him to the Grand Lodge of Wisconsin.
In considering the disbursement of its charities, Grand Lod!fe remembered the
widow of its first Grand Master, now a resident in Texas, among its beneficiaries.
It also voted $100 in aid of the Childrens' Home Society of Wisconsin.

To Bro. NORTH and his fourteen companions, in their answer to the summons, the

Grand Secretary KUYKENDALL presents the Report on Correspondence, giving a
review of a.ii the Grand Lodges that had come to hand. He notes the doings of
Grand Lodge under the direction of Grand Master STEVENS. He seems satisfied
with the Grand Master's Address, and notes nothing in the legislation to criticise,
but in his friendly reference to this writer he incidentally condemns the representative system as useless. iie disapproves of the system because it encroaches upon
the prerogatives and duties of the Grand Master. They hold beautiful commissions
and are rec•lived with Urand Honors, to which they are not entitled, etc.
Now, Bro. K., you have portrayed a representative that you consider of no possible
use. To illustrate the other side of the question: Suppose the Grand Lodge· of
Wyoming, in its wisdom, had named this writer as its representative near the Grand
Lodge of Oalifomia, and, as in duty bound, he should present himself at the ensuing
session of Grand Lodge and present the compliments and fraternal regal'ds of the
Grand Lodge of Wyoming to their brethren of California ; subsequently and at the
close of the session he ·(in short form) gives the important business of the session,
with the officers chosen for the ensuing year, in a concise report to the Grand Lodge
of Wyoming. Are the Grand Master's duties interfered with? Are they not positively benefited by the information received weeks in advance of publication in the
regular journal?
We think, Bro. KUYKENDALL, your objection to the system is shad,ed by brethren
commissioned as representatives who never representod anything except a neglect
of duties assumed and never performed. We do not care for tbe system because of
its geµeral neglect, bot we hold in remembrance during our nearly half century of
Masonic experience many useful and kindly acts recorded to the credit of the much
abused representative, who, appreciating the honor conferred by the appointment,
manifested an honest pride in performing its duties. A representative of a Grand
Lodge should be of direct aid and assistance to the Grand' Master of the Grand
Lodge to whose service his all&giance is doe.

CONCLUSION.
In closing the report of the past year we have no startlin!f events to chronicle;
indeed, we seem to have been but repeating the history of preceding yearsseasons of successful progress clouded by the loss of friends and brethren upon
whom we had become so accustomed to lean for guidance as to cause us to wonder
how and witb whom it were possible to fill the vacant places ; but with these
thoughts again comes the consoling knowledge tbat though the workman falls,
having fulfilled his purpose and passed to rest, yet the work goes on. Our brethren
die and are buried, bot the Grand Lodge lives, and will pass Into the future as a
great factor in the moral and social improvement of mankind.
Wbile writing tbis conclusion our attention has been claimed by tbe receipt of a
Masonic directory from tbe Master of Phwnfz Lodge, No. 178, with a name underscored which calls into action all our reverence for an elder brother, a veteran,
having a Masonic life of nearly three score and ten years.

Having dropped our sprig of acacia in memory of these four illustrious Masons,
we considered our work ended, but a book received from Comp. Hon. ~'REDERIO
SPEED, of Mississippi, " a reprint of tbe proceedings of the Grand Council of Royal
aod Select Masters of Mississippi for the years 1856-66, impresses us with a neglected
duty.
For twenty years there resided with us in California a remarkable man and an
eminent Mason. He came in 1850 and remained until his death, save a visit to his
mother in 1856. Bro. P11BEz SNELL had been a leader in Masonry, and was identified
with the Supreme Council of.the Southern Jurisdiction at Charleston, South Carolina.
He was commissioned a Deputy of the Conocil under date of Febrnary 10, 1829,
having, io addition to his genei-al dnties as Inspector-General, the authority to confer
the degrees of Royal and Select Master or" Select Masons of Twenty-seven" and to
establish bodies of the same. Through some conflict of jurisdiction Bro. SNELL was
expelled by a rebellions 13cottish Rite faction in Louisiana, and for that reason
excluded himself from Masonic association in California. As soon, however, as the
Scottish Rite was organized here his position became known, and his Masouichistory set right by Bro• .ALBERT PIKE, then Grand Commander. Meanwhile Bro.
SNELL had passed to rest, but before his death he snmmoued a prominent Mason, a
friend aod neighbor. Bro. FRBDEBIO FAXON, and communicated to him the degrees
of the Scottish Rite to aod including the thirty-second degree, aod placed io his
keeping his books aod papers. Subsequently Bro. FAXON was affiliated with the
Grand Consistory here aod gave to me the papers mentioned. They were delivered
to the then Grand Recorder of tbe Grand Council for deposit in the archives of the
A&me, but for some reason disappeared. To our satisfaction tbey are again brought
to light in this reprint of the Mississippi proceedings.

A good old man has gone. On Monday last Doctor P.11a.11z SNELL was borne to
bis .le.st resting place in the Me.sonic bnrie.I gronnd. Few men have ever lived
among ns more universally respected and esteemed than Doctor Snell. He was horn
in the Sta\e of Vermont on the 19th day of September, 1783 ;· fonght at Lnndy's
Lane under General Scott; was for a number of years in the .Medical College at·
New Orleans; had traveled extensively in his own and in foreign countries. and was
a man of great learning and scientific attainments. Be came to California in 1850,
and resided in Sonora from that time until hi& death, except for a few months in 1856,
when ho returned to visit his aged mother in his native State. During the tlme he
resided in Sonora he devoted his time chiefly to scientific pursnits, and collected a
large and valuable cabinet .of curiosities and geological specimens. He did not
entirely neglect the practice of his profession, though he did not seek or desire to
engage in it. Many a poor sufferer bas found relief from his charitable baud. He
was ever ready by night or day to minister to the affiicted. He was first and foremost in evePy public work and duty, and though in his eighty-seventh year he took
a zee.lons interest in everything for the public good. His step was as firm and
elastic as that of' a man in middle life. Be was the friend of the children and
delighted to add to their pleasures and enjoyments. As a geologist and man of
science he had few eqne.ls and no superior in the State. He believed in the great
•I am' and loved to medite.te on his.works; beyond that he songht not to penetrate
the mystery.
"Be was probe.bly the oldest Me.son in the United States, having been sixty-five
years a. Mason, and was Inspector-General of the Supreme Council of the Ancient
and Accepted Scottish Rite for the Southern Jnrisdiction of the United States of
America. Be lived and died an honest man, the noblest work of God."

The apparent excess of moneys refunded from California Lodges over the
amount spent for California Lodges, was caused by the refunding of_ moneys
expended during last year.
·
The amount i:eported above as expended for widows of California brethren·
($145 45) was all expended for the relief of the widow of M. PHELPS, formerly of Hiram Lodge, No. 43.
She will undoubtedly continue to be a charge upon this Board for at least
an equal amount during the ensuing year.
This Board has already called the attention of the Grand Master to this
case, and would suggest that the Grand Lodge take some action in regard to
it, as Hiram Lodge is reported to be unable to reimburse this Board.
There is still due to this Board the sum of one hundred and twenty
($120 00) dollars. expended for the care of Bro. DINGMAN, of Edgar Lodge,
No. 67, of the jurisdiction of Nebraska.
The amount was properly expended, but Edgar Lodge has persistently refuaed to repay the same.
This Board in March last requested the Grand Master to assist us in the
matter, but so far as we are advised nothing has been done.
A few weeks ago we placed the matter in the hands of Bro. Past Grand
Master WILLIAM A. DAVIES, the representative of the Nebraska Grand Lodge.
As appears from the above report, we have extended assistance to four
persons, after'wards proved to be unworthy.
In each of these cases the applicant was carefully examined and found to
be well posted in the work.
The cases have all been reported to the Secretary of the General Masonic
Relief Association of New York, and reported in their circular.
We are glad to be able to say that more impostors have been unsuccessful
than successful in their applications to the Board.
Dema:nds upon the Board have increased slightly over those of last year,
and will probably be larger for the year ensuing than during the present
year.
All which is respectfully submitted.
JAMES HALSTEAD LINDSLY, President.
FRANK HARTFORD SMITH, Secretary.

Dea.th is ae inevitable as the dawn of morning, or the shadows that thicken
as the sun sinks behind the western horizon ; yet, it too often comes suddenly
and un~xpectedly, and brings a throb of sorrow and anguish.
Life is the commingling of sunshine and shadow; a.nd the shadow deepens
into gloom for the moment, when .those whom we love and revere are laid to
rest forever from our eight. When a good man dies, the people put on the
habiliments of mourning, and recount the value bf character in the example
he has left to mankind. It is not possible to fully estimate the inftuence for
good of NATHANIBL GREENE CURTIS. It reaches out in countless avenues that
will go on multiplying as civilization advances to a better state of perfection.
It is a goodly thing to honor the memory of one whose life was de\•oted to the
elevation and amelioration of humanity, and in this respect our brother will
not be forgotten. The evidence of hie unflagging zeal and devotion to the
Order he eo dearly loved, are to be found in almost every volume of the
printed proceedings, since the formation of the Grand Lodge of Freemasonry
in California, over forty-seven years ago. He early took first rank in the
councils of Masonry, and maintained it to hie death. He grew old in the
service of the Grand Lodge ; and seldom has hie seat been vacant at Annual
or Special Communication. For four consecutive yea.rs he presided over the
Grand Lodge as its honored and well beloved Grand Master ; and during hie

members to vote as a unit on some question, when a ten minutes' talk from
him would carry the Grand Lodge with a perfect stampede in the opposite
· direction.
His f!MJulty for repartee was truly remarkable. No amount of interruption
ever disconcerted him, and his replies were sharp and instantaneous. His
sallies of wit and sarcasm, when fully aroused, were as decisive and witheringas the vollies from a gattling gun at short range. The man who dared to
measure words with ·him in controversial discussion would find cause to remember it afterwards. But the sympathetic element in his nature was one
of his strongest characteristics. Those of you who were present at the Annual
Communication in 1879, will remember the pathetic scene, when he presented
to the Grand Lodge the homeless orphan boy from the yellow fever stricken
district of New Orleans, the only survivor of his family; and how earnestly he
appealed to the Grand Lodge to become a mother to that poor child of misfortune. It was a subject just suited to the warmth of his noble nature ; and
before he had talked five minutes his pathos had brought the tears of sympathy to the cheeks of a hundred stalwart men.
An incident that occurred while he was a member of the legislature of this
State is in evidence of his nobility of ch&racter. He had been warmly advocating a proposition which he believed to be .right, but which was looked upon
in the light of a party measure. A young member of the opposing party went
to him and said : " I recognize the strength of your position and the force
of your argiim.ent ; and, out of regard for my warm friendship and personal
appreciation of you, I will vote for your measure." He promptly replied:
" I cannot allow you to do so. You are a young man with promising political
prospects ahead of you. To vote with me will place you in an awkw&rd attitude before your party, will cripple your influence, and may militate against
your future preferment, and as much as I desire to see the measure prevail, I
cannot consent for you to take this personal risk." In politics, as in everything else, a high standard was the guide of his life. He attributed to every
man the right of an honest opinion, though it might differ essentially from
his own. Sordid selfishness was foreign to his being. His was a superior
nature-grand in its capabilities-the embodiment of those graces and virtues
which cryst.a.lize human sympathy and sweeten existence. A close survey of·
his maturer life reveals the evenness of his well rounded character. Ask his
neighbors, those who were in daily close communion with him, how well he
bore the crucial test of intimate acquaintanceship, and they will tell you of
the delights of companionship with him, th~ sacredness of association that
broadened and deepened as the.years passed by. He had a remarkable personality. No matter where you fonnd him, whether in the social circle, the
Lodge-room, pleading at the bar, or in the halls of legislation, he towered
above the ordinary mlm like the stately pine above the dwarfed oak. In carriage he was erect, with a proud, dignified air, which at times had .the semblance of haughtiness, and which won for him the sobriquet of the Chesterfield
of the Grand Lodge. In conversation on business matters, his replies were
frank and blunt, 11-nd at times seemingly rude; but it was simply his earnest-

Bro. CURTIS was born in North Carolina, February 8, 1826. He died at
his home in Sacramento the twelfth day of .July, 1897. On the fifteenth, we
laid him to rest under a bed of flowers in the capital of the commonwealth,
-which had been his home for well nigh half a century. The day was far spent,
A!ld it seemed an appropriate hour for the solemn ceremonial over one who had
p11.ssed the noon time and was seeking repose in the evening of life. Ah, how
poignant the sorrow, as we face the stern fact to-day, that we shall never
more enjoy his companionship; nevermore listen to his warm pathetic eloquence; nevermore receive from his lips wise council and wholesome advice.
When the ideal Grand Master, LEONIDAS E. PRATT, lay enshrouded for
the tomb in this hall, Bro. CURTIS was chosen to pronounce the tribuM to his
memory. From that eloquent and touching eulogy, we extract the following
as a most appropriate and expreBSive tribute to the memory of this grand old
patriarch in Freemasonry : "In every walk of life he grandly and nobly
e.xemplified the sublime teachings of our Order by administering comfort and
consolation to the sorrowing, lifting up the downfallen and inspiring all with
hope and confidence. The poor, the friendless, the orphan, the widow may
indeed weep, for they have lost a friend. Their tears will be a nobler offering
to his memory than the most eloquent words of enlogy. The good that he
has done is not, cannot be, buried with him. It remains as a halo around his
name to make him remembered as long as charity exists, not a mere abstract,
but a living, glorious reality."
Resolved, That we profoundly sympathize with his bereaved widow, and
we suggest that a copy of these resolutions be forwarded to her.

CLAY WEBSTER TAYLOR was born at Howell, in the State of Michigan, on
·the 10th of September, 1844, and when a young boy migrated with hi~ parents
from Michigan to Shasta county, California. His father having died when
our brother was in his extreme youth, his education was left to the care of his
mother, who, with her small financial means, could only give him such education as could be obtained in the local schools of Shasta county and a short term
in Oakland, California. After a short experience at clerking and mining, he
adopted the profession of the law, and when he had sufficien' age and learning
he embarked in the practice of·his chosen profession at the town of Shasta.
Bro. TAYLOR was possessAd of great physical power, was a natural orator,
and an ever zealous devotee to his friends and to· any cause which he believed
to be just and honorable, and he was ever ready, with unceasing effort and
industry, to advance and accomplish what he believed to be right; his effort

Past Grand Master CoNKLIN was born in Pennsylvania in 1835. He graduated from Wyoming Univet"Rity in that State. For a time he edited a newspaper, then studied law and emigrated to the State of Missouri to commence
the practice. In 1861 he enlisted in the Fourth Missouri Volunteers, fought
with the Union Army until the end of the war, and was promoted from time
to time, until, when mustered out of the service, he was Judge Advocate on
General Brawn's Staff. After the close of the war Bro. CONKLIN resumetl the
practice of the law. He was elected Probate Judge of oue of the counties of
the State of Missouri, served out hie term of office," and came to California in
1875. Here he settled in Inyo County, practiced law with Patrick Reddy as
a partner. He afterwards removed to Kem County and served as SuperioiJudge of that county from 1891 to 1897. In 1882 he was a candidate foiLieutenant-Governor of this State, and, after a gallant fight, went down with
the rest of his ticket. In 1890 he was made Grand Master of the .Masonic
Order in this jurisdiction, which position he filled with great credit.
He possessed in. an eminent degree characteristics peculiar to noble natures. He was inspired with a remarkable courage of his convictions, and yet
he was as gentle as a child. He was rarely angry at others, and men seldom
had just cause to be angry at him. He was dignified in his deportment, just
and fair in his criticism, wise in his judgments and unwavering in his friend ships. While free anrl outspoken on all public qQestions, yet he avoided giving offense by the too open expression of his opinions.
But he is dead, and this G111-11d Lodge for t_he third time during this Masonic
year is called upon to close up the ranks, as another in the front line hae
fallen. Bro. CONKLIN was, indeed, a conspicuous character wherever and
with whomsoever his lot was cast; whether as a lawyer or a ,Judge, he was
always the same calm, dignified sincere man, modest and retiring in his social
relations, In his profession, when in the right, he was earnest and assertive.
No man could find a truer friend, no wife a more devoted husband, no child a.
more loving and indulgent parent. Need we say more? We loved him in
life, and revere his memory now that he is gone from us forever. Be it
Resolved, That this (hand Lodge most deeply mourns the death of Past
Grand Master ALvAH RusSEL CoNKLIN; that we profoundly sympathize with
his bereaved widow and orphaned children. Awl. we direct that a copy of
these resolutions be presented to his family.

follows:·
It is not often in the experience of a Grand Lodge that it is called upon to
mourn the loss of three of its passed presiding officers within the short course
of a twelve-month, and it is the reverent hope of him who addresses you today that it may be many years ere we engage in ceremonies like unto those of

the present time. May those who a.re left among us continue for many years
to come and go, exemplifying in their lives the beautiful and impressive lessons
of our noble Order, encouraging us by their presence, aiding us by their advice,
strengthening us by their example, and lea.ding us by the sweet simplicity of
their lives to a. just appreciation of the privilege we enjoy of being even humble
workers in a. cause that has enlisted the time, attention and energy of many of
the noblest and best men who have lived upon the earth. Past Grand Master
CLAY WEBSTER TAYLOR, of whom I am specially asked to speak, was a type of
man not unusual as the product of this comparatively new continent, and espe;
cially of that newer part of it, the western slope. He was, in all that th.e phrase
implies, a self.made man. Born under conditions not the most favorable;
coming up through youth to manhood without those educational advantages
considered so almost essential to the highest development of all the faculties,
he yet, by his indomitable pluck, his steady purpose of mind, his untirin1t
energy, his unquenchable thirst for knowledge, his unswerving integrity and
his fidelity to friends, attained an exalted position in his chosen profession, a.
notable influence among his people and his State, and received at the hands of
his beloved brethren the greatest honor that can be conferred upon a Californian Mason, that of presiding over the deliberations of this Grand Body and
guiding the destinies of Masonry in this Grand Jurisdiction, His was the
genius of ha.rd work. His success ca.me not by the ·chance of fortuitous circumstances, hut from the fact that whatever he undertook to do, he did with
all his soul, with all his strength and with all his mind; and he finally, at the
meridian of his splendid powers, sacrificed his magnificent physical manhood
to the attainment of the high ideal of accomplishment which he conceived to
be his duty. The conditions that surrounded the early settlement and marvelous development of this new Western Empire opene!i np questions which had
never before presented.themselves to the human race for solution, and in dealing with which no precedent had been handed down to us. ,This, like all
crises in the evolution of the race, necessitated the development of men capable
of blazing the pa.tbs leading the people through the wilderness of doubt and
uncertainty to the glorious mountain tops overlooking the promised fruition of
their hopes. As in all like conditions, men spra.ng up all over the land who
demonstrated by their snperior foresight, exalted characters and noblest intelligences their capacity for lea.demhip, and stamped their individuality for all
time in the.history of this commonwealth. Such a man was CLAY WEBSTER.
TAYLOR, and perhaps ~o man influenced to a. greater extent than he publie
sentiment in the northern part of ' this State. By his knowledge of human
nature, by his large eympa.thie~, by his intuiti·rn grasp of the very essence of
all questions, by his fidelity to friends, by his magnificent personal presence.
and by his superior magnetism, he was enabled to impre88 his own ideas on.
those with whom he ca.me in contact, and persuade the people to adopt his
views on all questions that ca.me before them for decision. I have been informed by members of his own profession,' who were his associates a.t the bar,
that he always sacredly fulfilled any verbal agreement as to the conduct of
cases. No competitor ever questioned his entire fairness in this respect.
Perhaps the most notable and influential of hie many.admirable characteristics
was his fidelity to his friends. No question of personal sacrifice would prevent.

Pa.st Grand Master MORRIS MARCH ESTEE spoke as follows : MosT WORBIDPFUL GRAND MASTER:Past Grand Master NATHANIEL GREENE CURTIS is dead. He died at Sacramento on the 12th day of July, 1897. He was born in North Carolina..
From North Carolina. he moved to Memphis in the State of Tennessee, where
he was ma.de a. Mason in 1845. In 1850 he ca.me to California., settled at Sacramento, and commenced the practice of the law. In the early fifties he was
Recorder or Police Judge of that city. In after yea.rs he was elected State
Sena.tor from Sacramento. These were the only official positions he ever occupied, both of ,which he tilled with fidelity and ability. For more than
twenty-five yea.rs as a. jury lawyer he was a.t the head of the Bar of this State.
He was always a leader of the Sacramento Bar. Thie is no common praise,
because that Bar was then composed of men illustrious in their profession, and
famed all over the Coast. There wa.e H. H. HARTLEY, once a. dietingniehed
member of this Grand· Lodge, Judge TOcl RObmson, Oen. Thomas H . Willia.Illll, Thomas Sunderland, Judge H. 0. Beatty, Milton H . ~m, Col.
Edwards, James W. Coffroth, and many others of equal a.1>1lity. In the practice of his profeuion, a.sin private life, Pa.st Grand Master CURTIS was open,
frank, manly, able and always a gentleman. As a.n advocate, he was e~oquent
without knowing it. He appealed to the reasons of men. He was not a. great
reader, nor was he what is ca.lied a. book lawyer, but he was deeply versed in
the principles of the law. He always declared that the law was intended to
educate men so that they would know how to "do unto others as they would
they should do unto them."
He was the young man's friend. I remember that in the early fifties a.
young, beardless and briefless lawyer was attempting to practice law in that
city; this young lawyer was one day appointed by the Court to defend a. notorious but pennilees criminal for murder. When the day of trial ca.me, an older
attorney arose and objected to so young a. man defending a. human being for
his life. CURTIS, although unacquainted with the youth, rose and ea.id : "I
will be responsible for the proper defense of this man." And for two week11,
during the trial, that venerable !Awyer, without compensation, sat in Court to
witne88 the young man's first effort in trying a great case. Finally the argument was reached, and the young lawyer ma.de possibly the best speech that
he ever ma.de before or afterwards. When he concluded, CURTIS, in the

presence"of the Court and jury, grasped the young man's hands and congratulated him.
I am here to-day to tell the story of his life-not to praise him. He needs
no eologiom from me ; his good deeds are his most enduring monument. He_
was always a true friend and a patriotic citizen. I remember io 1861, during
the rebellion, a few of us were talking with him of the war. He was born in
the Sooth and sympathized with his people. Some of us spoke most earnestly •
of the recent events, when he said : "I was born in the South ; my kindred
are there. I sympathize with them " But he ended by saying we ought all
of us to daily repeat this beaotif;J_ poetical benediction ; and he did repeat
this verse : " Great God, I thank Thee for this home,
This bounteous birth-land of the free ;
Where wanderers from afar may come
And breath the air of liberty."
When we separated we hadj more of the feeling. of human kindness
within us.
,
He had an abiding faith in man. He never sought to find the bad in our
nature. He was confiding, hopeful, manly and generous. In private life he
was eminently social. He never di;ank a drop, yet he was one of those temperate men who pitied but never defamed those who drank to excess. He be·
longed to no church, but believed in all churches. He never could understand
or appreciate how men should so widely differ as to the manner of worshipp~g
the same God; his faith was abiding and as broad as humanity. True, he was
human like all of us; and sometimes he erred. Bot more than once I have
known him to correct himself and apologize for errors which were trifling to
adegree. He was as sensitive as a woman and gentle as a child, yet no man
was stronger in his convictions. Io the hignest and best sense he was a man
of honor. He wronged no one, he imperiled no interest, he lived a peaceful,
kindly, harmleBB, but an honored life.
It was as a Mason that we knew him best. He was Grand Master of this
Grand Lodge during the Masonic yaars of 185i, 1858, 1859, 1860. Under his
leadership, Masonry prospered in California as it never had prospered before,
and since then he has been one of the most conspicuous characters in Masonic
history. His presence in this Grand Lodge was always hailed with delight·
by the Fraternity. He is gone and yet he has not wholly left us ; his noble
example remains ; his spirit cannot die. He will live on forever "in memory
dear," and though he is dead, he fell, "like the_struck eagle, stretched upon
the plain."
.
Methinks I see him, strong and well and young again, in all his vigor and
in all his manly graces. We can almost hear his eloquent voice to-day in this
hall. We seem to listen again to his words of wisdom, but when.we awaken
from this illusive reverie, he is not hero, and he will be here no more forever.
He has crossed the dark river to the limitless and endless beyond. •. The
machinery of his physical life has run down; his spiritual existence has just
begun. Troe, we can remember him as he was in the splendor of his sparkling
wit, in the brilliant sallies o! his great mental gifts, in the warmth of his generous friendship, in the restless eloquence of his convincing logic. And yet

The cause of the delay in forwarding this transcript is certified by the
Master and ~retary to be due to the loBB or misplacement of the original
summons, and of several letters, papers and documents used at the triaL
The record shows that the summons was properly issued and served, the
accused was preeent during the tria1, testified thereat, and waived all such
irregularities, if any.
The trial was fixed for the 21st day of October, 1896, but upon request of
the accused, by and with the consent of the Master, it was continued until
November 5th, at which time six of the nine CommiBBioners being present, the

15

226

Procwlings of the

[Oct. 14,

trial was proceeded with, and testimony was taken ; the proceedings were
regnl11.r until we come to the statement : " Here the further hearing was continued until Friday evening, November 27th, 1896, at half-past seven o'clock."
On November 27th, twenty.two days intervening, the Commiasioners assembled, with five of the Commiasioners preeent, two others making their first ap· .
pearance ; further testimony was taken, and the statement is then made :
"Here the Commissioners adjourned until Monday evening, November 30th,
1896, at 7 :30, when the be.lance of the testimony is to be read to the witneaseii
and signed by them."
The transcript shows no reasons for such continuances, nor that the Master
consented to the same.
In the case of BROCK, in Vol. 19 of Proceedings, page 556, it was held, that
where the Commission adjourns for a longer time than permitted by the Constitution and without the consent of the Master, that it lapses and diasolves·
itself by its own neglect and cannot reinvest itself with any of its powers.
At the meeting on November 30th, the matter was submitted to the commissioners, and, upon ballots being taken, the accnsed was found guilty on the
first and second specifications and not guilty on the balil.nce. ·
The following proceedings were then had :" Ballots on the punishment :
"First--Shall the accused be expelled? Result, five votes no.
"Second-Shall the accused be suspended! Result, three votes no ; two
votes aye.
"Second ballot-Shall the accused be suspended? Result, three votes no;
two votes aye.
"Third ballot--Shall the accnsed be suspended? Result, five votes aye,
being a majority of all the commissioners elected. The result of this ballot
having been declared, the Commiasion, having finished its work, adjourned."
Thia method of procedure was severely criticised by this committee in the
NEEL case, Vol. 20 Proceedings, page 686, and the conu:nittee there said:
"The utmost diligence of your committee fails to find a parallel to this action;
it is certainly contrary to common as well as Masonic law, and finds no war·
rant in sense or precedent. "
The transcript contains one hundred and thirty-nine pages of typewritten
matter : the evidence shows that the accused was guilty of the charge of unmasonic conduct, as contained in the first and second specifications ; no benefit
could be derived by a retrial; the verdict is warranted by the testimony and
the judgment merited.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the judgment of King Solomon'a Lodge, No. · 260, given on
the seventh day of December, 1896, whereby DANIEL SANFORD CuLP was
suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is
reversed, and that the said DANIEL SANFORD CULP be and he hereby is, by this
Grand Lodge, suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.

IV. Bro. ERNEST EDWIN HALL, representative of Alillal Lodge, No. 321,
proposes a plan for the organization of a Supreme Grand Lodge, to be composed of duly elected representatives from the several Grand Lodges throughout the United States, as follows:WHERlliAS, The work of the different jurisdictions of the United States
differs materially; therefore, be it
Resolved, That this Grand Lodge appoint a committee of three to confer
with all other jurisdictions of t.he United States, for the purpose of establishing a Supreme Grand Lodge, to meet once in three years, for the uniformity
of the work throughout the United States.
The adoption of the foregoing resolution would give the official sanction of
this Grand Lodge to an innovation far more revolutionizing and difficult of
attainment than the scheme of the Grand Lodge of Mississippi for the adoption of a code of uniform rules governing jurisdiction over candidates for the
degrees. That scheme was designed to promote harmony and good fellowship
among the Grand Lodges, by removing one of the causes which is a continual
source of controversy and ill feeling. Yet it was so vigorously assailed that
the Grand Lodge of Mississippi, with all of its merited prestige, failed to secure the concurrence of any considerable number of other Grand Lodges in an
effort to modify their laws to conform to the plan proposed. What, then,
would be the fate of an effort to promote the plan of the foregoing resolution,
which proposes the surrender of certain prerogatives of the Grand Lodges to a
higher tribunal of delegated authority ?
Section 1, of Article III, of. Part I, of our Constitution, reads as follows :. S~arroY 1. The G.rand Lodge is t~e supreme Masonic power and authority
in ~his . State, po~essmg ~ll ~h.e att':'1b~tes of sovereignty and govemmentlegts.lat1ve, executive and JUdic1al-hm1ted only by a strict adherence to the
Ancient Landmarks of the Order, and by the provisions of it11 own Constitution
and Regulations.
The plan of the resolution under consideration is a violation of the foregoing section of the Constitution. It proposes to destroy the suprema.ey of
this Grand Lodge.
We therefore recommend that it be not adopted.

4. On December 5th, 1896, I received a letter from Bro. MICHAEL Jos&l'H
SAVAGE, Worshipful Master of Occidental Lodge, No. 22, requesting that the
Lodge be allowed to decorate its altar with the American :flag. Without giving
the matter serious thought, and being in a patriotic mood, I granted the request. Since then, having seriously considered the question, I am compelled
to confess that I am of the opinion that I erred in so doing. I believe that the
best interests of Masonry will be subeerved by not allowing such permission.
We concur wit)l. the Grand Master in his amended decision. His reconsideration of the permission granted was wise and timely. All Masone owe
allegiance to God, but the political allegiance of our Masonic brethren is as
varied as the powers and principalities of earth. The Great Lights on our
altars are the mystic symbols of our loyalty to the Nation, and blue is the dis·
tinctive color of the three symbolic degrees. There is no Masonic authority
for the practice and we recommend its discontinuance.
5. On January let, 1897, I received a request from Enterprise Lodge, No.
70, to allow that Lodge to receive and act upon the peti~ion of LEROY JOHN•
STON COPE, of Yuba. City, he having lost three fingers of the left hand.
I
authorized the Lodge to receive the petition, which was done. Later I learned
that almost the entire left hand had been lost. * * * I am of the opinion
that I erred in allowing the Lodge to receive his petition.
We are satisfied that the Grand Master was misled as to the extent of the
deformity of the applicant, and that, had all the facts been presented to· him
in their proper relations to his disqualification, the Grand Master would and
should ha~e decided that the candidate was physically disqualified.
6. I might say here, brethren, that it appears to me that our regulations,
with refereLce to physical qualifications, are too exclusive when we come to
compare them with those of other and older jurisdictions. Is he a sound man 1

238

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 14,

Can he receive and impart the knowledge of the Craft? The in'ternal soundness or uns01:mdness of an apJ?licant is of far more importance to the Craft
than some slight injury or blemish. Under this head I might say that I ruled
that a chronic asthmatic was not proper material for a Lodge to receive.
It is the province of your committee to interpret and apply the law, as we
find it in our Constitution and General Regulatio~ rather than to draw comparisons for the covert purpose of giving an excuse for evading the laws as
they exist in this jurisdiction. General Regulation No. 11 is the law as to
physical qualification within the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, and the
Masters of Lodges are bound by their sacred obligations to observe and obey
the law. If the law is too severe it may be amended or repealed, but so long
as it is the law it must be obeyed. This is the requirement of our Constitution. Section 2 of Article III of Part I, reads as follows :SECTION 2. Its legislative powers extend to every case of legislation not
expressly delegated by itself to the Lodges; and the Constitution and Regulations, which it has an inalienable right to adopt and promulgate at its own
convenience, and to alter, amend or repeal at its own pleasure, under limitations therein imposed, are final and binding upon all Lodges and Masons within
its jurisdiction, until so altered, amended or repealed.
This section of the Constitution is still in force, and it would be highly
commendable for the Masters of Lodges to vie with each other in obeying,
rather than as is too frequently the case, in seeking to evade the law.
In deciding that a chronic asthmatic is not proper material ~or a Lodge to
accept, the Grand Master complied with the spirit and intent of the law relative to physical qualifications.

7. An Entered Apprentice nor a Fellow Craft Mason is not, as a right,
entitled to relief from the funds of a Lodge.
This is in conformity with a decision by this Grand Lodge as recorded in
Vol. XX, page 217, of the printed proceedings, which reads as follows:None but Master Masons can be members of a Lodge, or are entitled to all
the privileges and benefits of the Order.
We therefore recommend that the decision be approved.
S. The funds of a Lodge cannot be used to defray the expenses of the
accused in a Masonic trial, nor to repay money expended for attorney's fees.
The decision is in strict compliance with former decisions by this Grand
Lodge, and we recommend its approval.
9. A Lodge has no authority to use its funds to pay asses,sments on a life
insurance policy, even though made out in favor of the Lodge, especially where
there are grave doubts that the amount of the policy would be paid to the
Lodge in case of the death of the insured.
The decision is sound and should be approved. Under our Constitution
and Regulations the funds of a Lodge must be used for the legitimate expenses
of the Lodge aud for charitable purposes only. They were never intended for
speculative investment, such as was.contemplated in the transaction refe.rred to.

10. There was an appeal made to me to use my power to compel a Lodge
to render assistance to a widow of a deceased Mason. I declined to do so. As
there was no evidence that the lady was unable to support herself, I did not
consider the Lodge was under any moral or Masonic obligation to render her
financial assistance.
The propositioµ, as stated above, seems equitable and just, and we recommend its approval.
11. A complaint was made against one of the Lodges in. San Francisco on
account of a printed folder that is sent to the members of the Lodge prior to
each stated meeting. The folder contained an epitome of the business that
would be brought before the Lodge, together with the names, residence and
· occupation of the candidates for whom the Lodge would ballot. The objection
was, that the Lodge was publishing to the profane that which should be kept
within its tiled precincts. Upon a thorough investigation, I learned that most
of the Lod/Jes in San Francisco were doing this ; also that it was a custom
among the English Lodges ; Section 6, A;rticle II, Part III, of the Constitution,
requires Lodges having concurrent jurisdiction to send this information to the
other Lodges.
I decided that, in sending out the folder, no Masonic precedent was violated,
and allowed the Lodges to continue the use of the printed folder.
·
The section of the Constitution referred to as authorizing the issuance of a
printed folder reads as follows:SECTION 6. Each Lodge having concurrent jurisdiction with another Lodge,
or with othllr Lodges, shall immediately notify such other Lodge or Lodges of
any application it may receive for the degrees or for affiliation.
The law requires that the notification shall be sent to the Lodges, not to
the brethren. When Lodges, or officers of Lodges, begin to take liberties
with the law, they are liable to become law-breakers. We respectfully recommend that the Lodges in question be required to conform to the constitutional
requirement in such a manner as to avoid just criticism for publishing and
distributing information which should not be communicated to the profane.
We concur with the Grand Master in his decision that no Masonic precedent
is violated in sending out a printed folder, but add the restriction that the
names of the applicants for the degrees must not be printed and dispersed in
such folders. Neither should such names, when posted on bulletin boards, be
exposed to public view, except during the times of the meeting of the Masonic
Lodges in whose halls the names are posted.
12. Where there was no evidence of a legal marriage, a widow claiming to
be the widow of a deceased brother Mason should not be recognized as such,
and is not an object of a Lodge's charity.
This decision is in accord with the strict observance of the laws of morality
which is enjoined on all Masons, and should therefore receive the unqualified
approval of this Grand Lodge.
13. A rejected applicant for affiliation is not a special charge for charity
on the Lodge t~at rejected him.
This decision can apply to Masons only who are not in good standing in
this jurisdiction. A worthy distressed Mason who, at the time of his applica- •

15. Or.land Lodge, No. 265, ele~ted an applicant on November 16th, 1888.
He received the first two degrees of Masonry in t~at ~dge •. A brother M~on,
member of a neighboring Lodge, objected to his b~g raised. to th4: sublime
degree of a Master Mason. A committee was appomted to mvestigatt: the
objection. The committee brought in an unfavorable report and the candidate
was denied advancement.
. . . .
In the meantime the candidate removed to the JUnsdiction of Olay Lodge,
No. 101, at Dutch Flat. After having resided there several years, Olay1!o~ge
requested Orland Lodge to. grant it the privilege to confer the remammg

Being governed by a ruling made by Past Grand Master BELCHER m . ,
and the report of the Committee on Jurisprudence in regard 1'.<' that ruling

Let the petition take the usual course. If the petitioner were elected, Orland

.

Second-Let the applicant request 0~1?-nd Lo~ge t? grant Clay Lodge the

The second alternative was acted upon-and the candidate was, by Olay
Lodge-, rejected.
.
.
Olay Lodge desired to be informed to what Lodge did the candidate owe
allegiance as a Fellow Craft Mason. I ruled that he was a Fellow Craft
Mason under the jurisdiction of <Jl,ay Lodge.
We have had no opportunity for determining whether or not all provisio,ns
of the Constitution and Regulations were complied with in the various proceedings which led up to the question of the status of the Fellow Craft who~e
membership is to be determined, but for the purpose of the argu~ent we ~l
assume that the proceedings were regular. The Grand Master, m rendering
this decision, was manifestly guided by the laws and usages relative to a waiver
of jurisdiction. ' The weilht of authority justifies such an application ~f the
law to a candidate who, before receiving the degrees, asks for and receives a
waiver of jurisdiction. It applies with equal force to a general waiver of jurisdiction such as is authorized in Section 19 of Article III, Part III, of the Constitution. But the authority of a Lodge over a Fellow Craft is of a different
nature from its authority over a profane, or over an irregularly made Mason,
and is to be determined by constitutional limitations, rather than by the laws
and customs relative to a waiver of jurisdiction.

Gra'fld Lodge of Oalifornia.

241

A decision reported in '\"oL XIII, page 197, of the printed proceedings,
reads as follows :The Lodge in which an applicant is initiated gains, and can retain at its
pleasure, control over him .as an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft. He
cannot apply to another Lodge for advancement without the consent of such
Lodge.
The method by which such consent can be given is regulated by Section 3
of Article I, Part V, of the Constitution, which reads as follows :If ~ Mason shall have received the first degree, or the first and second degree_s, m one Lo.d~e, and shall simply receive permission from such Lodge to
receive the remamm~ degrees or degree in another Lodge, he must petition
the last Lodge mentioned for such other degrees or degree and the petition
shall be subject to the usual reference and ballot. If he ~ elected and receive the additional degrees or degree he shall be deemed a member of the
Lodge in which he received the degree of Master Mason.
In the last clause of this section we have the conditions precedent, and the
only conditions named in the Constitution whereby an Entered Apprentice or
a Fellow Craft can become a member of a Lodge other than the one in which
. he "'.as initiated. These conditions are that, after the neceBBary permission
by his own Lodge, he must be elected to receive· the remaining degrees in
another Lodge, and when he has received his last degree he becomes a member of the Lodge in which he received the degree of Master Mason.
The permiBBion referred to in this section of the Constitution cannot be
const:J:ued as a waiver of jurisdiction until the conditions named, whereby Olay
Lodge may acquire jurisdiction, have been complied with ; that is, until after
the candidate has been elected by, and has reccived the degree of Master
Mason in said Lodge. The permission referred to is clearly a privilege,
granted by one Lodge to another, to perform a specific act. The right to perform a ,specific act is exhausted where the act specified is performed. For
instance : Tha Master of a Lodge may grant permission to his Senior Warden
to occupy the East and confer a degree in Masonry ; when the degree has
been conferred the right is exhaused and the gavel must be surrendered to the
Master ; the Senior Warden cannot again occupy the East without another
penrission being given.
Olay Lodge received permission to perform a specific act, to wit : That of
receiving and acting on the petition of a Fellow Craft from another Lodge.
It performed that act and rejected the candidate. Its rights in the premises
have been exhausted. It can neither receive the petition again without
another permission from Orland Lodge, nor can it lawfully consent that the
Fellow Craft may petition another Lodge. Such consent can be given by
Orland Lodge only; hence, any jurisdiction which Olay Lodge might have
claimed is at an end and the Fellow Craft owes his Masonic allegiance to
Orland Lodge, which Lodge only can remove the obsta.cle to his receiving the
Third Degree.
Respectfully submitted.

Bro. CHARLES LEWIS PATTON presented the Report of the Board of
Trustees of the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home : To the M. ', W. ', WILLIAM THOMAS LUOAS,
Grond Master F. d: A. M. of California:-

The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home of
Calif?rnia herewith submits its sixth annual report of its work during the
year.
The Board organized by the election of the following officers :CHA~ES L. PATI'ON ......................... . ... President;
CH~LES F. CROOKER .• , ..•...••• . ....••....••.•• Vice-President;
EDWARD COLEMAN .............................. Treasurer;
GEORGE JOHNSON............... . ................ Secretary.
During the year Bro. NATHANIEL GREENE CURTIS; a member of the Board
since its organization, paased to the great majority, leaving behind him not
only the regrets of his fellow Trustees but also of the Fraternity of California.
We also lost a faithful and enthusiaatic co-worker in the death of Bro.
CHARLES F. CROCKER, of whom no eulogy is needed by us,
We also regret the loss of Bro. J A.MES W • .ANDK&'lON by resignation, who
was nnable to perform the duties of a member of the Board because of hie
residence at such a distance from this city.
The Board as now constituted consists ofBro. CHARLES LEWIS PATTON,
Bro. EDWARD PEABODY,
" JACOB VooRBANGER,
" THoM'.AS FLINT, Sr.,
" WILLIAM JOHNSTON,
" EDWIN WHIPPLE,

During the past year $7797.69 have been expended in payment of found&·
tion, grading, piping water, etc, ·
Cash on hand, September 30, 1897 ........ . ......... $ 3,178 60
Old subscriptions, unpa.id ........................... 11,382 77
Bro. .ANDERSON'S resolution of last year providing for ~r capita ta.x of $1
was almost nullified by changing the words "required " to " requested,'' and
instead of $17,000 to $18,000 expected, yielded in cash only $2464-a sad
shrinkage, which the Trustees can but' very much deplore.
The Board has labored under these as well as very many other unforeseen
difficulties and perplexities, causing delays in the completion of the building,
and though our hearts are in the work, lack of funds is the principal reason
why the building is not now ready for dedication by this Grand Lodge. The
Home so far is free from debt; $60,000 will complete it in brick and stone
ready for occupancy.
About $50,9<JO has been expended to date; another $50,000 will complete
buildings, and $10,000 more will furnish it and beautify the surrounding
ground.

1897.]

Grand Lorlge of California.

251

If this Board is expected to go on with the work let the Grand Lodge provide at least part of the money required, and we feel satisfied that we can
have the Home ready for dedication prior to the next Annual Communication
of the Gr~d Lodge.
We are willingly giving our time and best knowledge without price or stint
to make this Home a success, but the Fratemity, if in earnest in their wish
for a Home, has only to provide the funds. Let the individual Mason, the
Lodges, and, especially, the Grand Lodge, donate from their surplus funds to
this worthy object.
The Grand Lodge has now in its treasury some $100,000. This Board of
Trustees feels that no better use can be found for this money than to bestow
charity upon the indigent brother Mason, his widow and orphans, and this
Board of Trustees, your own creation, appeals to you ae a body to give us the
funds to complete the work you have authorized us to. commence. Over
$115,000 have been expended by this Grand Lodge for charity in the past, and
now is the opportunity to provide for the needy in the future by putting the
Home on a firm basis, and certainly, in the opinion of this Board, no better use
of some of the large amount of money in the Grand Lodge hands can be
·
found.
The completion of this Home would relieve the Lodges and Boards of Relief of much permanent charity, leaving only cases of temporary relief for
their consideration. Seventeen Grand Lodges of the United States make
liberal donations for establishment and .maintenance of Homes. Twelve ~
Grand Lodge1 make all their contributions to charity to Homes only. It is
the most practical and satisfactory form of dispensing Masonic charity from
Grand Lodge treasury for regular pensioners on our bounty.
The present Home, 'when completed, will be sightly, commanding, healthful, and easy of access. It now stands an uncompleted structure, appealing to
the Craft, a reflection upon the liberality of California Masons.
Times are now good throughout our State and if we commence building we
believe the subscriptions will come in. .
We again are under obligation to Alameda Lodge, who, during the put
year, have set out an orchard on the site, of twelve acres, comprising 1000
trees, without the expenditure of one cent to the Board.
In conclusion we unanimously request a donation of $20,ooO from this Grand
Lodge, to be pa.id upon the completion and acceptance of the building, and
if granted we pledge ourselves .to complete the building as rapidly as pos·
sible.
·
Respectfully submitted.
CHARLES LEWIS PATTON,
President.

To the M. •• W. ". <hand Lodge of Oalij<Yt'nia :Your committee have examined the papers relative to a consolidation, presented by Calaveras Lodge, No. 78, and Oampo Seco Lodge, No. 100, and find
that each of these Lodges has secured the written assent of more than threefourths of its members to the proposed consolidation, and has, in all its
proceedings, conformed to the requirements of Section II, Article II, Part III
of the Constitution. In the agreement between the Lodges it was stipulated:
lat. That the constituted Lodge shall be designated as Calaveras Lodge,
No. 78, F. & A. M., being the name and number of one of the Lodges desiring
consolidation.
2d. That the consolidated Lodge retain the charter and seal of said Oala·
veras Lodge, No. 78.
3d. That such consolidation take effect at the stated meeting of Oalaveras
Lodge, No. 78, in December next.
4th. That at such meeting the :Master of Calaveras Lodge, No. 78, shall
preside, and that all the members of both Lodges· shall have the right to participate in all the proceedings of such meeting, and shall from that date be
members of the consolidated Lodge.
5th. That the by-Jaws of Calaveras 1odge, No. 78, be declare! to be the
by-laws of the consolidated Lodge.
·
6th. That the property belonging to the res~tive Lodges shall become
the property of the consolidated Lodge.
Your committee therefore recommend that the consolidation of those Lodges
be approved, and offer the following resolution:Reaolved, That the proceedings of Oalaveras Lodge, No. 78, and Campo
Se.co Lodge, No. 100, looking to the consolidation of those Lodges into one
Lodge, under the name and number of Cal.aw:ras Lodge, No. 78, be and are
hereby approved; and that such consolidation shall take effect at the stated
meeting of Oalaveras Lodge, No. 78, to be held in December next.
RtJBOlved, That at such meeting the . Master of Calaveras Lodge, No. 78,
shall preside, and that all the members of both of said Lodges shall have the
right to participate in all the business and proceedings of such meeting, and
shall, from that date, be members of the consolidated Lodge.
Resolved, That the by-laws of Calaveras Lodge, No. 78, shall be the by-laws
of the consolidated Lodge.
RtJBOlved, That immediately after such conso},idation shall be effected, the
charter of Oampo Suo Lodge, No. 100, shall be transmitted to the Grand
Secretary.
ReAolved, That all the moneys, property and effects of the said Lodges
shall, immediately after such consolidation, be delivered by the custodians
thereof to the consolidated Lodge, to be by it held and administered for the
benefit of its members.
All which is respectfully submitted by

Your committee again take pleasure in reporting that during the past year
the Fraternity throughout the State has made marked improvement in accession of membership, the number of degrees conferred by the subordinate
Lodges, and is now numerically stronger than at any time in the history of
Masonry in the State of California. The Grand Lodge has l"l)ason to congrat-

Which was concurred in, and ihe resolution accompanying it
adopted.
·
was

ulate itself upon this ehowing.
But notwithstanding the flourishing condition of the Craft, and the.annual
admonitions of this committee with reference to the duties of Secretaries of
subordinate Lodges in the matter of their returns, it is with regret that we
have to report an unusually large falling off from the record of precediag years
in the number of reports from su,bordinate Lodges that were returned to the
Grand Secretary correct in every particnlar and prepared as they should have
been, and the consequent increase in the number of euch reports that are subject to criticism. Your committee can find no excuse for this state of affairs.
While it is true that the Secretaries of subordinate Lodges are primarily responsible for a strict adherence to the rules regarding this matter as laid down
by the Constitution, still it is the duty of Masters of Lodges to see that the
returns to which they certify are not only correct as to the matters therein·
contained, but that they are properly attested with the Lodge seal, and a.Itip
to see that the dues aocompany the returns forwarded to the Grand Secretary.
In the hope that great improvement will be made in the future with reference tQ the matters to which we have called attention, a.nd also in the hope of
relieving the office of the Grand Secretary of additional work caused by ·neglect
and oversight of many Secretaries of subordina.te Lodges, your committee beg
leave to present the fqllewing res<?lotion and recommend its adoption by the

The records of Redondo Lodge, located at Redondo Beach, in Los Angeles
Co~ty, are in proper form and well kept.· The first meeting under dispensation was held January 15, Hi97. It has twenty-six members, has conferred
eighteen degrees, has a balance of $138.30 in the treasury and is without indebtedness. The minutes of this Lodge disclose irregularities in the opening
and closing ceremonies·which should be corrected at once.
The records of Vallee de France Lodge, located at Los Angeles, in the
County of Los Angeles, have been handsomely kept, but are fall of matters
which a~ prohibited to be written. This departure from our regulations is
due to insufficient instruction in this respect, for our brethren in Vallee de
France Lodge have manifested in al.I other ways a zealous desire to strictly
conform to our laws and reqnirements, and are eiu-nest in their labors for the
Craft. This Lodge held its first meeting under diepensation on Janu.i.ry 29,
1897. It has met thirty-five tinies, has twenty-four members, has conferred
twenty-four degrees, has a balance of $377.60 in the treasury and has no debts.
The records of Kilauea Lodge, located at Hilo, Island of Hawaii, Repu~.­
lic of Ha.waii, dl!viate in many respects from the usual form of keeping Lodge
minutes. The brethren, however, are earnest and enthusiastic and are laboring well for the Fraternity.' The Lodge -has every prospect of becoming
vigorous and useful. The first meeting under dispensation was held February
27, 1897. It has twenty members, has conferred thirteen dt>grees and has no
debts.

inge, of t~e names of. brethren wh? may be suspended for non-compliance with

Relative to the jurisdiction of Lodges in incorporated towns, whose municipal limits a.re contiguous to each other.
Bro. F. W. Luc.AS, of Santa Cruz Lodge, No. 38, proposes the following:.fl1JBolved, That where there are two incorporated towns adjoining each
other, with but one Lodge in each town, does ea.ch Lodge h!'ve exclusive juri,ediction within its own municipal limits?
The question of territorial jurisdiction is to be decided by the provisions of
Article II, of Part V, of the Constitution, under the title of Jurisdiction,
which reads a.s follows :- ·
The jurisdiction of a Lodge include all its own members, wherever residing,
and all Mai!ons residing nearer to its place of meeting than to that of any other
Lodge within this State, except in towns or cities where more than one Lodge
exists, in which case each of such Lodges has separate jurisdiction over its
own members, and concurrent jurisdiction over all Ma.sons not members of
one of such Lodges, who reside in such town or city, nearer thereto than to
any other place where a Lodge exists.
On page 374, of Volume V, of the printed proceedings, the Grand Lodge
ruled a.s follows :The rlght of exclusive jurisdiction of a Lodge over parties living nearer to
its place of meeting than to that of any other Lodge in this i:ltate, except in
towns or cities where more than one Lodge exists, is a provision of the Uonetitution which must in all cases be strictly observed, in order that the harmony
of the Craft be not disturbed.
These enactments by the Grand Lodge leave no debatable questions as to
territorial jurisdiction of the Lodges within the incorporated towns referred
to. There is but one Lodge in either town and the question of jurisdiction ie
therefore to be determined by air line distances from the place of mee.ting.

re11pective Lodges to San Francisco. This entails much extra work on the
committee. It wa.s neceBBary to make this year sixty-eight changes in allow·
ances from the amounts ae returned to the Grand Secretary. It ie hoped that

firet claBB tare to San Francisco, and other costs of transportation, to the Grand
Secretary in their returns.
A.a the surplus, ae shown, will admit of there being a reduction of one-fifth
of the usual levy for the Representative Fund for the ensuing Masonic year
and still leave a very material surplus, your committee therefore offer the
following resolution and recommend its adoption :Resolve,d, That there be levied upon the subordinate Lodges of this jurisdiction for the current fiscal year, in addition to the dues prescribed by the
Constitution, the sum of twenty (20) cents for each member borne upon the
respective rolls at the date of the annual reports. Said levy sha.11 be made
for the Representative Fund, and sha.11 be paid at the ea.me time and in the
ma.oner prescribed for the payment of the annual dues.

The Grand Master then delivered his Annua.l Address to the Grand
Lodge as follows :BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LoDGE : -

Jn accordance with the Constitution of this Grand Lodge, I now submit
to you an a.ccount of my official acts during the year just passed, together
with such recommendations as the experience of the last twelve months has
demonstrated to be worthy of your consideration.
It is with great pleaeure that I am enabled to report to you the continued
prosperity of the Craft within this jurisdiction. Notwithstanding the financial
depression that has prevailed throughout the greater part of the State, the
increase in membership has been unusually large. The net gain in membership for the year is 734, which has been exceeded but four times in the entire
history of this Grand Lodge. Peace and prosperity have prevailed within our
borders, and our relations with sister .jurisdictions have been pleasa.nt and
harmonious.
The war clouds which for a time hung heavy over our country have been
diBBipa.ted, and peace again preva.ils in our beloved land.
Mant of our brethren have left their quiet homes to follow Old Glory to
victory with DEWEY at Manila, and have shown their loyalty and patriotism
in the battles that sealed the fate of that city.
To those who have demonstrated their manhood and devotion in this the
time of their country's need, we extend our moat sincere congratulations; and
may He who guides the destinies of nations return to us our soldier boys in
health and honor.
It is with pleasure that I note the presence at this Communication of so
many who have grown gray in the service of the Craft, and whoEe devotion to
the cause of MRBonry has tended so much to the elevation and enlighten·
ment of mankind. But there is one missing from our midst: one who for
many years was wont to welcome us to our deliberations and extend to us the
hand of fellowship at parting. Bro. JAMES OGLESBY is gone. That tall, stalwart form is absent, and we miss the kind, genial presence of our Grand
Tyler. Bro. OGLESBY was born in the North of Ireland on February 29th,
1811, and died in the City of San Francisco on December 20th, 1897, having
nearly reached the age of 87 years. He received the first three degrees of
Masonry before leaving Ireland and affiliated with Oalijornia Lodge, No. 1,
on July 5th, 1865. In October, 1864, he was appointed Grand Tyler, and
continously reappointed up to the time of his death. On the 23d day of December last, under the auspices of this Grand Lodge, in the hall which for
nearly two generations had been his especial charge, in the midst of sorrowing brethren and friends, the last sad rites of the Order were performed over
all that remained on earth of our beloved brother. We mournfully bore his
remains to the place of interment, and then left him to rest beneath the soil of
the State of his adoption. When we, too, shall have crossed the dark river,
and stand before the outer door of the Grand Lodge above, may we not be·
