DECISIONS.
Durin<> the year I have received many communications desiring the proper
interpre,;tion of questions that have arisen in the subordinate Lodges. Most
of these could readily be answered by reference to the Constitution and to

1898.J

Grand Lodge of Oalifomia.

597

decisions heretofore made. Believing it to be unnecessary to reiterate
decisions a.lrea.dy recognized as la.w, and adopted by this Grand Lodge, I
submit those only that present some point not already passed upon by this
Grand Body.
The following are the decisions ma.de:An application to a Lodge for permission to form a new Lodge must be
accompanied by a proper dimit in the case of each brother signing the application. No one while a member of a Lodge should vote on his own application to form a new Lodge.

A brother who has been refused advancement is entitled to know only that
he has been refused, that the matter has been referred to a proper committee,
that his rights ha.ve been preserved, and that the Lodge has, by a proper vote,
refused to advance him.
A person having been elected to receive the degrees may, at the request of
the Lodge in which he was elected, receive the three degrees in another Lodge.
Charges may be withdrawn previous to the commencement of a trial, but
not afterward.

I -'

When a. brother has received certain sums of money as charity from his
Lodge, the money thus given him cannot be charged to his account as dues or
as money due from him to the Lodge.
•
An amendment to the By-laws of a Lodge, remitting the dues of all members suspended for non-payment of dues, would be neither wise nor constitutional. It is the duty of every Mason to pay his dues when financially a.ble,
hot when he can no longer do so his Lodge, on a proper showing made, may
either remit them or extend the time of payment. Having been suspended,
a member may be reinstated either by paying all arrearages, or hie does ma.y
be remitted by the Lodge; but a By-law, the effect of which would be practically to l'.tlquire no dues at a.II from any member after a certain period of
delinquency, would not be constitntional.
.
There is nothing unconstitutional in the adoption by a Lodge of the following· resolution:-

. "!f~olved! That every application for dues being rflmitted must be made
~ w_i:tmg or m person by the delinquent himself, stating his reasons for his

mabihty to comply with the financial requisitions of the laws of the Lodge."

To the query, "Can an Italian gentleman, speaking neither English nor
French, receive the three degrees of Masonry in a Lodge, working in the
French language, by the medium of an interpreter or dragoman ?" I replied
that he could not.

HEADQUARTERS AT CAMP MERBITr.

At the suggestion of a number of the brethren I authorized the erection of
Ma.sonic headquarters among the soldiers located at Camp Merritt.
By this means the brethren of the different Grand Jurisdictions were
enabled to become acquainted, information of a Masonic character was furnished to all inquirers, an opportnnity was given for reading, writing and
social intercourse, and, in general, everything possible was done for the com·
fort and accommodation of our soldier brethren.
To those who conceived the idea, and so faithfully carried out the plan in
all its details, I extend my personal thanks and trust that the Grand Lodge
·will give its approval of the same.
.AltMY LODGES.

Two applications have been received by me during the past six months
asking for dispensations to form Lodges among the soldiers enlisted from this
State.
.
A careful examination of the reports of various Grand Masters from 1861
to 1865, upon the so-called Army Lodges, convinced me that for .various
reasons it would not be for the best interests of the Craft to gra.nt dISpensations of such a. character, at least until the Grand Lodge had determined the
manner and method by which such dispensations were to be granted.
When the Philippines shall have come under the authority of the United
States and something of political and social permanency shall have been secured, the location of Masonic Lodges in that far away land to a.esiet in the
up-building of the State and the elevation of mankind will be the duty of
this great Order.
I refer this subject to you fqr your consideration and for such action as
may .by you be deemed wise and proper for the future .

W1Dows' AND ORPHANS' HoME.

I congratulate you, brethren, upon the fact that the Ma.sonic Widows' and
Orphans' Home, which for so many years has engaged the time and attention
of the Craft, has at last been completed, and that this Grand Lodge will at
this Communication dedicate it to the purposes for which it has been erected.
May those in whose minds the idea was conceived, and those by whose
intelligence, business ability and pertenacity this work has been accomplished,
receive from this Grand Lodge the thanks that to them a.re due. The strnggle
has been long, the task difficult, but at last success has been achieved, and on
to-morrow the widows and fatherless will have a "Home " to shelter them
from the cold blasts of adversity and from the trials and vexations of life.
The future support and maintenance of this institution should now receive
the attention of the Fraternity, and I urge upon you a. careful consideration
of this subject.
GRAND LoDGE DIPLOMAS.

The rush to the Klondike and the war with Spain have created an unusual
demand for Grand Lodge diplomss from the brethren of this jurisdiction. The
price fixed for the issuance of each diploma. has heretofore been $1, but I
am informed by the Grand Secretary that the actual cost to the Grand Lodge
exceeds that amount, and would, therefore, recommend tba.t the price of ea.ch
diploma. be increased to such an a.mount as will at least reimburse the Grand
Lodge for money expended.
HA w AllAN !sLANDS.

The recent acquisition by the United States of the Hawaiian Islands has
added, in a certain sense, to the responsibilities of this Grand Lodge. The two
Lodges chartered by this Grand Body have thus become nearer and dearer to
us, and a territory has been opened that, to a. certain degree, may be considered
our own, in a Masonic sense. While the several Lodges situated in Hawaii
have derived their charters froll' different Grand Jurisdictions, it would seem
to be for the beet interests of Freemasonry that they be, if possible, comprised within the ea.me jurisdiction, and from the fact that the Grand Lodge
of California is nearer than any other Gra.nd Lodge ; and from the further
fact that our Masonic relations are, and must be, in the future brought
nearer and closer, it would appear that the most natural affiliation of
the Lodges situated in Hawaii should be with the Grand Lodge of California.
We are not unmindful of the fact that the territory of Hawaii is a concur·
rent one, and that the Lodges heretofore charti,red have been so chartered in

602

[Oct. 11,

Proce,edings of tM

a regular manner, nor would we in a.ny way ~eek to infringe upon the jnriadiction of any other regular Grand Lodge; but the nearness of Hawaii ~ thia
jurisdiction, the close relations that must hereafter exist between our peoples
and the fraternal friendship that has in the past been a source of pleasure to
us both, would seem to indicate that a closer union would be advisable. I
therefore recommend that the subject of a closer union of the Lodges in
Hawaii with those of this jurisdiction be referred to the Committee on
Jurisprudence, and . that said committee report to this Grand Lodge at this
Communication such reoommendationa as they may think proper nuder the
circumstances.

At the last Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, the surrender of
the charter of Michigan City Lodge was accepted, and the Grand Secretary
was directed to take the usual measures for closing up its affairs. In accordance with that direction, on the first day of November last, Bro. MICHAXL D.
LININGER, Inspector of the Tenth District, was appointed to act as the agent
of the Grand Lodge in the settlement of its affairs ; and it is pleA.Sing to note
that all the business connected, therewith has been transacted in a manner
most praiseworthy and satisfactory. The final settlement shows a balance due
to the Grand Lodge, after payment of all the liabilities of the Lodge; of
$158.65, which amount has been received and will be found accounted for in
the financial portion of this report which follows. The correspondence and accounts relative to this settlement are herewith submitted.
No report has been received from Contra Costa Lodge, No. 227, the surrender of whose charter was accepted at the same Communication.
At date of la.et report there were two hundred and sixty-seven Lodges
borne upon the roll of the Grand Lodge, with a membership of eighteen thousand eight hundred and· eight. Since that time one dispensation to form a
new Lodge has been granted. Cala11era3 Lodge, No. 78, and Campo Seco
Lodge, No. 100, have consolidated; -Michigan City Lodge, No. 47, and Contra
Costa Lodge, No. 227, have surrendered their char~rs, which leaves a loss of
two Lodges, and deducted from above, makes total number of Lodges now
in existence in -this jurisdiction two-hundred and sixty-five, with a membership of nineteen thousand five hundred and forty-two, being a net gain for
the year of seven hundred and thirty-four.

Of the proposed amendments to the By-Lawe of Lodges, which have been •
received during the year, the approval of the Grand Master in nineteen .cases
has been filed in this office. Of these, four, being from Lodges Nos. 158, 210,
224 and 326, proposed to reduce the dues of members ; four, being from Lodges ,.
Nos. 12, 136, 1S6 and 233, proposed to reduce the fee for the degrees; seven,
being from Lodges Nos . 77, 180, 252, 295, 305, 330 and 333, proposed
changes in the time for st11.ted meeting; and four, being from Lodges Nos. 61,
65, 224 arid 330, proposed to abolish the affiliation fee.
Proposed amendments to the By-Lawe, relative to the reduction of dues of
members, from Lodges Nos. 301 and 316, were disapproved by the Grand
Master, for the reason that the rate proposei was thought to be too low for
the Lodges to maintain a healthy and useful existence.
The approval of the Grand Master being but a temporary authorization,
the foregoing amendments, as required by our law, have been placed in the
hands of the Chairman of the Committee on By-Laws of Lodges, and will be
submitted to the Grand Lodge for final action, as have the book of By-La~s
of the Lodge now working under dispensation.

In this connection we would beg leave to call again the attention of your
Worshipful Body to the expenditure of $73.50 made in February, 1891,
already thrice reported to the Grand Lodge.
This amount was advanced on the telegraphic order of the Master of Mount
Olivet Lodge, No. 3, Parkesburg, West Virginia, for the burial of a deceased
member of that Lodge, and although there has been considerable correspond·
ence on the subject, both by the officers of the Grand Lodge and of this
Body, the same has never been paid and probably never will be.
All which is respectfully submitted.

The Grand Lecturer presented hie Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :To tlie M. •• W. ·• Grand Lodge of California:In accordance with the usual custom, I herewith present a report of my
Masonic work during the year, and my ideas of what ought to be done to
obtain uniformity of work and a reasonable amount of proficiency in conferring degrees.
I have spent one hundred and twenty days visiting Lodges throughout the
State and everywhere have' been received with fraternal conrtesy, and the

1898.]

Grand Lodge of OaUfornia.

647

brethren have shown an earnest desire to learn the correct work. I could
have visited a good many more Lodges had I remained but one night in a
place ; but where I found a Lodge badly in need, of instruction I considered it
better to remain long enough to teach the work thoroughly than to cover so
much ground and do little good. I have not in this report given many details,
as such details must, of necessity, be mere repetitions, and I would rather be
judged by results than by any report I might make of my work. I am content
to leave these resnlte to the judgment of the brethren whom I have visited o.nd
with whom I have spent so many pleasant hours.
I have constituted two new Lodges during _the year-Redondo Lodge at
Redondo, Loe Angeles county, and San Pedro Lodge at San Pedro, Loe
Angeles county.
February 13th, in company with the V. •. W. •• JAMES A. fosHAY, Junior
Grand Warden, I visited San Bernardino, and attended the fnneral of our late
brother GEORGE LoRD. A very large number of Masonic brethren were present
to pay the last sad tribute of respect to the memory of our venerable brother.
In accordance with a reaolution passed at the last session of this Grand
Lodge, I called a meeting of Inspectors in the City of San Francisco for the
19th day of April last. Twenty.five of the number were in attendance part of
the timll and a few all of the time. Lodges of Instruction were held during
the week. Broe. EDwARDS and PK&RINE were present most of the time and
rendered very valuable assistance in teaching the work. Considerable good
was accomplished by teaching the manner of doing the floor work ; but it was
impossible to thoroughly teach ,the exact wording of the ritual to all the
brethren present. My experience has been that the only successful way to
teach a. man the work is to sit down with him privately and go over it again
and again until he has learned it. This meeting cost abont five hundred
dollars, and I do not believe the good done was worth the expenditure of so
large a sum of money.
Several of the Inspectors have the work perfectly, but the larger half have
it imperfectly, and always will until the Grand Lecturer visits them at their
homes and stays with them until they learn it. In two or three cases Inspectors have refnsed to adopt the work as taught by me. In such cases there
ought to be a. change. From the reports of Inspectors I find that most of the
Lodges are in a fair condition financially, and that harmony generally prevails.
From my own observations I find that in the large cities and towns, and
in a few of the small ones, the work is almost perfectly rendered, but in most
of the small Lodges there is Yery much to yet learn. In my judgment the
Grand Lecturer ought to devote hie entire time to the work of teaching the
ritual and that he should be paid. a reasonable sum for his services and traveling expenses. He conld then visit every district during the year and devote
Beveral days to each one.
In the course of my travels I found several Lodge-rooms that I did not qpnsider safe. I warned the brethren tha.t the defects ought to be remedied, and
in one case reported the matter to the Grand Master for his action.
In conclnsion, l wish to thank the M. '. W. •• Grand Master for my appoint·
ment as Grand Lecturer. To Bros. PERRINE and EDWARDS I wish to express

1898.]

Procudinga of the

648

my appreciation of their kindness duriD.g my term of office, and to the officers
and members of the Lodges which I have visited I will say that if I have con;.
tributed some little toward your better understanding of our beautiful ritual,
I am amply repaid.
Most respectfully submitted.
CHARLES E. MITCHELL,
<hand Lecturer.

Bro. JACOB H. NEFP presented the following:Suspension of a Master Mason by a Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California carries with it suspension in all other
legitimate Masonic Bodies of which he is a member, it is but an act of jtlstioe
and Masonic comity that those Bodies, if recognized by the Grand Lodge of
California, should be notified of ea.ch suspension ; therefore be it ·
Resolved, That the Grand Secretary, upon receiving notice of the suspen·.
sion, expulsion, or restoration by a Lodge of this jurisdiction of any of its
members, shall transmit such information to the Grand Secretary of the Grand
Cqapter and the Grand Recorder of the Grand Commandery as so~n as practicable.
And for the purpose of including this among the duties of the Grand Secretary it shall be made one of the standing regulations of this Grand Lodge.

The Report on Correspondence is presented· by Bro. A. B. GRAOE, Grand Junior Deaoon, who, after submitting an excellent report, in his excess of modesty
declares his disappointment, says he could see the goal, and worked hard through
many a midnight hour, but could not reach it.
Excuse us, Bro. GRACE, but we dissent from your conclusions and predict that
by the time vou are Grand Master you will look back with pardonable pride to the
report of 1897.
Reviewing California, Bro. GRACE quotes us as writing of several decisions of
the Grand Master, etc. Now what was intended was no reflection upon the decisions, but upon the character of the "questions." We would not for a moruent question the right of a Master to ask of the Grand Master advice upon any legitimate
Masonic subject, but there is such a thing as making a foolish inquiry that no
"gentleman found worthy by the voice of his brethren to be chosen Master of a
Lodge of Freemasons would for a moment entertain." No legislation, however
plain, and no expre88ion, however clear, can forestall the questioner. Some make
inquiries simply in order to hold correspondence with the Grand Master, and others
ask because no printed law or regulation is so satisfactory to them as the personal
aBBurance of the Grand Master. So let the brethren ask and be enlightened; that's
what Grand Masters are for.
He quotes with approval the Address of Grand Master PRESTON, and from the
reports and doings of the forty-seventh Annual Communication concludes that
"prosperity has reached the brethren in the land of the setting sun ahead of
schedule time."

In accordance with the order of Grand Lodge, at 9 A. M. of November 10,
1897, the Grand Marshal formed the procesaion, and, clothed in white gloves and
aprons, the two hundred men in line ma.de an imposing appearance as they ~arched
from the Lodge to the hoisting works from which they were to descend i~to the
mines and cave. In the line of march the Grand Lodge was in the rear, but on
reaching the works the column halted, opened ranks, and Grand Lodge passed
through, and were, of course, the first to enter the mine. They were scientifically
stood on the cage a. ha.If dozen at a. time, when down they went about two hundred
feet in a. second to the level by which the cave was reached. Then began the long
march in single file through the winding, angling tunnel, which was . illuminated
the entire distance by candles set about ten feet apart, and each turn and cross-cut
carefully guarded by Mason• who are employed in the mine, till at length the individual passed through a. temporary door into a scene of inexpressible splendor and
beauty- the illuminated cave. The figure, the strength, the symmetry, the polished alabaster, the glittering wealth of gold and jewela of King Solomon's
'l'emple, were here dazed ond dimmed into insignificance by the brilliancy, the
aboonding wealth of exquisite forms of beauty, the majestic splendor of huge abutments literally covered by the most delicate tracery, the flash of a million jewels;
the bold outline of grandeur and strength clothed in glittering delicate chiseling,
such as no human hand has ever wrought, the stupendous dome of the mountains
above borne upon these noble and beautiful pillars, and a.II fresh from the hand of
the Supreme Architect of the Universe, filled one with overwhelming emotions of
surprise, of delight, of adoration. StalactiteR from the size of a. drop of water to
that of the giant tusks of some antediluvian monster, hung suspended from the
roof, and beneath the white glare of the electric light they danced and shimmered
like icicles in the sun. Singly ancl in cluster, some in blue and some in white, of a.II
lengths and shapes, these stalactites cover the roof~ while among them in labyrinthine irregularity glitters the crystal ooze.
On the north side, almost opposite to where the cave was first broken into the
lime, God has created the fairest creatures of his handiwork, and what King Solomon wrought in yea.rs was hl're fashioned in a. single night; but a night that knew
no day, nor the sound of ax!!, hammer or tool of iron, till the operative workman,
agreeably to the designs drawn upon the trestle board, revealed its hidden treas·

urea. Here are the steps, the pots of incem1e, the bee hive, the hour glass and
waterfall. The steps, whiter than Parian marble, lead upward and into an unexplored beyond; the bee hives, apparently ma.de from great coils of a.la.baster rope,
are from two to ten feet in diameter and six feet high. East of these is the waterfall, stayed midway in its descent by some hypnotic hand; white and a.weinspiring in its silent grandeur is the seemingly stilled torrent of foaming waters
that ere it slept had dashed it~ spray on hummocks of ice in a. thousand fantastic
shapes sparkled in the light. There a.re curtains and veils behind which no man
may enter, woven white and transparent in the cimmeria.n darkness. The whole
aspect of the cave is one of entrancing and bewildering loveliness, and he who can
gaze without a.we upon the grand scene has no beauty in his soul.
The cave, which is probably one hundred and fifty by two hundred and fifty
feet in dimensions, and an extreme height of a.bout one hundred feet from the lowest to the highest point, was lighted by electricity. Eighteen thousand feet of
wire had been used for the purpose, and one hundred and thirty-five lamps were
used, some of th.,m one hundred candle power. In the East hung a. brilliant letter
"G," three feet in height and studded by thirty-five electric lights of sixteen candle
power, a. thing of beauty and joy in itself. In the vast space overhead the lights
formed a. great square and compass, the distance between the extended points being
one hundred feet and the length of ea.ch leg being one hundred and thirty feet. A
sufficient portfon of the cave for the use of the Ma.sons had been floored aivI
seated, and there beneath that great dome, seventy feet overhead and surrounded
by such glitter, such beauty, such strength, such overwhelming s~nse of location,

CANADA.

The Grand Lodge of Canada held three Special Communications during the
year. The first, August 4, 1896, for the purpose of placing the corner-stone of Holy
Trinity Church, in the village of Chesley; the second, August 25, 1896, for the purpose of placing the corner-stone of Grace Methodist Church in the town of Gananoque; and the third, for the placing of the corner-stone of the new Victoria School
building in the City of Beautford, all of which ceremonies were performed with
due regard for the formalities of the Ancient Craft, except that Grand Lodge performed all this labor while "called off," or, in other words, "at refreshment." Do
the brethren of Canada habitually refresh themselves by handling Big Stones?
Grand Lodge held its forty-second Annual Communieation in the City of Beautford July 21, 1897,-M. ·. W. '. WILLIAM GIBSON, Grand Master, on the throne;

and a large number of Past Deputy Grand Masters, Wardens and other Grand

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

In this number of the proceedings we have another of the eloquent reports of
Past Grand Master GREENLEAF. The doings of fifty-nine Grand Lodges are
reviewed, including California under the administration of· Grand Master PRESTON; he comments favorably upon tM Grand Master's Address, the placing of the
(lorner-stone of the Home at Decoto, the general relief work and the oration of the
Grand Orator, ihe Rev. Bro. VooRSANGER, which he pronounces "a gem."
In reviewing Ohio and commenting upon the Address of Grand Master MEL·
LISH, we find these thoughtful words-as we think, words of wisdom:The subject of physical qualification is discussed at length and with much facetious comment. He is in favor of relaxing the law and admitting large numbers of
those hitherto excluded. We have no disposition to enter into a discussion at this
time; there is to our mind only one phase t,, be co11sidered, and that is, was the law
establishert for pecuniary reasons, or for a symbolic purpose? If for the latter, the
Jaw should stand; if for the former, the sooner it is repealed the better. We are
among the number who cling to the idea that the restriction is enforced by symbolic requirements. "
Under Wyoming we note the following comments upon the method of electing
officers in that jurisdiction, applicable to any Lodge of Freemasons :The election of Grand Officers was in this wise: Upon motion, in each instance,
the Grand Secretary was directed to cast the unanimous vote of the Grand Lodge
for Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Senior Grand Warden,. Junior Grand
Warden and Grand Treasurer, and then a good brother was instructed to cast the
unanimous vote of Grand Lodge for Grand Secretary, and all went merry as a
fnarriage bell with our Wyoming brethren.
Colorado has "shut down" on that sort of thing, and a ballot must be had for
every elective office. We are pleased to note the unanimity of sentiment among
our neighboring brethren, but with the growth of jurisdiction they will find it more
desirable to require a ballot of the member• individually instead of collectively,
and, we would add, thereby avoiding the possible disatisfaction which results in
a lack of interest in everything pertaining to Masonry.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
Past Grand Master JOHN H. BARLOW, as usual, presents his report, which in
this instance measures the doings of half a hundred Grand Lodges. But before
writing a word of notice or criticism, we would offer our only consolation to our
highly esteemed brother, the sympathy of a Mason for one of bis brethren in distress. While writing his report our brother was visited with an afHiction that God,
in his unseen ways, inflicted upon him. Our brother says: "We are compelled to
write this report somewhat hurriedly, and for a portion of the time while under
sore bereavement. Death has invaded our family circle 1md taken away our only
son, who, but a few months before, had finished his college and legal courile,
and had commenced the practice of his chosen profesoion. It has left a wound i11
our heart which time alone can heal."
Referring to Mexican Masonry, Bro. BARLOW says : The condition of Mexican Masonry is again prominently presented, and the
Gran Dieta, so called, has received recognition from the Grand Lodges of Iowa,
Montana and New Hampshire, in addition to those reported last y~ar. We have
41olluded to this subject under its proper head, and have no doubt that its former
violation• of the Landmarks of Freemasonry are now strictly prohibited, but that
It is the sole governing power of Masonry in that republic is not so clear, and we
cannot advise its immediate recognition by our Grand Lodge.
Bro. BARLOW'S notice of California is of the administration of Grand Master
E. M. PRESTON. He quotes from the Address of the Grand Master the progress
of the Masonic Home, with its probable effect upon extensive buaineBB of the
Masonic Board of Relief. He giY'es the legislation of the session his general
approval.

To the ladies of the Eastern Star throughout the jurisdiction I can only say,
Life at best is not very long. A few more sighs or smiles, a few
more tears, some pleasures, much pain, cloud and darkness, hasty greetings, abrupt
farewells, and our little play of life is over. We need the assistance of the ladies,
so let us encourage the growth of the Eastern Star.

God bless them.

First. An unaffiliated Mason is still bound by all those Masonic duties and
obligations which refer to the Order in general, but not by those which relate to
Lodge organization.
Second. He possesses reciprocally all those rights which are derived from membership in the Order, but none of those which result from membership in a Lodge.
Thfrd. He ho.a a right to assistance when in imminent peril, if he asks for that
1188istance in the conventfonal way.
Fourth. Re has no right to _pecuniary aid from a Lodge.
Fifth. He has no right to visit Lodges, or to walk in Masonic processions.
Sixth. He has no right to Masonic burial.
Seventh. He still remains subject to the government of the Order, and may be
tried and punished for any offense by the Lodge within whose geographical jurisdiction he resides.
EighJ;h. And lastly, as non-affiliation is a violation of Masonic law, he may, if
he refuses to abandon that condition, be tried and punished for it even by expulirion, if deemed necel!Bary or expedient by any Grand Lodge within whose jurisdic'
tion he lives.
The committee add :As far back as the Gothic Constit.ution of A. D. 926, it was proclaimed that
"the workman shall labor diligently on workdays that he may deserve the holidays." Such an obligation is implied from all the subsequent charges and constitution• which speak of Masons as "working members" of the Order.
The ninth landmark of Masonry asserts the necessity for Masons to congregate
in Lodges. How can unaffiliated Masons congregate in Lodges when, by their
own violation of their obligations and of Masonic law, they prevent themselves
from visitmg a Lodge? It is a well established rule that no man can take advanta"8 of his own wrong.
If a Mason is a non-affiliate through no fault of his own, for instance, when he
has petitioned for membership and been rejected, he would not be subject to discipline; but where Masons live for years with dimits in their possession and make
no effort to affiliate, and therefore pay no dues, nor contribute in any manner to
¥be welfare of the Order, they are indifferent to its interests, and ·their conduct
imtifies the conclusion that they were poor material when made, and are stones
lbat should have remained in the quarries.

The Grand Master bears the following testimony of the benefits the Fraternity

Progress has been made during the past year in teaching the standard work.
The five schools have been largely attended. The zeal of the Craft has been
unabated. '!'he humblest brothers.spires to great proficiency in the work. Nearer
approach is made year by year towards a perfect uniformity in work among the

of instruction as those which follow our superior system of schools. One was held
in Chicago. It has been difficult heretofore to make a school in Chicago successful.
owing to the great numbers which have overcrowded the largest halls. To avoid

there were throo schools held in Chicago, as each continued for three full days.

city and Cook County.

RRPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
The report is another of Bro. JOSEPH RoBBINS' excellent papers. He reviews
'fifty-seven North American and five foreign Grand Lodges in a paper of three
hundred and fifteen pages. He concludes from the proceedings examined, that the
two subjects attracting the most attention, and of course the most discussion, are
the subjects of relief and jurisdiction over rejected candidates, the one being the
text of the Wisconsin and the o.t her of the Maine resolution•.
Bro: ROBBINS writes confidently of the non-recognition of the Gran Dieta.
SRys in his direct and positive manner:It seem• probable that the final dissolution of the Gran Dieta is imminent, and
that the "unveracious factotum," who was its chief projector and has been its chief
manager and pro·noter in Mexico, will soon startle the Masonic world with some
tiew project to enlist the missionary zeal of those American Masons who have
"1ddenly become so devoured by a desire to demonstrate the "uni versaJity of
,Masonry," that they are ready to call anything Masonry which claims the name.
It has been erron<'ously stated in some jurisdictionR that California had recognized the Gran Die.ta, which is a mistake ; the matter h•s as yet not been before
our Grand Lodge. In these matters of recognition our Grand Lodite has always
been conservative, aiming to be right before going ahead.
Under California, Bro RoBBINS reviews the administration of Grand Master
PBEKTON. He quotes the Address, with his decisions, without dissent and with
general approval. Speaking of the decision in regard to cremation not being in
larmony with the Masonic burial ser•ice, he truly and pointedly observes:If cremation should become general, Masonry would adapt itself to the change,
as we are not bound by any unchangeable law.

HONORS TO A DEAD VETERAN.
By invitation of Grand Secretary WILLIAM H. SMYTHE, I accompanied him in
September last to Cape Girardeau, in the 8tate of Missouri, where I assisted in removing the remains of Past Grand Master ALEXANDER BuoKNER from the un1Darked and lonely place where they had laid for sixty-four years to the old and
beautiful cemetery.in the city of Cape Girardeau.
'.
Both Bro. SMYTHE and myself, as representatives of this Grand Lodge, received
every attention and courtesy from our Masonic brethren and the citizens generally
of Cape Girardeau that could possibly be extended to us.
During the funeral ceremonies the court adjourned and the business houses
were closed. Many citizens were present at the burial, and every mark of respect
was shown to the memory of the able and distinguished man who had been so
great and important a factor in the early history of the great 8tate of Missouri.
Fraternal greeth:gs were extended to the Grand Lodges of Canada and Utah
through their representatives present in Grand Lodge.
A Grand Secretary's twenty years record, one of which our It.·. W. •• Bro. WILLIAM H. SMYTHE needeth not to be ashamed.
Passing the financial portion of the Grand Secretary's report, with his very interesting account of the raising of the body of Indiana's first Grand Master from
his unmarked grave "for more decent interment nearer the Temple," we are interested in a retrospective view drawn by the Grand Secretary of his past twenty
years' i!Brvioe as Grand St:cretary of the Grand Lodll0 of Indiana. We q note :A brief review of the past twenty years may not be entirely uninteresting.
When you called me to this high and responsible office May 29, 1878, the Grand
Lodge was in debt $103,666.66, with the sum of $327. 78 in cash in the hands of the
Grand Treasurer. . Creditors were clamorous for thPir money. Interest and prini!ipal had· been defaulted, and the blackness of darkness almost encompassed the
Grand Lodge. That year many of the representatives came up to Grand Lodge
fully expectinir to defray their expenses from mileage and per diem as in the years
before, and they were sorely disappointed when the trae condition of affairs was
laid before them.
Notwithstanding the fact that the Grand Lodge was sorely distressed financially,
and notwithstanding the fact also that the members thereof werP forced to suffer
inconvenience, yet the Freemasons of that Grand Lodge provided for the great
debt which was subsequent!} paid to the uttermost farthing. This action of the
Grand Lodge proves that Indiana Freemasons, like Indiana •oldiers, may be relied upon at all times and under all circum•tances and conditions.
Eighteen of the members of the Grand Lodge present here to-dav were also
mbors of the Grand Lodge of 187ll, with the right to vote both then and now;
eir names are as follows, to wit : Martin H. Rice, Christian Fetta Lucien, A .
ote, Daniel McDonald, Calvin W. Prather, Mortimer Nye, Isaac ·P. Leyden,
ank E. Gavin, Orlando W. Brownhaek, William W. Tiffany, John Castor, Wm.
J. Bethel, Isaac Johnson, Wm. L. Fraley, John Fable, Wm. L. Waltman, Jae.
Crooks and,Wm. H. 8mythe.
Look on the other pictures: Tu-day the Grand Lodge is free from debt, has
lte property released from mortgage and unincumbered by liens of any sort, has
100,974.79 securely invested in interest bearing securities, and it also has a cash
balance of $14,239.68 in the hands of the Grand Treasurer, making sure the fact
that all ex!lflnses of this meeting will be paid in cash, and that each member of the
Grand Lodge present here to-day will receive his mile~e and per diem.
In the twenty years that I have acted as your servant I have written 14, 798 receipts for the collection of the gross sum of $494,856.91, and I have dr&wn 1,952

To conduct the correspondence and other business connected with my office, I
have expended the gross sum of $4,848.50 for postage. This sum for postage in a
measure shows the extent and magnitude of the duties devolving upon me. As
Grand Secretary I have answered thous1mds upon thousands of letters, telegrams
and other communications since May, 1878. Every call made upon my time by a
Master Mason hae been honored. I have performed the duties of a Dun or a
Bradstreet. I have investigated chaiacter and have frequently found myself acting as chief of a bureau of information upon matters entirely foreifCD to the requirements of my vow of office. I have even been asked t0 give my opinion upon matters that should be answered by lawyers, and for which an attorney would exact a
good stiff fee. These things are not related here to be taken or coosidered as a
complaint, but to impress upon {our minds the fact that I have enjoyed g1muine
pleasure in the knowledge that have rendered ycm service, which you have duly
appreciated, and my pleasure is intensified by the further knowledge that the most
humble Master Mason in the State receives as prompt attention as the Grand
Master himself. My delight has been and always will be to perform the duties
assigned to me in suoh a way as to meet the approval of the Master Masons of
Indiana. Their kindness, forbearance and fraternal courtesy have endeared th&m
to me now and always.
Since 1878 I have been subject to the command of sixteen Grand Masters, viz :
Robert Van Valzah, Bellamy S. Sutton, Calvin W. Prather, Bruce Carr, Albert P.
Charles, Mortimer Nye, Isaac P. Leyden, Thomas B. Long, Jacoh J. · Todd,
NicholasR. Ruckle, S1dnev W. Douglo.s, Daniel Noyes, Frank E. Gavin, Edward
O'Rouke, Simeon P. Gillett and Mason J . Niblack. Three of these have been

Charles.
When the Congress of the United States declared war against the destroyers
of the Maine-the treacherous Spanish aseaesins of the brave American seaman
thereon, and the oppreasors of the libertv loving Cubans-patriotic motives
prompted me to cause the star spangled banner to be unfurled and allowed to float
from the flagstaff on top of Masonic Temple, where it has continued almost every
day since that time. For this act of patriotism and devotion to country and emblem of liberty I have been criticised, both favorably and unfavorably, while the
Grand Lodge of Indiana, in the light of the patriotic record made dunng the war
for the preservation of the Union, needs no farther-outward evidence of her devotion to country and flag, and while we, as Freemasons, have been taught in the
first degree thereof that, as citizens, we are to be "true to our government and
just b our country," yet I can see no goon reason why the flag of our country
should not float from the top of every Masonic Temple in this great Union-knit
together and cemented with the blood of patriots, and so long as I have charge of
thia Masonic Temple, and so long as the "land of the free and the home of the
brave " is confronted by an armed foe, the stars and stripes will continue to wave
from the flSoRstaff on top of the M .. sonic Temple of the Grand Lridge of Free and
Accepted Masone of the State of Indiana, unless otherwi•e ordered by you.
Patriotism, !ova of a united and free go'lern°'ent, obedience to the requirements ·
and teachin11;s of Freemasonry, veneration for the memory of the dead defenders
of the flag, viz: Washington, Lincoln, Grant, Sherman, Sheridan and unnumbered thousands of others; respect and love for Fitzhugh Lee and Admiral Dewey,
and admiration for the brave soldier boys of Indiana (many of whom are Freemasons), who ho.ve gone forth to bare their breasts to Spanish bullets and to do
battle in the cause of liberty and humanity, and as ,. token of appreciation of the
blessings vouchsafed to us under her protecting folds, the star spangled bA.Dner
should float from every public building ae well as from every residence in this
glorious country, "dedicatOO to liberty and to the service of God according to the
dictates of conscience. Freemasonry adds to her fame and to her glory by rendering moral and loyal support to the flag of the country, and Freemasons should be
the first as well as the last to exclaim "the star spangled banner; long may it wave
o'er the land of the free and the home of the brave."

R. RUCKLE made the following report concerning Mexican Masonry:Your Committee on Correspondence fraternally report that there has been referred to i~ ~ circular l~tter from Master Masons of Monterey, Mexico, looking to
the recogmt1on of Mexican Masonry by the Grand Lodges of the United States.
The circular or letter does not emanate officially from any body claiming to be
Masonic, but from a meeting of Master Masons, and is accompanied by no information in regard to the status of ·the Fraternity in that portion of Mexico.
While your committee has the sincerest sympathy with the efforts of American
Masons in Mexico to establish Freemasonry on such basis as will secu"' its recognition by the Grand Lodges of the United States, this letter furnishes no information that will assist this Grand Lodge in arriving at a safe and just conclusion, and
therefore recommends that no action be taken upon said communication.
The report was concurred in.

The ritualistic work of the Grand Lodge of Iowa is in charge of a Board of
three Custodians, who are elected by Grand Lodge. The present Board consists
of two Past Grand Masters and a Past Junior Grand Warden. The present session
determined the law in regard to its dissemination as follows:Section 230. Within sixty days after the Annual Communication of 1898, the
Board of Custodians shall divide the State into such number of districts as to it
1hall be advisable for the purpot!eS hereinafter specified, having particular refor·
ence to the extent of territory; they shali then number said districts in some convenient manner.
Section 230a. There shall be held in each of said districts so established schools
of instruction in the work and lectures of the Order. Such place shall be chosen
as will furnish free a suitable room with light and heat. The schools shall he in
general charge of the Board of Custodian!, who shall, within thirty-days after each
Annual C'.ommunication of the Grand Lodge, select one of their number to act as
Traveling Custodian, and under his particular care the said schools shall be held.
The Board shall make such rules and regulations as to time, place, duration and
general management of said schools as may seem best for the accompli~hment of
the purpose for which they are held, which is declared to be the uniform rendition
of the work of the ritual throuirhout the State.
Section 230b. It is hereby made the duty of each Lodge within the district
wherein such school is held to send thereto the Master of the Lodge, or one repre~ntative to be selected by him, who when proficient in the lectures and work,
llhall receive from the Custodian in cbarj!'e a certificate thereof, and the said repre110ntative shall thereafter he the authority for the Lodge on questions as to the
'Wording of the work and lectures, until his certificate ehall he revoked by the
Grand Master on recommendation of the Board of Custodians or another certificate
1ball be issued to a member of the Lodge.
It is hereby made the duty of said instructor to thoroughly instruct the Lodge
in the work and lectures prescribed in this jurisdiction.
Section 230c. There shall be paid to the person selected as Traveling Cueto·
dian an annual compensation of twelve hundred dollars ($1200), to be paid monthly,
upon the order of the Grand Master knd Grand Secretary; and also his traveling
Hpenses and board in attending said schools and expenses for printing ; to be paid
bv the Grand Lodge quarterly, upon the order of the Grand Master and Grand
,Secretary, when audited by the Finance Committee.

"Books are friends which every man may call his own."
Broe. GRANT, STAroN and WILSON-there's a Library Committee for you-in
closing their report, philosophize on the book question as follows:Books furnish food for thought, and thought moves the farm and the factory,
the pulpit and the President, arts and armies, mountains and men-in abort, the
world. Books are our moral and Masonic trestle-boards which furnish the rules
and designs for our guidance in the great work of our Fraternity. More th1m four
hundred years ago the Bishop of Durham said that books "are the master• who
instruct ua without rods and ferrules, without hard words and anger, without
clothes or monev . If you .. pproach them they are not asleep ; if investigating,
you interrogate them, they conceal nothinl('; if you mietakP them, they will not
grumble ; if you are ignorant, they cannot laugh at you. The Library, therefore,
of wisdom is more precious than all riches, and nothing that can be wished for is
worthy to be C<'lmpared with it. Whoever, therefore, ack.nowledgeii himself to be
a zealous follower of truth, of happineBB, of wisdom, of science or even of faith,
mnsL of neceAeity make himself a lover of books."
ROBERT COLLIER worked at the anvil and became a distinguished minister
through the knowledge gained from hie books while pumping the bellows. ELIHU
BURRITT, while wearing the leathern apron, ma•tered eighteen langu•ges by his
study of books. FRANKLIN lived on potatoes, pudding and rice, that he might eave
money with which to purchase books, and thus became one of the greatest of
American statesmen and a Mason whom the world delights to honor.
A worthy object that should have the practical sympathy of every Kentucky
Mason.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
The able Chairman of Correspondence, Past Grand Master W. W. CLABKE,
submits his fifth report, a paper as noted for close reasoning and thoroughness as
any of its predecessors. He reviews fifty-one Grand Bodies, and says, in his conclusion:Some questions of moment we have not attempted ~o discuss,. for the re\lson
that we did not feel sufficiently informed. Among such is the question of ~exican
Masonry.
The question of perpetual jurisdiction has happily passed the acrimonious stage,
and while still unsettled, is not acute. Manifestations of the doctrine in the form
of propositions to limit the time of jurisdiction are manifesting themselves here

One hundred and twenty-eight Lodges were represented, with twenty-six other
Grand Jurisdictions. California was not represented owing to the death of Past
Grand Master JOHN QUINCY ADAMS FELLOWS, for whose passim~ away the
Masons of every degree in the Nation are in mourning. He was born in Orange
County, Vermont; was a graduate of the University of Vermont and, as be told
us in Boston in 1895, under the immediate supervision of our lamented brother
WILLIAM C. BELCHER. He has repreaented the Grand Lodge of California near
the Grand Lodge of Louisiana since 1869. Three Past Grand Masters were. in
attendance.
Grand Lodge was opened in the Third Degree in Ample Form; with prayer by
the Rev. H. C. DUNCAN, Grand Chaplain.
After appointing the committees, the G~and Master delivered his Address.
With a retrospective view of the history and conditions of Masonry in the
jurisdiction he claimed their earnest attention to the needed legislation ot the
aession before them. He referred to the unusual death roll of the year and among
the 130 brethren called home was that Prince in Masonry, Brother JOHN QUINCY
ADAMS FELLOWS.
The Committee on Correspondence reported that owing tu the long illness
and subsequent death of Past Grand Master FELLOWS, chairman of the committee,
no report had been prepared for the Grand Lodge at this Annual Grand
Communication. The remaining members of the committee would, therefore,
claim indulgence for the unavoidable omission.
The Committee on Correspondence recommended and Grand Lodge resolved
Th ..t the Grand Lodge of Peru having extinguished the Great Light upon its
Altars has ceased to be a true Masonic Body, and that the action of the Grand
Master in respect to said Grand Lodge and its Representatives be sustained and
perpetuated. This action to remain in force until that light shall be again rekindled.
A communication was received from the Grand Royal Arch Chapter of
J.ouisiana donating a claim held by it of $2, 700, with accrued interest to date, to aid
in the redemption of the debt of the Grand Lodge. The Grand Master elect was
ftquested to properly convey the thanks of Grand Lodge for the magnificent
donation.

Past Grand Master BocK at the request of the Gr:Lnd Master.

The great Masonic Fraternity throughJut the land knew and honored our
departed Brother.
The lament over his grave has traveroed Lodge-room and Temple, Asylum and
Consistory, and from everywhere the voice telling of our loss and attesting our
reverence for the dead has gone forth. It is on the records and will there remain
a lasting testimonial to his devotion as a Mason, and of our esteem for his manhood and his Masonic virtues.
But that this last tribute should be complete in itself for the information and
benefit of those who came afte1· us, we should not deem it necessary to repeat
what has been made known and placed on record in the official announcements of
his death: the story of his life-the details of his Masonic career, the work he has
don11-tbe services he has rendered. With this view we incorporate and make part
hereof:"The Masonic History of the deceued," is given to the brethren of the
Grand Jurisdiction by the M. •. W. ·. Grand Master in his official announcement
of his death, as follows :
Bro. FELLOWS was born at Topsam, Orange County, Vermont, April 3d,
. 1825, and passed to the Temple of Infinite on the Lords day, November 28,
1897, in this Uity of New Orleans, at the age of seventy-two years, seven· months
and twenty-five days.
We have seen that he was made a Mason on the 29th day of November 1849,being then just a little over twenty-four years of age-showing that practically,
the whole of his life's struggle and thi. whole of his life's work, from the years of
first manhood to the decline of his days, were accomplished under the inspiration
of M !\>Onie thought and the guidance of Masonic light
Of his services to Freemasonry it is not necessary to Sl!eak-the above record
tells its own story. Nothing less than a perfect devotion,-a sacrifice of ev~ry
other study or pursuit, could have yielded such results. The history of It is told,
therefore, when we say that his life, his appre<"iation ·of it< dignity, its loftiness
and mission were involved in his conception of tbe ·study and practice of the
principles of Freemasonry. He was skilled in the knowledge of its' laws, profound in the appreciation of its philosophy, exalted by his abiding faith in the
fundamental logic upon which it is erected-the belief in God and the immortality
of the soul.
His Masonic writings, mainly consisting of his work as chairman of the
Committee on Correspondence, are full of the true spirit of Masonry. A Mason
born, truly made in the heart ere ever that friendly and brotherly grasp welcomed
him as an actual brother-to him the great faith in the brotherhood of man was a
practical reality.
We abstain from mere eulogy of words, and expre~aions of grief and sorrow pale
in the presence of that which is both inexplicable and inevitable. It is ordained that
"All who Jive must diePassing through nature to eternity."
His distinguished personality and his earnest presence are impressed in our
hearts. Though forever gone from our sight, we shall long seem to see him
before us-urgin~ the ,good of the Fraternity, upholding the integrity of Freemasonry, expounding its humanity, expostulating against error, defending the
truth.
Bowing in humble submission to tbe divine ordinance which has removed him
from our midst-let W. remember that the miBBion of our human existence is to
come nearer God. Upward is the hope and the struggle, to cast sin off and vice
and degrading passions and attain the Joftinf;BB of the true, the pure, and the
beautiful. In that struggle the memory of the good and the beautiful of those who
have gone before us lights up our hope and guides i1:1 the difficult ascent.
For that let the record be made, let the living sanctify the dead and be themsdvea exalted in the consecration.
Let him who has so let his light shine before mnn as to glorify God be forever a
leBSon and example.

This report is probably awaited with interest by a greater number of Masons than
any other issued. Bro. DBUXMOND's position lo Masonry was not acquired by his

tflotoria-tbe reports forming a book of almost three hundred pages.

ldhere to their go·as-you·please rule, a large number have appreciated the situation
and been willlo1t to modify their laws to seoure the harmony of the Craft.

of the jurisdiction in which he i• rejected, and this ha~ met uoexpect.ed favor. While
we may believe that in many jurisdictions the time during which the effect of a rejection continues Is too short for the good of the Craft, still, if the status of rejected

lighting and ventilation, the expense of which will be, in round numbers, about
$70,000.

izatioos comprising 40,000 Master Masons, 13,000 Royal Arch Masons and 5000 Royal
and Select Masters, and then as 11 surprise presents a paper or 300 pages reviewing
fifty-eight Grand Bodies embr...:ing the Masonic world. That the report is a good

Bro, C0Nov11:B'S notice of California is of the administration of Grand Master
PBEBTON, whose recommendations and opinions be la in harmony with. He quotes
the Addre88 fully concerning the condition of the jorisdictioo, statistics referring to
Boards of Relief and Masonic Homes, and hie supervision ot the work.
He notices the a88ef!8ment per capita of twenty.five cents upon the membership
for the Representative Food, and says it nearly equals the entire per capita tax of
Michigan for all purposes.
Troe, Bro. CONOVER, bot then our Representative Fond accomplishes the object
for which it was created, viz: to insure the representation ot small Lodges at the
Annual Communication of Grand Lodge. Territorially considered , we have an im·
meose State; the smallest Lodges are always located at places most remote from the
place of meeting of Grand Lodge. The Reprel!'lntative Food iosores their representation by the allowance of the actual expense of the 'ransportation of one person by
the nearest route to the place of meeting. Ot' course, the fund is a tax upon the
larger or city Lodges for the benefit of the generally poorer or smaller ones-for
exampleOalifornia Lodge, located at the place of meeting of Grand Lodge, pays into the
Representative Fund this year $119 and draws nothing, while Lodge No. 248 pays in
$5 and draws $57, Lodge No. 287 pays $6.50 and draws $62. The measure also acts
as an incentive for tbe prompt payment of dnee, as no Lodge that baa not made re·
turns and paid its dues can receive the benefit of the Representative Fond.
Bro. CONOVER bas a good word for the Eastern Star folks, and advises us " to
declare our intentions" and see bow it is ourselves.

MISSOURI.
The Grand Lodge of Mil!Bouri held its seventy-l!Elventh Annual Communication
in tha city of St. Louis, October 19, 1897,-M.'. W.'. DoBSll:Y A. J.AMIBON, Grand
Master; R.-. W.'. JOHN D. VINOIL, Grand Secretary. Chartered Lodges, five
hundred and fifty-six; 31,000 Master Mason•. Three hundred and twelve chartered Lodges and one U. D. were represented, with ten other Grand Jrrisdiotions,
California not included. Seventeen Past Grand Masters were in attendance •.
A portrait of Grand Master JAMISON appears on the opening page.
Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with praver by the Grand Chaplain,
and music by the" Singing Section" of Erwin Lodge, No. 121.
Grand Master JAMISON appointed the committees and then delivered his
Address. He referred to the organization of Grand Lodge in 1821, and that during
the seventy-six years of its existence it had kept pace with and materially aided
civilization in its wonderful progreBB in the western country. He said:We must recognize that He, in whom w~, as ¥asons\ put our t~ust, has been
our guide in the past, and we confidentlr believe will contmue to be ID the future,
so long as we live up to the teachings of Freemasonry and His revealed law.
He granted five dispensations for the formation of new Lod1tes, and caused the
arrest of four charters for failure to comply with the law.
The Grand Master visitP.d officially forty Lodges in various parts of the jurisdiction.
Taking up the subject of Mexican Masonry, the Grand Master says:-

717

<hand Lodge of OaJ,if<>rnW..

1898.]

With the aim of arriving at a proper conolusion as to the merita of their cause
and as to whether they 11ire entitled to the desired recognition, I bave given much
thought to the subject; have read much that has been written pro an ii C<Yn by those
who are considered among our ablest Masonic students, and have conversed with
eeveral prominent Masons who have visited and sat in Lodges which held chartel'I!
from the Gran Dieta.
He recites these points in the history of the Gran Dieta.

He says :-

. It cannot be denied that the Gran Dieta, for several years subsequent to 1890,
permitted and did acts that were irregular and contrary to the ancient charges and
?egulations and contrary to the teachings, usages and customs of the Grand Lodges
of the United States of America. It issued charters to and permitted women to
be initiated and become members of Lodges. It did not require the Bible to be
placed upon the altar, yet at no time did it prohibit it from being placed thererm,
Becoming convinood, however, of the error of its ways, it in 1895 and 1896 took
radical measures to remedy these errors and mistakes.
Article 539 of the Statutes of 1895 provides that there shall be a Holy Bible on
the altar.
From the best information at hand, it appears tbat the said Gran Dieta,
since tbe adof.tion of said Constitution and Statutes, has lived up to the requirements thereo , and has compelled the subordinate Lodges to do likewise, and has
aince then been makh1g its ritual similar in all essential respects to that of the
Grand Lod~es of the United States of America.
If our brethren of Mexico have been guilty of irregularities and errors, should
we not overlook them, if we are satisfied that they have corrected them and are
now Jiving up to the true principles of Freemuonry!

In conclusion, he si.ys :Much has been said ..nd ";\'rit~n upon the subject during the last three VP.Are,
•nd in many instances some of the brethren have drifted into personalities, and
have in that way drifted from the real issuee in tbe case. I trust that in determining this matter the brethren will lay aside all bias and prejudice, and endMvor to
considP.r the caae upon its merits, and do justice to our brethren of our sister
Republic. From the consideration which I have given to the matter, I feel constrained to recommend that this Grand Lodge recognize and establish fraternal
relations with said Gran Dieta Simbolica. But in order that this question may
be duly considere<i before final action is taken thereon, I further recommend that
it be referred to a special committee of five members to fully consider the matter
and report thereon.
The committee was appointed and r•ported as follows :Your committee appointed to investigate the matter of Mexican Masonry,
*'fapectfully ask leave, in view of the import:1nce of the question, that the committlee be granted until the next meeting of Grand Lodge to report.
And Grand Lodge so ordered.

by reason of there not being sufficient room to comforts.hly_ accommodate those who
had been admitted and were seekilllt admission into the Home.

mcrea.sed about seventy-four cots. It has all the modem improvements and appliances, so that the members of the Home will be fa.r more comfortable than tbev

The Grand Lodge of Nebraska held its fortieth Annual Communication in the
city of Lincoln, June 16, 1897,-Jl.·. W.·. VHABLES J. PH&LPS, Grand Master;
R.-. W.·. W11r. R. Bow.111N, Grand Secretary. Two hundred and twenty-eight
chertered Lodges; 11, 763 Master Masons. Two huudred and twenty-one Lodges

Brn. DAVID M. MolLHINNEY of Hastings, Nineteen Paet Grand Masters were in

A Lodge of Master Masons was opened in Ample Form, as required by the law
of Nebraska. It being then ascertained by roll call that a constitutional number
i>f Lodgee was represe11ted, the Grand Master declared Grand Ledge open for the
transaction of businl!llll, and proclamation thereof was made by the Grand Marshal.
The Grand Master delivered his Addre88. He extP.nded to all a fraternal
greeting and congratulated Grand Lodge upon being permitted to a88emble in its
fortieth Annual Communication under conditions favorable to all as men and as

722

Proceedi.'tuJB of the

[Oct: 11,

1898.]

. Masons. After a philosophical essay upon the political and religious conditions of
the world, from the Turkish cruelties in Armenia to the Spanish persecutions in
Cuba, he rdports with satisfaction the "good news," that in their own Nebraska
"abundan~ rains and bounteous crops crowned the labors of the husbandmen in
the year last past, and now in early summer presents a beauty of landscape,
abounding in luxurious foliage and growing crops which is altogether gratifying to
the eye and pride of her citizens," and Freemasonry shares in the general prosperity.
In presenting the death roll of the year, upon which are inscribed the names of
one hundred and seventeen brethren, he paid fraternal tribute to the memory of
Past Grand Master GEORGE ARMSTRONG, a veteran Mason and soldier, and the
first Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Nebraska ; also Bro. UHARLES W.
HAMILTON, Grand Senio1· Deacon at the organization of Grand Lodj!'0, and subsequently Grand Junior Warden. He recommended suitable action by Grand Lodge
in remembrance of their useful Ii ves.
He reported forty-one decisions and says, but for the fact that our law seems to
require it, I should deem it unneoessary to report all the decisions that I have been
called upon to make, for Mme of them are no more than transcripts of former decisions and of the law bound in our code. With few exceptions the decisions were
approved by the Committee on Jurisprudence. Decision 36 was" that the fact that
a man is a bookkeeper for a brewery association does not bar him from being made
·a Mason."
Tbe Committee on Jurisprudence disapproved, by which they virtually say "a
bookkeeper for a brewing aasociation may never become a Mason in Nebraska."
Wby not amend the obligation to include bookkeepers with the other prescribed
people and make it strong.
Grand Master PHELPS reported that, by virtue of his prerogative, and following
· the example of the Grand Master of Pennsyl~ania, he had made his son a Mason
at sight, and that said son is now a member of Acacia Lodge, No. 34.
The Committee on Jurisprudence had the matter under consideration, and their
report was adopted by Grand Lodge, as follows :Your Committee on Jurisprndence be!{ leave to report that we have bad under
consideration the matter of making HARBY E. PHELPS a Mason, as reported in
the AddreM of the Grand Master. "Without entering into a discussion of the
question of whether or not the preroiiative of making Masons at sight ever inhered in the office of Grand Master, we are of the opinion that, by reason of our
situation and Masonic traditions, such prerogative does not inhere in the office of
Grand Master in Nebraska. We therefore disapprove the action of the Grand
Master in making his son, HARBY E. PHELPS, a Mason at eight, as reported in his
Address. The Grand Master is the creature of the Constitution of this Grand
_Lodge, and his prerogatives are defined and limited thereby."

We quote the first few lines of this interesting recital, illustrated by colored
maps 1, 2 and 3 as specimens of this "historical summary" or "abstract of title"
to the property now known as the New Jersey "-Home."
Situate at the southwest corner of the intersection of the Oxmead road with the
road from Burlirtgton to Jacksonville, in the township and county of Burlington,
and 8tate of New Jersey, as described in a deed from GEoBGE FoBTMEYER, et ux,
et al, to the Grand Lodge of the ancient and honorable society of Free add Accepted Masons of the State of New .Jersey, bearing date January 17, 1898, and
recorded in book No. 332, page 136, etc., in the Clerk's office of Burlington County,
at Mount Holly.
This tract lies upon and forms part of two original surveys, one made to
THOMAS WBIGHT, October 15, 1683, and marked with green bordered lines on map
No. 1, appended hereto, and the other made to DANIEL LEEDS, April 16, 1694, and
marked with red bordered lines on the map aforedllid, the title to which surveys
is briefty shown as follows : England claimed sovereignty over part of America, embracing New Jersey, by
virtue of the commission granted by King HKNR\' VII, in 1496 to JOHN CABOT
and his three sons, authorizing them to sail in search of new land for annexation
to that kingdom. This resulted during the following year, 1497, in the voyage of
John and Sebastian Cabot, who formally took poBSession of a iarge territory,
embracing New Jersey, in the name of the English crown, and so on down through

preroa-ative to make Masons by looking at them, down to the right of a Lodge to
instruct its Representative upon any pending proposition.
Constitutional government has no friends in the Masonic organization of New
Jersey.
Grand Lodge ordered a large portrait of the retiring Grand Master prepared,
and that he he presented with a Past Grand Master's jewel, in token of its appreciation of his faithful service.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
Bro. GEORGE B. EDWARDS, Chairman of Correspondence, submits, as W!ual, a
first rate Report on Correspondence well worthy a place in this unusually brilliant
number of this New Jersey journal. Bro. EDWARDS reviews sixty-one Grand
Masonic Bodies in his report, and does it thoroughly in a paper of one hundred
and fifty-six pages. He admires the Address of Grand Master PRESTON, and gives
hie approval to the general routine legislation; but he dissents, with emphasis,
when this Correspondent is dispo!Wd to ridicule the pretensions of a Grand Master
who would preoume, in the exercise of his royal prerogative, to make a Mason at
light. He quotes our opinion of the humbu&', and, by way of comment, says:-

When 'California passed a law restraining its Grand Master from makiiw •
l\faeon at sight, it gave significant testimony as to the existence of the prerogative
inherent to the office of Grand Master.
We do not think your oonelusion warranted by the facts in the case referred
to, Bro. EDWARDS. The attention of Grand Lodge was undoubtedly called to the
exercise of this assumed prerogative by the unlawful, unmaeonic and corrupt acts
of tb,e then Gr11nd Master, when he, admitting the truth of the charges, fell back
upon his "prerogaiive," that though hie acts tended to evil he could do no wrong;
that as Grand Master he was superior to all Masonic authority; that his will was
above all law, and that he to himself alone was accountable.
The oommittee. considering the l)hargea in their report, said :We think the Graud Master should possess no prerogative, the full exerch!e of
which is wrong; and they cannot believe that ~he spirit and genius of Freemf18oary
evj!r iAtended that be should possess an_y such prerogative. Neither cr,n thej
believe that in electing a brother to the office of Grand Master, we abeolve him
fr91D all or from any of his Maaonic obliKations, or from the proper consequences
of their reckless and wanton violation. They cannot believe that in electing him
we elevate him to a pinnacle so lofty that he cannot be reached ; that we have tbe
right or power to place him in a position thll.t enables him to scorn, wit la impuuitv,
the principles and laws of the Fraternity, and trample under foot our time-honored
Institution. In assuming his office, the Grand Master is obligated to support and
enforce our Constitution and laws, and the dignity of the station should render
him, if po!!l!ible, far more observant of such obligations than other brethren, and
far more responsible for their violation. It is, perhaps, owing to this fact that no
written law exists to govern this case.
We can be guided only by preoedente, and as no ease like this has before
occurred, we have not even a precedent for our guide. Indeed, it seems never to
have been imagined that a brother could by any mean~ reach the elevated place
of Grand Master who was capable of forfeiting Masonic confidence by unmasonic
deeds. The ancient Romans bad no law by which to punish fratricide, they not
supposing it possible that a man could be so vile as to commit a crime so terrible.
But when a case occurred a law was made for the occasion ; and the committee
quote the General Regulations of the Grand. Lod!fe of England :Il the Grand MIWlter should abuse hie power and render himself unworthy of
the obedience of the Lrxiges, he shall be subjected to some DAW regulations, to be
dictated by the occasion; because hitherto the Ancient Fraternity have had no
reason to provide for an e¥ent which they have presumed would never happen.
But among the different opinions held by brethren well instructed in Masonio
knowledge they were most inftuenced by the opinion of Bro. ,JoHN QOINOY ADAMS
Fi.:LLOWB (recently deceased), as Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence
c.f the Grand Lodge of Louisiana, and the effect of his judgment found expr088fon
in Grand Lodge in these words : This Grand Lodge does not acknowledge the doctrine that a Grand MaAter may

powers except tho10 contained in the Constitution of Masom·y and those clearly

ln the metropolis the applicants for the degrees have been fairly numerous; and,
evidently, due cantion is observed In the Lodges to ensure that men -of s1erllog

excellence Is noticeable in the proceedings of the m~jority of the Lodges, and only
In a few isolated cases was It apparent that more care and application than were
evinced'were necessary to produce the requisite satisfactory standard of rroflciency.
I have noticed with pleasure the growing tendency to exchange fraterna visits. On
one occasion no less than three Lodges simultaneously visited a sister Lodge, aud
materially added to the attractiveness and enjoyment of the proceedings. I trnet
this custom will be zealonsiy cnltivated and the brethren enjoined to ·perform so
necessary a dnty.
In order to secure the fullest 111dvantage from visitations, it is desirable that they
should not be confined to flourishing Lodges, but that the etrong.ehonld, as frequently
as expedient, visit the weak and laognlshiog, and by their presence and assistance
induce the despairing remnant of a Lodge to strive for its restoration to life and vigor.
A struggling and disheartened Lodge, neglected and Jen to its fate, may very readily
become a source of danger to the Craft in its eagerness to gain members, and pose!·
bly qnestionable proceedings and methods may result If the fraternal critic is eon·
tinnally absent.
In the suburbs the same carefnl rontine and high standard that have hitherto
di8'ingulshed the Lodges are still observable, and it is extremely creditable that
some Lodges which have had no accession of new members for lengthy periods are
still flonrishing, harmonious and eangnioe as to the fntnre.

Although the work, as a whole, h88 been conducted eat!efactorily, yet in a considerable minority of cases improvement is greatly to be desired, and Masters should
strive to op bold the credit of their Lodges by careful work on their own part, by close
scrutiny of the Lodge's affairs, and by exhortation of their officers to higher ideals
and results.
Amongst the defects observed, I would mention the habit, noticeable with
Deacons, of whispering instead of speakiq audibly at the times they are expecte~
to instruct, and of prompting when lnstrnotion Is not required of them. The habit
of prompting is not confined to Deacons alone; many Past Masters, whose experi·
eoce should otherwise teach them, frequently cause a nervous man to p~r.pet~ate the
very fault from which they desire to deliver him, by too eagerly ant1c1patiug the
worker's necessity.
The duty of vouching Is often performed in a perfunctory manner; the bald statement by the Tyler that a visitor is vouched for. is accepted, where88 the voucher
eboold be declared and verified by the Junior War.den before admission is authorized. The Junior Warden, not the Tyler, is the arbiter.

Mexico, presented the following report, which was adopted by Grand l.odge :-

To the Grand Lodge of Ne1JJ York:On the 15th day of February, 1898, the United States battleship Maine, while ou
a friendly mission in the harbor or Havana, was deetroyd by an explosion, due, there
is painful reason to believe, to malign agency; two hundred and eixty·eix American
sallors, of whom eigbty·tbree were Freemasons, lost their lives.
As citizens of this great Republic, as memberR of a brotherhood whose aim It bas
ever been to cnltivate right, justice and good·will to all men, the members of the
Grand Lodge or the State of New York mourn over this appalling catastrophe, which
sent a thrill of horror through the entire civilized world. We deplore the cruel loRe
that has befallen our nation and onr brotherhood ; we declare onr deep sympathy
with those who have been most honored by the loss we have all sustained, and we
express to our brethren from other jurisdictions onr heartfelt thanks for the fraternal
condolence they have tendered us in the dark hour of our amiction.
To our sister Grand Lodge, the Grau Diets Simbolica of Mexico, we return our
special acknowledgments. Tbroorch Its Grand Master (M'.-. W.-. PoRPIBlO DIAZ,
th'l Preeiden\ of the Republic of Mexico), it bas omcially •eat to this Grand Lodge
the expression of its sorrow, becanee of the sad fate of many of our brethren and
fellow ~itizene. It bas announced to us that nil Lodges of its obedience in the Repablic of Mexico, pul'8aant tG the order of the Grand Master, have draped their
altars in monrnlog, to show their sympathy with us in this affiictiug calamity.
Lodges of 8orrow have been held by the Mexicau Freemasons in memory or oar
unfortunate brethren, and eloquent tributes to their worth have been pronoanced.
At these mourafnl solemnities were uttered words of friendship for the United
States that embody tlte foremost principles of onr beloved brotherhood, and manl ·
fest the universality of Masonry, for they show, by a common sorrow, distinctions of
speech, nationality, religion and political opinion, are obliterated in our great Fra·
teruity.

REPOBT ON CORBESPONDENCE.
Doctor and Bro. JoaN A.. COLLINS present.II another, and hie second, aouoal review of the MMonic world. Bro. COLLINS work is elaborate, to be kept within one
bundred pages.
Referring to the questions which seemingly attract the most attention in the
Grnod Lodg61l reviewed, he says:That of a time limit to jurisdiction over rejected candidates, as proposed by the
Grand Lodge of Ma.lne, bas been made a subject of discussion in almost every
American Grand Lodge, and of serious consideration. A minority hold to the doctrine of perpetual jurisdiction, but a great majority repudiate it entirely, and require only a short time limit of one or two · ears, and it is not oolikely that within a
few years there will be practically uniformity lo this respect.
The request for recognition by the Grnn Diets Simbolica of Mexico as a legitimate Masonic Body h81! perhaps elicited more heated controversy within the last
few years than any other single topic. The origin and the practice of the Gran
Dieta have been very thorongbly investigated, and the result of the ioqniry eo far is
to make the Grand Lodges very slow In according reco(tnitioo. This policy of delay
in taking the Gren Oleta into the sisterhood of Grand Lodges is not accepted as joet
or Masonic by a few Grand Juriedfctione, notably those of TexM, New York and

[Oct. 11,

Iowa, each of which has recognized the Mexican Grand Lodge as an independent
nod sovereign Grand Body. The general conBeosus of Grand Lodges, however, is
to " make baste slowly" in this matter and wait for developments.
On the snbject of Masonic Relief, the Wisconsin plan of uniformity bas been be-·
fore Grand Lodges for several years, and is generally declined because it is be.
lieved to be dangerous, unwise and not in accord with the teachings of Masonry.
But the Fraternity is now, as it always bas been, a ooit on the subject of extending
relief to the needy brother within her gates, and after be is gone, to his dependents,
There is no difference except as to the beei method of bestowing it. Some believe
that the beneficiaries should be cared for in a home, where there would be no sense
of receiving aim;, and where all the inmates could be officially attended to. Many
Grand Lodges. acting oo these views, have erected costly homes, and tbroogb their
agency are doing incalculable good.
The influence of the Oxford Orphan Asylum, under its earnest, faitliful and God.
fearing management, will be potent for good io the years to come, when the names
and memories of these good men and Masons who bethought them of this noble
wprk shall have faded from lhe minds of men, and shall nowhere be fonod exc/pt io
the record book of that Supreme Lodge where the Great Architect of the Uoivene
presides.

Grand Stewards and Grand Tyler, 'imd invested those officers, for which he received the thanks of Grand Lodge.

Most High upon the deliberations of the session, he announced the death of

The condition of the jurisdiction was satisfactory. That the Grand Master
was competent to make the declaration, it is only necessary to say that he visited
personally ever.v Lodge in the jurisdiction and made a close and searching examination of the financial condition, and, as a close examination always discloses,
found a large amount of back dues owing. He says :-

1 hope the day is not far distant when this "innovation" of dut-s will be done
awa:v with altogethe~ . The Craft would be more united and harmonious, and there
would be no suspensions for non-payment-thid terrible insect which is eating our
very existence.
But this question will be asked, "If we do away with Lodge dues how a.re we
to meet our expenses?" H.,w? Why raise your fees. Masonry is altogether too
cheap. Retailing it out, as is too frequently done, is the whole cause of the trouble.
Cheap Masonry brings cheap material, and hence shoddy goods. Decay must follow. Let us hear from our able and distinguished writers a better remedy, if they
have one.
We believe, Most Worshipful, you have indicated the only "cure" for the
l!l"eatest evil we have to deal with in the Masonry of to-day. We have always
been an advocate of "maximum fees and minimum dues." Let the burthens fall
on the initiate rather than on the faithful worker.
Referring to the Maine resolutions concerning the "limiting of the effect of re"jections," the Committee on Constitutions and Regulations said: "That whilst
viewing with great respect the communication of our sister Grand Lodge regard·
ing the position of rejected candidates, we see no good reason why this Grand
Lodge should depart from the Constitution now in force in thie jurisdiction, which
we believe to be in strict accordance with ancient usage."
