Under the bead of "Conflict of Joriadiotioo" the Grand Master, In biB Addresa,
refers to four cases involving correspondence between himself and Grand Mastera of
other Grand J urisdictioos :These caaes call·atteotioo to the well known-fact that the same governmental
olicy does not prevail throughout all the Grand Jurisdictions. While Masonry,
n its character, conceptions and high purposes, is essentially the same the
world over, yet we mu•t not expect its administration to be the same so long
as the doctrine of Grand Lodge sovereignty prevails. The Grand Lodges,
although always agreeing opoo essentials, and ever remaining within the Ancient
Landmarks, will s~ill have dl.lferent_ideas, opioio~a and seot~meota about receiving
members, goveromg Lodges, making and enforcmg regulations, and kindred subjects, and they will, each for itself, adopt rnles, provide lawli, Issue orders, and
arrange plans to build np, maintain and extend the Fraternity within their respective
territories. And now, since there is no world-wide central authority to review these
laws, rules, orders and plans, and to mold them after oor pattern, ooitormity in these
things is impossible, even if desirable.
The only way it could be obtained would be by some general system of conference
and agreement among l\ll the Grllnd Lodges, adoµting and maintaining a plan with
all the oomerooa details modeled alike. Thia can moat probably never be accom·
plh>hed. Difference in laogol\ge, literature, laws and institutions, diversity in local
needs, sentiments and conditions, different degrees of education, civilization and
,hveloµmeot, render this not only difficult bot impossible.
J It cannot now, probably cannot ever, be aocomplisbed even by the Grand Lodges
of America.
Some of the cases referred to by the Grand Master relate to the ao-oalled doctrine
of perpetual jurisdiction-a rule that a candidate once rejected by a Lodge, no matter
why, is forever disqualified for Masonry, except by consent of such Lodge; no matter
where or how long he may reRide elsewhere; no matter bow wise, worthy, strong,
noble. manly, good and pure he may thereafter become. This rule enables a single
member of a Lodge, be he never so nowise or ooJoat, in a moment of anger or under
a temporary beat of petty personal grievance, either real or i111agin11.ry, or under a
mistaken belief based on idle gossip or untrue information, not only to oloae the
door of bis own Lodge llgaiaat the candidate, bot to drive him thence, and to place
a brand upon him, that be may wear it, like CAIN, throogboot life, no matter bow
long be may live, where be may go, nor how pure and noble be may be or thereafter
become. A minority of the American Grand Lodges adhere to this doctrine; the
others bold the doctrine of temporary jurisdiction-if we may nae this as a counter
expression.
Thia latter doctrine gives rise to the rule that a rejected candidate, who thereafter
removes into another jurisdiction, may, after be baa resided there a fixed period, and

r.

748

Pr~edim.ga of the

[Oct. 11,

•rt.er a definite time has expired since his rejection, properly apply to the Lodge in
whose jnrisdiction he resides for .Masonr.y, and that this Lodge is the sole jndge of
his fitness or unfl.tness; and that while his previous rejection should be carefully
investigated, yet the Lodge may reject or receive him, as it may determine, withont
let or hindrance from the Lodge previously rejecting him. Your committee believe
that this Is tbe best role, for it is oonsonant witb philosophy, philanthrophy and
human nature, and it reoognizes in man the po88ihility of growth, lmprove1'ent and
~
reformation.
Besides, which Lodge has the best ordinary opportunities to judge of the candi·
date's physical, mental and moral qualities, tne LOdge wlrere he resided years ago,
or the one where he now resides, and for a number of years last past haSoreeided?
Why should the latter appeal to the former for judgment? The candidate may have
been rejected years ago, either with or withontjuet cause, and some time before his
character had been formed as it is formed In after years. In the mean time he has
lived many lears within the Jurisdiction of another Lodge, and if the latter apply to
the former odge, the record discloses the candidate's rejection . The me.mbers do
not know or remember him ; they do not know who or how manv opposed him, or
why ; they only know he was rejected, and presume their Masonic fathers had good
reason for his rejection, and therefore refuse consent.
. The only wise, jnst and philanthropic rule, In the opinion of yonr committee, is
to let every State and every Lodge judge for itiielf of the fitness or unfitness for
Masonry of those who have resided within its territory a snfficient time to enable
their merits or demerits to be known. ludeed , no other rule can be fairly, uniformly
and satisfactorily enforced or even enforced at all against Lodges of another Grand
J urisdictioo.
This Gra11d Lodge once entertained the view of perpetnal jurisdiction, and found
itself often embarrassed and entangled with other Grand Anthorlty, until it amended
Section 18 of its Code, since which time it has upheld the other role.
Bot the Address of the Grand Master presents to ns the query, whether we should
not at times depart from our own law, out of comity and courteous consideration
for the laws of other Grand Lodges on this subject. Your committee think not. If
a question on this point arises between one ol' our Lodges and a Lodge .of another
Grand Jurisdiction, we must either follow our own law, or, setting it aside, follow the
foreign law. There would be no dignity, self-respect or justice in the latter course.
It i~ a maxim in government that a law enacted by one principality or power can
have no extra tel'l'itorial etleci. It wonld be wrong, not to say insolent, for this
Grand Lodge to insist that some other Grand Lodge, in violation or disregard of its
own laws, should follow our law in its application to one of itii Lodges or members,
or woo Id-be members, simply because he once residecl within our territory and once
vainly songht admls•ion to our membership. Besides, it would be impracticable to
attempt to apply the law of another Grand Jurisdiction to one seeking initiation or
preferment in one of our Lodges. Buch a course would require the subordinat4'
Lodge to overlook our own Constitution, Code and Laws, and to become a student
of the jorisprndenoe of a foreign and· sister Grand Lodge. It Is hard enough for our
Lodge officers to understand our own Jaws; and if we required more, it would involve the Grand :Master and Grand Lodge in endless and froltle88 difficnlties to e;r:plain and enlighten them on the laws of other Grand Lodges. Then, if this plan
could be soccessfol!y carried out. oor system of government would become as varied
and checkered as the Autumn foliage, and we would introduce within one jurisdiction, and that one our own, all the discord which exists, not in one, but among a.II
the others.
We think we need add nothing fnrth er In regard to the Pennsylvania case referred to by the 'Grand Master. With feelings of regard and veneraiion for that
jurisdiction, we think ii has no cause of complaint.

TENNESSEE.
The Grand Lodge of Tennessee held its eighty-fourth Annual Communication In
the city of Nashville, January 26, 1898,-M.·. lV.·. A. N. SLOAN, Grand Master;
B.'. W.-. JOHN B. GABRBTT, Grand Secretary. Four bnndred and twenty-nine
Lodges; 17,088 Master Ma~ons. Four hnndred and nine chartered Lodges were represented, with six under dispensalion. Sixteen Past Grand Masters, one Past Deputy
Grand Master and two Past Grand Wardens were in attendance.
An elegant steel portrait of the Grand Master elect, M.-. W.'. W1LLiil! B. BuHPAB, appears on •he opening page of the jonrnal.
Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with prayer by the Grand Chaplain,
and the Grand Master delivered his Address.
The Grand Master bad been visited by a serious misfortune. He said:The report of my year's work as your Grand Master is incomplete, and must ever
remain so, from the fact that on April 3, 1897, my office and ite entire contents were
destroyed by fire. Not a vestige was saved. All records and papers pertaining to
the office of Grand Master, as well as the jewel and apron, were losi. Also my personal records ot' a lifetime, together with a large number of Masonic and other vain·
able books. To me it was not only a heavy loea, bot a very great inconvenience
I attempted to duplicate correspondence pertaining to the Grand Master's office,
bnt with little success. My report must, therefore, be Incomplete.
No deaths among the Grand or Paet Grand Officers had occurred during the past
year, although many faithful brethrel) had answered the dread summons.
Grand Master SLOAN Is one of the three custodians of the work in Tennessee.
He believes the Widows' and Orphans' Home "the great charity" which demands the attention of every Mason in Tennessee, and pleads earnestly for its maintenance and ample support.
The work was exemplified, under the direction of the Board of Custodians, dur.
ing the evenings of the session.
The Tennessee Centennial induced many brethren to visit the city from afar, and
Grand Secretary GABBETT acknowledges calls from disUnguished members of the
Fraternity during the continuance of the Exposition, among others the venerable
POWKR, of .Mississippi, MKLLISH, of Ohio, Dr. RoBBINB, of Illinois, H:&NDEI180N, of
Pennsylvania, E10eBAUH, of the same State, nod Gov. ATKlNBON, of West Virginia.
Grand Lodge extended its cordial greetings to Its Senior Past Grand Master,
M.'. W.·. Bro. A. M. 8UGHER, Grand Master during the years 1802-3 and 1863, and
now in his eighty-sixth year. He desired to attend the present session, but the infirmities of age prevented, The Grand Lodge recognizes bis lifelong devotion to
Freemasonry, his attachment to its principles and his earnest efforts for its best in·
terests.

The Depnty Grand Master reported a nnmber of Lodges constituted, and hie official acts of discipline, decisions and ceremonials, from which it appears the .Depnty
Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Texas has "fish of his own to fry'' besides
waiting for the absence of the Most Worsbipfal from the jurisdiction.
Grand Lodge, after recapitulating Lhe action of 1892-3, referring to the " liquor
question," said:WBEBBAB, The time bas folly come to relieve the snbordinate Lodges of the animosities and retaliations so often engendered by being compellell to reject by ballot
applicants engaged in the Jiqnor traffic ; and inasmnch as a large number of other
Grand Jurisdictions have already taken in snbstance the same action; therefore be it
Resolvea, 1. That hereafter persons engaged in the manufactnre or sale, at
wholesale or retail, of intoxicating liqnors, shall be Ineligible to receive the degrees
of Masonry or to affiliate with Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction.
2. That it shall be unlawful for any Mason.in this Grand Jurisdiction, not in said
business, to hereafter engage in the ~ame.
The above. the majority report, was adopted by the Grand Lodge. The minority
report was as follows:A minority of your special commiitee, to whom was submitted the resolntion of
Bro. S. M. 'l'EMPLKTON, proposing a new quallftcation for membership in onr Order,
not being able to agree with a majority of the committee, and believing the pro·
posed legislation nuconstitntional nnd inexpedient, feel constrained to submit this
minority report. In onr opinion, the ancient tests, which have stood unchanged
d11ring the centuries that Masonry has existed, are amply secnre and satisfactory;
and having been incorporated into our fundamental law, cannot be changed witbont
destroying a landmark and violating the Grand Lodge Oonstitntion. We think that
(snbject to the Constitution and Ancient Landmarks) the subordinate Lodges and
indlvidnals also should be let\ undistnrbed In the right to decide whom they shall
elect to membership. We, iherefore, recommend tliat the resolntions do not pass.
As before stated, the majority report was adopted. Who will forteil the next
innovation ?

Procudinga of the

Ami jnst here I woold call attention 1o the too common error of re-electing the
same person :Master of a Lodge for a numbe.r of years in sooceBBlou. In mv jildg·
ment this is the most frnitfnl soorce of apathy and want of interest amongst the
members. While *he young members of a Lodge naturally shrink from taking
opon themselves the labors and reRponslbilities of office, and especially that of
Worshipful Master, yet there is also. a natnral and laodablA ambition in every ma.nly
bosom to attain to that distinction, and to be honored by snob ao expression of t.be
confidence and esteem of their brethren, and these sboold be encouraged, and, if need
be, forced into office by those who have pa.seed through the chairs. To do this the
Master, after serving one or two terms, shonld peremptorily refuse re-election, and
thus compel the Lodge to take up some of these brethren and force them to bear the
honors they secretly desire, but are too modest or timid to acknowledge the fact.

REPORT ON OoBBEBPONDENCE.
Bro. KUYKENDALL presents a report full of meat, and well @easoned, He must
have his shot at the Representative system, and selects a proper cnse to exemplify
his side of the question. He finds it In the following, under Arizona. He quotes:The time set for the reception of Grand Representatives, the record says, " they
were introdnced and received with the Grand Honors. " Upon examination we find
fifteen reported as present at opening of session : the Grand Master, Depoty Grand
Master, Senior Grand Warden, Junior Grand Warden, Grand Treasurer, Grand Sec·
retary, Grand Lecturer, Senior Grand Deacon, and the pro tem. Grand Oratol', Grand
Pursuivanl and Grand Organist, constitnting eleven of the fifteen. The record does
not explain the mode of introduction. From the expression "received with the
Grand Honors," it would be reasonably inferred that the whole number wa@ lined
up outside, then introduced to the inner chamber and the court as Ambassadors
Extraordinary and Ministers Plenipotentiary ; but we are met with the solemn fact
that there was no court to receive them. Then the Grand Master, In a speech of
welcome, " addressed himself" and the other officers of the Grand Lodge as
"Brethren of the Diplomatic Corps," 11dding: "It would hava been sad, indeed, if,
d nring the year now clo•ing, either or any of yoo should have found it necessary to
ask for yonr passports, or that it shonld have become necessary for us to present
you with the same."
Bro. KUYKENDALL. adds:As a joke and a farce it may be well enough for those wbo enjoy such perform·
ances to 11:0 tbrou11:h with the same annually, as that isaboot all there is to tbe system.
We say all this whilst holding the highest respect for the Grand Master and Grand
Lodge of Arizona.
The joke is a good one, Bro. KUYKENDALL ; but ~imply proves the role t.hat it's
unfair to judge any system by an exception.
Under Uolorado, discussing the Maine resolutions to limit the effect of rejection&,
Bro. KUYKENDALL very pertinently remarks :Now, perpetual jurisdiction over rejected material is either all right or all wrong.
If right, Just and io keeping with Masonic law and general principles of Masonry,
then the attempt to limit the same to any specifien time is and woold be illegal and
wrong. If wrong, and baA no fundamental law backing it, then all should do away
with it.

brother fallen into poverty and decay, bot of none else; but every particnlar Lodge
shall dispose of their own charity for poor brethren according to their own by-laws,

io order to make a common stock or it for the more handsome relief of poor brethren.
This looks to ns as though the four London Lodges that then composed the
Grand Lodge of England bad and meant to express the idea that not only the constituent Lodges, but, as well, the Grand Lodge, bad a duty to perform towards "trne
brethren fallen Into poverty and decay;" that a J,odge ooold dispense charity more
efficiently than its individoal members, and that the Grand Lodge conld dispense it
more efficiently than its constitneots-that is, that every Lodge ahonld have a fund
for the relief of those in need, and it could, through a proper committee, much more
readily and certainly than its individnal members, determine the necesiities of the
applicant and the character and extent of the relief that onght to be given.
It is trne that the rlnty of a Lodge to care for its own members, when they need
CBl'e, is not expressly declared in the Ancient Charges or the Old Regulations, bot
seems to have been so patent and so recognized as to need no expression in words,
and we think it follows as a necessary corollary from what is said.
In 1883, on this same snbject, our committee said:The dnty or the Lodge is to its members and to their families, withont regard to
their place of residence; and the fact that one of its memberR, or the widow or a
deceased member, has removed to some 'place beyond its territorial jnrisdiction,
does not absolve the Lodge from the performance of this well-known and necessary
dnty.
If a member of a Lodge in Caliloroiashonld visit Florida or England and be taken
sick and die, we should expect the Lodge in whose jurisdiction be might happen to
be, would, if he needed assist11nce and bis condition was known, give snch assistance
as he might reasonably reqnire in sickness, and bury him decently, and we
should expect that this Lodge here wonld properly repay the amonot so expended
and that, if it were unable to do so, this Grand Lodge would come to its aid and
make the repayment. Jt baa never yet failed to recognize snch an obligation, and,
we trust, never will.
Some of our brethren of other jnrisdictlons tell ns, "true, yon relieved the distress of a member of our family, but yon were bound by yonr tennre to do that, and
to do It without hope or expectation of reward or reimbursement, and to do it so
on ostentatiously and qnietly that even the left hand shoo Id not be ad vised of the
kindly act done by the right." That kind of instrnction sonnds well, bot is not, under
the ciri:umstances, at all satisfactory, because we have a very distinct belief that
every Mw;onic family ought to exercise some care over all its members and make
·
some provision to protect and care for snch as need care and protection.
We do not think that the whole duty of a Lodge consists in making Masons and
using them so long as they are healthy and strong, and turning them adrift when by
sickness or misfortnne they are no longer able to care for themselves. Oases have
been brcmght to our attention where a Lodge has furnished to one of its owo mem·
bers, who was sick and poor and absolutely needed assistance to provide the necessaries of life, funds sufficient to transport him to another jnrisdlction, and then left
him to the care of strangers. A Lodge is an organized society, and we insist that
one of the first and most importan.t pnrposes ol its organization is that it shall pro·
tect and relieve its own members when they need protection or relief, and that,
except nnder extraordinary clrcnmstances, it is false to its trnst when it fails to do its
dnty in that regard, and that when another Lodge in the same or another Grand Jnr-

The severest criticisms of Mexican Masonry emanate from one who claimed to
be, and doobtlesa wae, the ·worshipfol Master of Toltec Lodge, No. 520, at the Ofty
of Mexico. Including the documents mentioned by the Grand Master, Tolteo Lodge
was chartered in 1882 by the Grand Lodge of .Missoori, with the consent of the then
existing Grand Bodies of Mexican Masonry, and wae composed in the name of
Americans residing in Mexico. From facts in possession of yonr committee we are
fully warranted in saying that these criticisms were not inspired so mnch by a zeal
for .Masonry as by a desire to retain the charter of their Lodge and the prestige of
their position as the only Masonic Lodge in Mexico with an American charter. All
of these criticiams have been ably- met and fully answered by the Gran Dieta, and
the regularity of the work of the Mexican Lodges is also folly attested by well·
informed brethren of this jurisdiction who have recently visited the City or Mexico.
We would not be onderstood a• intending ia this report to dignify with any
attempted reply the varioas pamphlets, letters, circulars, etc., emanating from the
above mentioned indivldnal, and which have been scattered broadcast ove'r the land,
for we regard theee pablicatioas as the oataral resalt of chagrin on the part of their
author, aad so befog, we do not believe they caa properly come before this Grand
Lodge tor notice, and they are only referred to here (and by our Grand Master, we
&11snme,) because they have been very generally circulated among the American
Grand Lodges, aad have, we think, been accorded more notice than they deserved.
Having recognized the Gran Oleta, and aow holding fraternal correspoatlence
with that Grand Body, the Grand Lodge of Texas does aot propose to take notice of
strictares apoa itself and apon the Gran Oleta by individual Masons or lndividaal
Lodges, .eapecially when soch strictures are coached ia terms, to say tho very least,
too disconrteoas for :M.asoaic discussion, and more especially so since these strictures
are aot warranted by the facts.
At its recent Aaauaf Oommunicatioa the GraaJ Lodge of .Missouri instructed its
Grand Master to take proper steps to withdraw the charter of Toltec Lodge, No. 520,
and this prompt, very proper and eminently Masonic act of the Grand l.odge of
Missouri will doubtless end all disputes in this matter, and leave .Mexican Masonry
in the full and indisputable control of its own alfairs, and the Grand Lodge of Texas
heartily approves . this action of the Grand Lodge of Missouri, and extends to the
Gran Oleta of Mexico most cordial greetings and fraternal congratulations thereupon.
In the proceedings of the last Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Missouri, embodied lo the Grand Master's Address, is an extended accoootof Mexillao
.Masonry, in which allosioo is made to the coarse of that Grllnd Lodge in annulling
the authority granted to Tolteo J,odge, No. 520, located lo Mexico and under its Joris·
diction, and adtiising that acharterbeallOt>pledfrom the f:kan Dieta Simbolica. The
Grand Master, M.·. w.·. DORSEY A. JAHISON, seye :It has been and is contended by many prominent Muons, that the actions of oar
Grand Lodge in regard to Tolteo Lodge, constitute a tacit recognition by this Grand
Lodge of tho Gran Dieta Simbolico of Mexico. · Be that as It may, much light has
been thrown on this subject since 189~. Io my opinion, the time has arrived when
this Grand Lodge should come oat squarely and unequivocally and either recogr.ize
or refuse to recognize the Gran Dieta Simbollca or Mexico.
.Mu\Jh has been aaid· and written upon this subject during the last three years, and
In many instances some of the brethren have drifted into personalities, and have in
'bat way drifted from the real issues in the case. I trust that in determining this
matter the brethren will lay R~fde all bias and prejudice, and ·endeavor to consider
the case opoo its merits and do justice to our brethr~o lo our sister Republic. From
the consideration which I have given to the matter, I feel constrained to recommend
tbat this Grand Lodge recognize and eatablish fraternal relations with said Gran
Diet& Simbolica. But in order that this question may be dnly considered before Onal
acti.o.o is taken thereon, I further recommend that it be referred to a special com

of valued brethren. Worshipful Bro. JAMllB OGLESBY, wb.o for thirty·three yea.rs
past he.s guarded• the Grand Lodge from the approach of cowe.ns and eavesdroppers, B.·. w.·. Bro. GEORGE HINDS, Jr., Grand Warden in 1882, e.nd FRANCIS

seen of men no more forever.

age.in alarmed by the passage of our old friend e.nd brother, Pe.st Senior Grand

We tree.sure his memory and commend his spirit to God who gave it.

Phami,x Lodge, No.178, was born io New York io the year 1800; made a. Mason lo

All great results have begun in struggle-at most times against the con·
sent of the majority-for the world, usually indisposed to listen to progressive ideas, will turn its face to the suirgeetion that as time goes on the
oondition of man might improve. And our noble structure which we consecrate to-day, a.midst the benisons of 20,000 Masons, is an exception to the

motives which every Ma.eon places before himself, and permits him to execute
the mandates of his Craft, not only in obedience to those who command him,
bot with willing sacrifice, because the Constitution which he obeys teaches

all who confess themselves by his name, unto all who are weary and heavily
la.den, unto a.ll who, themselves, are imbued with the love of God which
shines in the heart of man.
I said that we conclude to-day a chapter of struggle. I use not the word
inadvisedly. It ha.a been my privilege to watch the progress of this Institu·
tion from its very inception. I know all the difficulties with which it has
contended, and, whilst appreciating the wealth of love that has been lavished
upon it, I know also of some antagonism that it created. Those among us
felt it to be a bounden duty to. provide for the widow and the orphan. We
understood that that was an obligation resting upon the Master Mason-an
obligation that we were anxious to discharge. Those among us were yea.re
a.go ready to engage in labor tending to the discharge of that sacred duty.
We were met with the cry that the jurisdiction of California was. unable to
cope with the responsibilities that thus would be created. The objections
were made in good faith. They were made by true and worthy men who,
according to their own judgment, desired to eave the Order from the mistake
of going forward too rapidly. Too rapid progress oftentimes results in retro·
peeion. There are no mistakes so felt as the mistake of failure ih an enterprue held as essential and necessary to the welfare of the community.
But, on the other hand, those who advocated the erection of this structure,

a.nd the organization of this noble Inatitntion, felt that Masonry in.California,
being twenty thouaa.nd strong, was like an invincible army that would destroy

Masonry iu California. could achieve anything that it decided to un~ertake, pro.
vided that the undertaking was founded in reason and in jnstice, provided that
it appealed to the sense of charity and the sentiment of love of the brethren,
and provided that its essential character and its necessity could be ])roved to
satisfaction. Masonry in California, with a due regard to the noble precepts
of the Craft and to the lofty history of its founders, had finally come to
the conclusion that it owed the world a pledge of its sincerity, that the time
had come when all the eloquent proofs of hope and faith and charity and fra.
terna.l love should finally be made concrete, in an expression that should con.
vince the world that the foundations of Masonry were well and truly laid; that
this character of love and justioe and righteouantiss and charity was not the
mere lip service of the social organization, but was the absolute confession of
· faith of the whole band of men, who, through their own lives and through
the ties of love that were put into others, would convince the wodd that He
whom they acknowledged to be their Grand Master was indeed the God of
humanity, worshiped by them with equal fervor, if not with more, swinging
incense and bringing burnt offerings, the·sweet spirit of which rises heavenward, yet for those conditions among themselves through which they could
appreciate all the blessings of God among them. Thia, then, was the beginning, the expreBSion of the neceBSity to appear before the world with tangible
works of love and kindpess.
I believe that this sentiment was for years a.live in the Grand Lodge of California, until it culminated in the introduction of a number of resolutions in
the seBSion of 1890, the Most Worshipful MORRIS MARCH ESTEE being Grand
Master, and which resolutions tended to emphasize this sentiment, "that the
Grand Lodge recommends that there be established in its jnrisdiction a Home
for the intellectual, moral and physical culture of the children of deceased
Master Masons of the Sta.te of California and a temporary asylum for the sick
and indigent widows of such deceased Freemasons."
This sentiment, it appeared, did not find much favor among the brethren.
It was thought that, to combine a home for orphans with an institution that
partook of the characteristics of a hospital, the brethren would indeed assume
burdens which, in the end, would be found too heavy to bear. Eager a.nd
anxious as the majority proved at the time to express their Masonic sentiment
in some tangible manner or form, the plan proposed was not to their liking for
the reason stated above. And it is to be stated that the resolutions were defeated; but at the same time another committee was appointed to review the
whole matter and present a plan for organization at the next Grand ¥ge
seBSion.
During the year 1891 the matter of establishing a Home for widows and
orphans was thoroughly canvassed, and at the Gra.nd Lodge session of that
year new resolutions were introduced which resulted in t~e api:>0intment of
nine brethren to act as a committee to devise a plan for the organization and

The plan of organization was simple enough and pertained merely to the
form of organizing the Trustees. Of essential importance to this aasembly
are the seventh and eighth clauses of the first plan of organization, namely,
"that all property rights and all contributions of money shall pa.BS through
the hands of the Grand Secretary of this Grand Lodge, and that the Trustees
are to administer the affairs of the Home to the extent of the means contributed, without any power or authority to create any financial liability binding
on the Grand Lodge or a.ny subordinate Lodge."
These two sections of the original plan were designed to confirm for all
time to come the right and title of the Grand Lodge of California. in any property that the Home might acquire, and limited the powers of the Trustees to
those of a mere standing committee, which is strictly in a.ccorda.nce with the
Constitution of this Grand Lodge and conforming to all Masonic tradition and
Masonic law.
The first Boa.rd of Trustellll, as well as all others who came after, understood that they were simply an agency created by the Grand Lodge of California. for the purpose of carrying out the plans matured in the Grand Lodge
it.self; and the Boa.rd felt the necessity from the very start of surrounding the
Home with everj safeguard, so that its close connection-nay, its very identity
-with the Grand Lodge of California. could never be qn811tioned.
On October 11th, 1898, Bro. EDWARD MYERS PBEBTON, now Past Grand
Master, presiding, presented the report of the transactions of the Boa.rd, together with By-Laws and reports of the Secretary and Treasurer.
From the report of the Secretary it appeared that during the ten months
of its organization-that is to say, from December 10th, 1891, to October 10th,
1892-the subscriptions toward the contemplated Home had a.mounted to $44,.
759.50, the then Secretary reporting that a.BSurancea of further snbacriptions
were not lacking. And I submit, brethren, that this subscription of very
nearly $50,000 during the short space of ten months, in the year noted in
California·for financial depression, was one of the most remarkable as well as
the most eloquent evidences of the disposition of Masonry in California to do
its whole duty toward the widow and the orphan who would apply to them.
The Grand Lodge, with mnch applause, approved the action of Grand Master JoHNBTO.ll, confirming the Board in its position, and sending it on its way
to found the great charity, tile work of which is now actively commenced.
The Grand Lodge, as well as Masonry in general, owes a debt of gratitude
to ma.ny of the brethren represented on this first Board, some of whom have
now passed beyond the gate, to meet us a.gain in the realms beyond the skies.

by means of organizing the Masonic Fair. There were gathered a slorions host
of men and women, boys and girls, even children of all ages and cl1188es and
conditions, who welded together in a strong instrument of charity to achieve
a most glorious result. The reports which have been submitted to yon prove
that the net proceeds of the Fair were very nearly $40,000, and this sum, added
to the liberal endowment of the Grand Lodge, enabled the Trustees to push
the work 80 rapidly that, thanks be to God, we are able to consecrate it today. But· the Fair did more. Had it not been for it we would have been
compelled to content ourselves with the main building, in which accommodations for both widows and orphans would have been neceBSarily som11wha.t
cramped, if not inadequate; but the Fair enabled the Trustees to design this
very large and handsome addition, and to include in it the dormitory, which
was contemplated in the original design, so that, ladies and gentlemen, the
womanhood of California has really enabled Masonry to extend its usefulness.
Whereas the original plan contemplated merely a housing of widows and
orphans, we are enabled to say, definitely, that the poor brother, also, will be
welcome, and that the beneficent heart of Masonry beats for him as well as for
the widow and the orphan.
And so we atand here to-day, Most Worshipful Grand Master and brethren,
with the work of organization practically completed-the Home finished, its
doors open, and awaiting the call 'of tho~e who will need our protecting care.
It is meet, indeed, that before entering upon the second stage of the workthat is, the practical ca.re and maintenance of our wards, being a great and
important undertaking-we should first invoke the blessing of Him, without
whose aid no work can prosper, for be it understood, &nd let there be no miata.ke a.bout it, we are but at the beginning of the aecond chapter. We have
written up a glorious indication of a more glorious work, and its success or its
failure will depend entirely t>.pon us. Shall we build upon these noble foundations? Shall we emulate the eloquent traditions here established from the
noble precedent here witnessed, or shall we fall back upon laurels easily earned
and contemplate the joy of success that was won by the workers who were
engaged in it? Brethren, the Boa.rd of Trustees is still ready to go on with
the work, but it finally commits the enterprise to your loving care. May you

The Proceedings or the Gran Dieta Symholica of Mexico for 1897.

The question of the relation of this Grand Body with the Ma.sons of Mexico
has been _brou~ht before this Gr~nd Lodge at two different times pr\or to this
date. First m October, 1883, which matter was then examined into and
elaborately reported upon by the Committee on Jurisprudence, and which
report is found on page 691, volume XVII, of the Proceedings of this Grand
Lodge.
At that time the Grand Lodge of Mexico was known as the "Grand Lodge
of the Federal District of Mexico." In the discusaion of the matter as
presented to this Grand Body, the Committee on Jurisprudence rec~m­
mended the "recognition of the Grand Lodge of the Federal District of Mex·
ico," because the committee, upon a careful examination of its Constitution,
Statutes a.nd Proceedings, and the Proceedings of the Convention which established it, believed that it was regularly formed and that it had declared
and adopted the la.ndm&rks of Masonry as its fnndamenta.l law, and further
because it showed that it wa.s and gave promise that it would continue to be
"permanent and nseful."
The following resolution was then reported and adopted:-

R_esolved, That the Grand Lodge of California. recognizes the Gran Logia
de L~bres y ~ceptados Masonas de! Distrito l''ederel of the United States of
Mexico as a iust and !~gaily formed Grand Lodge, and cordially accepts its
proposal. for the establishment of friendly relations and an interchange of representatives.
This report, as before stated, is found in volume XVII of the Proceedings
of the Grand Lodge, on page 691.
The matter was again brought before this Grand Body in 1892. At tba.t
session of the Grand Lodge there was pl'etlE'nted by Bro. Ju AN C. FARBER, as
the representative of the Gran Symbolic Dieta of Mexico, which was another

from the unfinished business of the preceding Annual Communication, and
report as follows : Bro. JOHN D. GLIDDEN presented the following:-

Resolved, That any Master Ma.son in good standing in this Grand J urisdiction, who has been a. contributing member of any eubordinat.e Lodge therein for
twenty-five yea.re or more, may, at the request of two members in writing, and
by a. vote of three-fourths of the members present, at a. stated meeting of the
particular Lodge of which he is a member, be plaoed on the honorary list and
thereby relieved from a:ll Lodge dues theres.ft.er.: and that this Grand Lodge relieve the subordinate Lodge from the payment of Grand Lodge dues on such
members.
(Proceedings of 1897, p. 196.)
Your oommittee find several previous rulings on the proposition of creating
life membership by remitting the dues of members, among which are the following:At the Annual Communication of 1888 the Committee on Jurisprudence
reportt-d that if);uelsior Lodge, No. 166, adopt.ad a standing resolution to the
effect that any one of its members who had paid hie dues to the Lodge and
had maintained good standing therein for a period of twenty.five yea.re should
thereafter be exempt from the payment of dues.
The resolution was in direct conflict with the By-Laws of that Lodge,
which declares that " the 4ues of each member of the Lodge shall be one
dollar per month, payable quarterly in advance." The Grand Master very
properly declared thiA resolution void, as it is clear that no Lodge can amend,
repeal or nullify one of its by-laws by a standing resolution.
Your committee join with him in hie disapproval of the plan proposed by
that resolution, evt>n if it were lawful, and in his suggestion that the better
plan, if there be any good plan at all in regard to life membership, would be
to grant such exemption only upon the payment of a sum of money which the
Lodge shall judge to be at least. a fair equivalent for its monthly dues. (See
Vol. XVIII, p. 677.)
The foregoing decision, which was unanimously approved by the Grand
Lodge, clearly prohibi.ts any subordinate Lodge from creating life memberships by resolution releasing its members from the payment of dues.
We find in the proceedings of 1891 another decision relating to the same
subject matter.
In Los Angeles Lodge, No. 42, a brother, who was abundantly able to pay
hie dues, the same were remitted for all time.
The Grand Master decided that this was a matter over which the Lodge,
only, had control. The Committee on Jurisprudence, in reviewing this decision, rendered their decision aa follows : 25. That a Lodge may release one of its members from the further payment of dues.
Thie decision is in accord with a rule adopted by this Grand Lodge in 1862
in the Golden Gate Lodge election case (Proceedings, Vol. V, p. 376), and followed in the Shepherd case in 1879 and 1884 (Proceedings, Vol. XIV, p. 190
Vol. XVI, p. 723.) In the former of these cases, the committee ~ta.te the
rule:"A subordinate Lodge may, for good reasons of its own, release a member
from the requirements which impose on him active duties, and relieve him
from contributions."
The case before the Grand Master did not commend itself to him as
right or just, but he could not do otherwise than follow tlte rule thus settled.

Bro. TBoMAB L. JoNES presented the following:To the M. '. W. ·. Grand Lodge of California:On the 29th day of July last Hope Lodge, No. 234, met with the misfortune
of having its Lodge building,. with ne&rly all its contents, destroyed by fire

While others (alas ! we miss their familiar faces) have fallen in life's battle-some crowned with laurels of a victorious contest and ripe for the Master's
garner--some in the blush of their young manhood, but with a name fragrant
with good works having built well the temple of character. To us who are
left devolves the great work to which they gave their best efforts, of lifting
up our common manhood, and strengthening the cords of friendship and
brotherly love throughout all lands.
The traditional account of the rise and formation of the Masonic Order was
in the organization of the workmen under the three Grand Masters in the
erection of Solomon's Temple at Jerusalem. Orders of workmen had nndoubf
edly existed long prior thereto, as shown by symbols found in the ruins of
Nineveh, Babylon, Persepolis and Egypt. Under the direction of the three
illustrious Grand Masters the workmen were organized as Entered Apprentices,
Fellow Crafts and Master Masons, and the thousands thus employed erected
the Temple to Jehovah upon the sacred Mount of Moriah. For a foundation
of the outer wall, on three sides the rock of the mountain wa.s laid bare ; on
the fourth, from the Tyropean Valley, a titanic wall was built up, which remains to this day the wonder of modern architects. From this wall a mighty
arch led over to the King's Palace on the hill of Zion, affording a. broad high.
way from the palaces on Zion to the temple. The stones for the building of
this great edifice were quarried in the caverns of the mountain, squared and
numbered, and placed in position without the sound of hammer, but by the
setting maul alone. The wood wa.s cut in the far north, in the mountains of
Libanus, shipped to Joppa, and thence transported to Jerusalem and placed in
the cloisters of the temple. From Ophir was brought talents of gold that over.
la.id the decorations of the structure, while from far and near came precious
stones to adorn and beautify the building, until, a.s JOSEPHUS says, it shone

[Oct. 13,

from afar as a monntain of snow, whose gilded minarets flashed in the sunlight
of the pure air of Palestine.
It was a marvel of etrength, magnificence and beauty, whose fame ~prea.d
far and wide, and yet the Queen of Sheba, as she stood in its courts, alilld the
gorgeous pa.laces by which it was surrounded, &nd gazing upon its unourpa.ssed
.
splendor, exclaimed, "the half was not told me."
Silently in the quarries and in the mountains and upon the site the gr~at
temple was reared; first a.ronnd the base of the mount the court.of the gentil11s
with· its cloisters ; then within and above the court of the Is~a.ehtes ; and t~en
still within and above, by regular steps, the court of the Pri.ests and t~e tribe
of Levi; and still within and above, crowning _the summit of Moriah, t~e
Sanctum Sanctorum, or most holy place; and thus the temple was complete 10
all its parts and dedicated to the worship of JEHOVAH.
.
So, in later days, the Craft in Europe have erected the migh~y c~tqedra.ls,
whose.chiseled beauty e.nrl magnificent proportions a.re the ad~nra.tion of ~he
world, not only for the conception of the architect, but the faithful devot10n
ot the workmen.
But Masonry is no longer operative, but symbolic. No longer do we h~ve
to do with the square, the trowel and the maul. No longer do we. deal. with
woo· d , or stone , or meta.le • or other plastic substance. But we a.re
. still builders
d
of temples, more enduring than SoLOMON's, and upon a. foun~tion a.a sure an
sacred. We a.re build.era of character, upon the foundation of. manhood.
M&&<>nry deals with me.n in his free, individual personality. There 1e no other
foundation on which the full.developed structure of humanity c_an be erec~d.
The patriarchal foundation has failed-now a.lone preserved i~ the f~lhng,

Through all the ages, from Egypt to Spain, the rule of the priest has been
the degrada.tion of the people. It has been the dogma of king and priest, ' that
men were for their benefit, having no inalienable rights in themselves. In
Masonry, king and priest and peasant are brothers, having the ea.me Great
Father and the same common destiny. Man must stand alone. No king or
priest ca.n act as proxy for him, in respect to the laws of nature or the mandates of heaven. He a.lone must investigate, he a.lone decide. No priest or
church can answer for him. It is his glory that he stands alone in his environ·
ment, with full power to freely think and act.
Man, ideally coneidered, is great. " What a piece of work is man ! In
action how like an angel ! In apprehension how like a god ! "
The Psalmist exclaimed : " When I consider thy heavens the work of thy
fingers-the moon and stars which thou hast ordained, what is man that
thou art mindful of him, or the son of man that thou visitest him? Thou hast
made him a. little lower than the angels ! Thou ha.st crowned him with glory
and honor ! " Crowned him with the glory and honor to weigh, measure and
trace th11 movements of the myriad of worlds that flash like diamond dust in
the evening sky. To read the history of this world, a.a revealed in the indu·
rated leaves of the rock-ribbed earth ; to analyze the elements of nature, learn
their substance and powers, and subject them to his use and pleasur~, and, in

of all truth. Upon a constitution so· grand, capacities so vast, e.nd range of
being so exalted, as a founda.tion-Masonry proposes, by precept and example,
to assist each for himself, to erect a. temple of immortal and imperishable
character. This it does in ite three degrees by inculcating the lessons of
obedience, intelligence and integrity.
Character is what a. man is in the light of his own consciousness and in the
eye of omniscience. We commence life without character, and we build for
ourselves under the environment of our lives . We may be moulded by that
environment, or we may use it to our growth and development. The utmost
freedom is required on the part of each man in that work; freedom from every
force that would enslave the soul, or hinder his highest effort, and yet he must
build under law. It is wondrously true that the environment of law aids
rather than hinders, the evolution of man and mind. He must work ~
harmony with the law of nature e.nd nature's God-or he will be found fighting
foes of his own creation.
Obedience to law, then, is thP. comer-stone of every truly great character.
Masonry teaches obedience to the laws of family and friend, to the laws of his
country-to the law of righteousness, which is the law of God.
In this land we have no SQvereign but law, and good citizenship depends
upon our obedience to law. For one to disobey is for a!l to d1sobey, a.nd
anarchy follows. Disobedience to law is the source of all our evils. It fills our
streets with the idle and dissolute, our jails With criminals, and our country
with strife. The conflict of labor and capital would lose its perilous character

Masonry teaches obedience to the laws of friendship and brotherly love.
This binds the Fraternity by the strongest tie. Every Mason is my brother,
whatever his station iu life, and my obligation to him, as such, is not changed
or lost by change of situation or condition. He is a. brother man. Secretly,
or openly, a. thousand instances could be cited, where this la.w has been obeyed
even at great peril.

Masonry teaches obedience to the moral law, the law of righteousness.
Every faculty of mind and body, every desire, emotion and passion, were
bestowed for a wise purpose. But all are to be used and enjoyed under a.n
enlightened judgment and a sovereign will. There can be no supreme obedience to law without supreme control of self. The appetites and passions are
loyal servants, but tyrannous ma9ters; when subdued to the power of the
will, they add zest to life, and strengthen every faculty of the soul. The will
is the helmsman of the man.

In the second degree, Masonry urges the acquirement of a knowledge of
the liberal sciences. The ignorant man is the slave or dupe of his fellownia.n.
Placed in the midst of conflicting opinions, he can only act wisely who acts
intelligently. Lack of knowledge is the source of all the isms of the age.
Truth is one and universal. The rough ashlar must be cut, squared and finished for its place in the structure ; so all the faculties of man must be rounded
out by culture, to erect the temple of a truly sublime character. A Mason is
not to be a mummy; enshrouded in the habiliments of death, but a strong,
living force in the world, c~h in his sphere.
American citizenship demands the educated man. Many of the States,
including our own, require an educational test in order to vote. It is not only
necessary to know the form of our Government, and the officers to carry on its
various functions, but great questions are constantly being presented for consideration, that require study and thought rightly to decide. We boast of
beiag a well educated people. In some senses we are. Most of us know how to
read and write; hut in the sense of a capability to master the great problems
in the science of government, there is a profound ignorance. How few know
aught of the laws of tariff or finance, or are able to discern between truth and
error in the discussion of the same. One asserts that we have become a rich
and prosperous people by reason of a protective tariff, and another holds that
we have become such from other causes, and have been handicapped rather
than helped by a protective tariff. One asserts that gold is the only stable
measure of values, and another insists that silver is the most reliable measure;
while a third declares that greenQa.cks and an unlimited issue of paper currency is the only panacea. of our financial troubles; and another holds that
government is a business corporation, only fixing the standard of weights and
measures, and receiving and paying out money in the strict order of business.
How shall we act in the matter! for we must act.
BoLINBBOKE deolared thoi.t history was philosophy teaching by example.
What does history say on all these questioDS? They are not new. It is the
Ma.son's duty to learn, that he may fulfill his vows of fidelity to his country ;
to know the truth rather than the shibboleth of party.
Man, uneducated, is a hewer of wood and a drawer of water. He exhibits
only a vital force. Independent thought and action only result from education. I do not mean the learning of the schools alone. Too often the school
has dwarfed rather than enlarged the scope of the man's being; but the evolution of the faculties of the soul by training and acquisition of faots. Knowledge
is power. But mere knowledge, without the ability to use it by a trained

We are in the midst of a political campaign. The press and the itinerant
orator are daily before the people, with their dogmatic statements, as to the
condition of the country, its finances, and its prosperity, and its necessities.
How full of sophistries both papers and orators are. Cunditions of the country
are given as having the relation of cause and effect, which are merely coincident. All the evils of Pandora's box are likely to follow the elevation of one
party, in the view of the other, and all prosperity of the country due to its
dethronement. With one, whatever it is or does, is right, and w.hat the other
does or believes, is wrong. An opinion is correct· when held by us, and wrong
when held by our opponent. Is it any wonder that confusion follows, and the
country is often imperiled by lack of stability, because we trifle with these
matters for the sake of place and power!
Sound learning would enable us to separate the logical from the illogical
the true from the specious and false, and place country before party or place:
&~d so secure for our land lasting peace and unbounded prosperity. Masonry
bids her followers to study well, that they may act wisely.

whatever field his labors were cast. He was well equipped for hie life laborthe law. He had a sturdy constitution, that brought him to the age of fifty.
eight years without a serious illne88. He was born October 2, 1839, in
Quillcy, Michigan, which was hie home until he ca.me to California in the
spring of 1865. He was educated in the schools of ·hie native State, graduat.
ing from the law department of Ann Arbor College March 31, 1864, and was
admitted by the Supreme Court of that State to practice as an attorney and
counselor a.t law, April o, 1864, and by the Supreme Court of the State of
Califor.nia, J a.nuary 3, 1871. On hie arrival in this, the State of hie adoption,
he first located in Sonoma county. He ca.me via the Isthmus, and before
reaching San Francisco he was shipwrecked, losing his law library and all the
property he had except the clothes he wore. He moved to Yolo county in
1867, where'·he taught school until he wa.e admitted to practice his profession
by the Supreme Court of this State. He then opened a law office in the city
of W oodla.nd, where he continued to practice with eminent success until death
closed hie labors on the 6th day of May, 1898.
In the fall of 1873 he was elected District Attorney of Yolo county, and
re-elected two yea.rs later, holditig the office four succe88ive years. He was
married in Woodland, July 19, 1874, to Mies Addie E. Thomae, who survives
hitn. Always regarding a. public office as a public trust, so well and faithfully
did he discharge it, that his friends and neighbors elected him to the Legislature
in 1880. He wa.e truly one of God's noblemen, always taking a great interest
in the welfare of the community in which he lived, being at different times
school trustee, lib~ry trustee, and a. trustee of the Masonic Ha.II Association
of the city in which the more mature years of hia life were P8.88ed.
About the year 1872 he became a member of Woodland Lodge, No. 106,
F. and A. M. He was a zealous and earnest member of the Fraternity, and
served his Lodge at different times faithfully and efficiently as Master, and
in variou·a subordinate positions. On October 17th·, 1896, the Grand Master
appointed him Grand Ora.tor. And on October 13th, 1897, he delivered the
oration so replete with historical research and the pithy deductions and application of a master mind.
.

In whatever station or place we behold him we always find him the same
nnll8lluming, courteous gentleman. With a mind stored in the classics and in
the law, with a thorough knowledge from a personal observation and historical
research of his own and foreign countries, with a clear head, a pure heart, a
trained intellect, a cultivated t&11te, a vigorous constitution and indomitable
will, he poll8e8sed, in the highest degree, the elements requisite for the de·
velopment and perpetuity of this Western Empire, the home of bis adoption ..
He was one of the almost countless number whom the East has given to
build up the West. As a rule, this influx was composed of men of Bro. BAKER'S
type, young, full of energy, scant ID material resources, relying upon the ta.lent
conferred by nature, upon habits of industry primitive to the northeastern
portion of our country., with a keen sense of right, of independence and of
eelf-reliance which so characterize the Anglo Saxon race, he ca.et bis lot

The past yea.r has been fraught with interest to the· Home, a.s since our last
report we have been able to erect two large buildings, the exterior and interior fittings of which need no commendations from us, as you have all seen
them for yourselves.
During the yea.r a. project originating with several of the brethren of San
Francisco materialized into a. Masonic Festival, or Fair, which, through the
zealous energy of many brethren and ladies, proved to be a stupendous success, and although only held from May 9th to 14th (one week), realized a. net
profit for the Home of over $39,000. This a.mount represents the zeal of the
Lodges, Cha.pteFs, Commanderies, Consistory, Shrine, Ea.stern Star Chapters,
and ladies of Ma.sonic families. Donations of money and supplitll! were most
liberal. We especially tha.nk

and many other Lodges, Chapters of Eastern Star, and individual Masons,
too numerous to mention in this brief report, the donations of cash amounting
to some $19,000.
With the Fair money, the prior subscriptions of Lodges, a.nd tho money
donated by the last Grand Lodge, the l!oard of Directors entered into contract
of building No. 1, and when the money from the Fair exceeded our estimate
we contracted for bnildiog No. 2. As first provided, building No. l included
kitchen and dining room in basement, which was not a good arrangement, but
the best we could do with the amount of funds on band, bat when we con·
eluded to build No. 2 building, or, as it ma.y now be called, the anna, we
placed the kitchen, pantries a.nd dining room on the first floor of the annex,
and the second floor is partitioned into small rooms, and we now have room
for eighteen men. The basement has the ba.ke l'oom, servants' dining room,
work-room and boiler for heating purposes. The large basement of the main
building can be used for the children's play-room in wet wea.tber, a.od, in time,

Many, many things are still needed to place the Home ~n run~mg order,
and it is for you to provide the means, and your Trustees will find the way.
A mistaken idea seems to exist among the Masone of Southern California
that this Masonic Home is a Northern California Home.
Thie is in no way, shape or form correct. It is intended for tb.e orphan
children, the widows of Master Masone, and indigent brethren of the whole
State.
The Masonic Home of California is your Home, my brother. Your children if they are in need and poverty, are entitled to its benefits.
I~ being yom· Home, we ask your support for it, that all deserving may
p&rtake of your bounty. Eight and one.third cents per month from every
Mason of this State will support this, your Home.
To every member of this Grand Lodge we make this appeal.. We want
every Mason in the StRte to know what this grand charity is intended for,
and to understand that it is for him and those dear to him.
We would recommend a capitation tax of $LOO per year, or $20,000 from
Grand Lodge funds, or increased assessment of Grand Lodge from 95c. to
$1.95, and let the item of $20,000 for support of Home be one of the necessary · and legitimate expenses Qf the Grand Lodge, just as the item of $3000,
Gr&nd Secretary's salary, is now. We can only recomhiend, it is for you to
act. Masonic Homes in ten States receive their support by capitation tax.
In view of the fact that a State allowance can be secured for orphans a.nd
half orphans by any corporation in the State, we deem it wise t~at your
Board of Trustees be given permission by this Grand Lodge to incorporate, if
they shall deem it 11dvieable, so that the State aid may be received by them
as a corporate body, if necessary.
Our thanks are due to Bro. w. H. LILLIE, the architect of the work, for
faithful performance of his duties.
Respectfully submitted.

Bro. WILLIAM S. WEr.LS, Chairman of the Grievance Col!lmittee,
presented the following reports : To tM M. •. W. ·. G1·ood Lodge of Califr:rrnia :-

your committee, to whom was referred the tranecript of trial record in the
case of RUSSELL WARREN BROWN, of Ionic Lodge, No. 121, suspended by
lllinoistown Lodge, No. 51, on July let, 1898, have had the same under con·
sideration, and report as follows : The accused was charged by a member of Eureka Lodge, No. 16, with unmasonic conduct in having made an assault upon the accuser, a Master Mason
by etriking him and applying to him vile names.
'
The accused filed an answer to the charges, in which he set out that he had
no knowledge or legal information that the accuser was a Master MBBOn
plead guilty ·to the assault and asked to introduce evidence showing juetifica'.
tfon and extenuating circumstances. The accused appealed, the time for
which, however, had expired, it being three days h~te.
There is no testimony to show that the accused knew the accuser to be a
Master Mason, and the accuser admits that be bad never eat in Lodge with

/

836

Proce,ed,i,ngs of tM

[Oct. 13,

the accused. The a.censer was represented on the trial by an attorney, the
accused without attorney, representing himself. After the testimony on the
pa.rt of the a.censer bad been presented, the accused offered to present testimony in justification; which testimony was objected to by the counsel for the
accuser on the ground that it was incompetent, irrelevant and improper.
The objection was sustained by the Master, to which the accused excepted.
. There seems to be a growing tendency in Masonic trials where parties are
represented by attorneys to strictly apply the rules of civil law to evidence
produced before the Commission. This is wrong ; the Master has no right to
exclude any testimony-the accuser should have every opportunity to present
evidence to the Commission in his defense, and the Commission should judge
its' competency. The testimony offered by the accused in this case should
have been received by the CommiBSion.
The trial w~ held on June 14th, and after all the testimony had been produced, the Commission, without any reason, adjourned until June 25th, or
for eieven days, when they met and proceeded to deliberate and discuss the
verdict without any further testimony being produced. This was' grievous
error. Immediately upon hearing the testimony the Commission should proceed to deliberate upon their verdict and sentence, :md should continue such
deliberations until an agreement is reached. This question was ably discussed and decided in the case of STEVENS, volume XXI, Grand Lodge ·Proceedings, page 729.
The record states "after deliberation and discussion proceeded to ballot, and
the accused was found guilty on each specification, and also guilty of uoma·
sonic· conduct, and the vel'dict of the Commissioners was suspension."
The record should show the vote upon each specification and upon the
charge, and also on the vote on the question '' shall the accused be expelled,"
and the vote on the question ".shall the accused be suspended," all of which
the record in this case fails to show and it is error.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the judgment of lllinoistown Lodge, No. 51, made on July
] st, 1898, whereby Ross ELL W A.RREN BROWN was suspended from all the
rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby reversed, with
directions to ea.id Lodge to retry the accused in accordance with Ma.sonic law.

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of the record of trial
of Bro. ALEXANDER RosBOROOGH FRASER, of South Gate. Lodge, No. 320, adjudged to be reprimanded by Sunset Lodge, No. 290, together with the. appeal of the accuser from said judgment, have had the same under· considera.
tion, and report as follows :The accused was charged with having an inordinate and unreasonable
craving for office and of writing a. threatening, defamatory and scandalous
letter to the wife of a brother Mason. Objections to the charges were ma.de,
some of which were sustained, the Master permitting a.mended charges to be

1898.]

837

filed and the trial to. proceed thereon. The practice seems to be increasing;
and cannot be upheld.
It is the duty of the Master, when charges are presented, to judge of their
sufficiency ; if insufficient he should refllBe to entertain them, and we know of
no rule which justifies the filing of amended charges and proceeding with the
trial upon suc.h new charges.
A brother must be tried upon the charges as originally presented, and to
which he has been summoned to answer; if it appears that they are insufficient they should be dismissed and new charges preferred.
The transcript contains seventy odd pages of dosely written 111atter, and
the only charge which is worthy of serious consideration is that of writing a
defamatory letter.
From a careful examination of the rl!CQrd and testimony we are inclin!ld to
the belief that the accused should not alone be ma.de to suffer, and that he is
by no means the only one a.t fa.ult. The testimony shows that the accused
bas been an enthusiastic, worthy and exemplary member of South Go.te Lodge;
that the letter complained of was written and handed by t)le accused to the
person to whom it was addressed at a lfleeting of the Eastern Star; that it
was written only after the accused had been informed that such person had
repeatedly, at divers times and to ma.i;iy persons, sneeringly and disrespectfully spoken of and slandered him-all clearly established by the j;estimpny.
Driven to desperation by her conduct, he wrote the lettiir complaioed·of, and
for the writing of which he ha.a on several occasions exprefll!ed, not ,only to
herself, but to others, his sorrow and regret. The same spirit exhibited by
all members of South Gate Lodge would have avQided all the trouble.
This case was transferred by the Grand Master from Soutli Gate Lodge to
Sunset Lodge. Nine CommiBBioners were elected to try the case; they were
from another Lodge, had no p'r ejudice or bias, and both part_ies expressed
themselves as having no objection to any of them.
,
The conclusion of such a CommiBBion, who hear the evidence and see all
the witnesses, as to the punishment which sbonld be inflicted, should not be
interfered with except for good cause shown. There is nothing in the circumstances of this case to take it out of the operation of this rule.
Your committee therefore offer the following resol11tion and recommend its
adoption:Re11olved, That the judgment of ,unset Lodge, No. 200, rendered April 8th!
1898, whereby Bro. ALEXANDER ROSBOROUGH FRASER was adj11dged to suffer
reprimand, be and the saioe is hereby affirmed.

ing her and wasting hie earnings in drunken debauchee, and of obtaining
money under false pretenses.
The accused was represented by counsel, who made a motion to strike out
certain of the charges and portions of the charges, the Master overruling some
and sustaining others. As an illustration, the second specification is as
follows : "That the said brother has been guilty of unmasonic conduct in
thi*: that during a large portion of the time during the past two years, he
having the ability so to do, has neirlected to providfl for hie wife the common
necessaries of life, and that during said time he has neglected her, and without just cause or excuse has abandoned her and has wasted hie earnings in
drunken debauches while she wad compelled to provide for herself ~nd be snpported in part by charity." Which charge the accused moved to strike out,
as follows : " All of charge two, for the reason that such charge contains no
clear and dertain offense, and because it is uncertain, unsatisfactory and insufficient." Which motion was sustained and granted by the Master.
Your committee must admit that it cannot conceive or imagine the argument used by the learned counsel to comince the Master that facts stated as
in this specification do not constitute a Masonic offense and are not clear and
certain. It certainly reflects great credit upon the eminent counsel, but
l!lbowe the absolute folly of pennitting such motions to be made in Masonic
trials. All the charges are clearly and 'specifically stated, and the Master had
no right to change or alter them in any particular, he 'having once passed
upon them and determined that they were sufficient to constitute a Masonic
offense. We trust that this committee will not again be called upon to disprove of this practice, and that no cause for complaint will be given in the
fa tu re.
The transcript comes to us carefully and properly prepared, and the proceedings, exept as herein noted, are re~lar and can be approved, There was
no testimony offered tO sustain the charges of obtaining money under false
pretenses ; the testimony shows that the accused has been justly adjudged
guilty of anmasonic conduct in being drunk and intoxicated on the public
streets of San Diego and Los Angeles.
We therefore offer th~ following resolution and recommend its adoption :ReBolved, That the judgment of Southwe11t Lodge, No. 283, made on Jane
lat, 1898, whereby DUNCAN SMITH McCLRLLAN was suspended from all the
righ~ and privileges of Masonry, be anc;I the same is hereby affirmed.

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of trial record in the
case of EUGENE C. SHAVER of Pnjaro Lodge, No. llO, expelled by Lompoc
Lodge, No. 262, on April 29th, 1898, have had the same under consideration
and report as follows :There are six specificatione, all allegin~ disobedience of summons to appear
for reprimand, and the accused was adjudged guilty on all six. He was tried

r .

Grand Lodge of OaUfornia.

839

on February 12th, 1897, by a Commission of Lompoc Lodge, for unmasonic
oonduct and adjudged to suffer reprimand.
The transcript was improperly before this committee at the last Annual
Communication and the same was returned to Lompoc Lodge.
Your committee has carefully examined the record and facts and heard
additional testimony in this matter, from all of which it appears that the
accused was summoned by Lompoc Lodge to appear for reprimand five
separate times, each time sending an excuse, which the Lodge accepted, and
fixed a new date. After the return of the trial record, and on October 29th,
1897, he was again summoned to appear on November 5th, and to this summons he re\ilied by letter, saying that he was financially unable to be present ;
that he had no means; that to go to Lompoc would work a serious hardship
and injury to himself and family; that by reason of his financial condition,
it would be impossible for him to attend. There is no certificate of service of
this last summons, or any showing that the same has been served, except the
letter of the accused giving his excuse.
We are convinced that the accused brother did not willfully disobey or
disregard any of the summons sent him by Lompoc Lodge, and that he intended no disrespect to the Master or the brethren of .the said Lodge, but
that he could not obey its mandates by reason of the fact that he had no
means to pay his way and the expenses of the trip from Watsonville, where
he resided and now resides, to Lompoc, a distance of three hundred miles and
more. That he should suffer reprimand in accordance with the judgment of
February 12th, 1897, we are thoroughly convinced, but to compel him to travel
that distance and expend the sum of money necessary, when sa.tisfied that his
circumstances will not permit and that it will work a serious injury to himself
and those whom it is his duty to aid and support, is not Masonic and is not
just. Lompoc Lodge desires this matter to be finally settled and determined,
and carefully weighing and considering all the facts and the entire case, as
presented to us, we offer, as the proper, just and Masonic solution, the following resolution and recommend its adoption:~
ReBolved, That the judgment of Lorn.pot Lodge, No. 262, made on April
29th, 1898, whereby EUGENE C. SHA.VER of Pa;aro Lodge, No. llO, was expelled from all the rights and privileges of Maeonry, be and the same is hereby
reversed, with instructions to said Lodge to dismiss the said charges.
Resolved, That a copy of the transcript of the trial record in the case of

The right to the fees in controversy is to be determined by. the ~onstl·
tutiona.l regulation governing a waiver of jurisdiction, as prescribed m Sec.
2, Art. III, Part Ill of the Constitution, a.s amended in 1892. That section of the C<>nstitution, at the time of its adoption, repealed all laws and
deci~ions which conflict with its provisions. The Lodge which grants a waiver
of jurisdiction over one who is not a Mason surrenders all of its jurisdictional
rights over the person mentioned, including its right to re_ceive his pe~ition
for the degrees, and its right to claim or demand the fees which were paid by
the ea.id applicant for the degrees in Masonry. From the evidence before us it
appears that Brooklyn Lodge unconditionally surrendered its jurisdiction over
the person in question. Under these conditions the fees for the degrees belong
to the Lodge of which the applicant became a member.

Bro. ADOLl'B WESKE states that he holds a certificate of .life membership in a Lodge that has gone out of existence and asks where he now stand•

We reply that hie relation to the Fraternity is now that of a dimitted
Ma.son. Ris life membership was a special contract between himself and his
Lodge. When the Lodge ceased to exist his life membership ceased also.
When he affiliates with another Lodge he will be required to pay dues the
same as any other member.

Bro. TAYLOR has manifestly misquoted· -the numbers of the section and
article of the Constitution, which .he wishes . defined, Sec. l of Art. II, of
part V of the Constitution, simply declares that a non-affiliate who resides in
this State for a period of eix months without applying to a Lodge in this jurisdiction for membership is a 8uspended Ma.sou.
The subject matter to which Bro. TAYLOR refers is found in Sec. 8 of Art.
V, of par~ VI of the Constitution, which was one of the amendments which
was adopted in 1883, and embodied certain provision1 which were formerly
embraced in General Reguia.tion No. 16. The section reads a.s follows:--:
SKC'l'ION 8. Non-affiliated Masons who, under the provisions of Sec. l of
Art. II, of part V, are deemed to occupy the same position as those euspen~e~ for non-payment of dues, and who desire to restore themselves by

if any, required by its By-Laws.
'
We a.re asked to define the exact meaning of this section. Conciaely
stated, it is this : A nou-affiliate Mason who has resided in this State for a period of six
montbs after he has withdrawn from hie Lodge, and who has, during that
time, neglected to apply for membership in eome Lodge within this jurisdiction, is an excluded Mason. He ha.e no recognized Ma.sonic standing here.
He has no Ma.sonic rights nor privileges-not even the right of paying dues,
nor the privilege of applying for membership in a. Lodge until after he hae
paid to the Secretary of such Lodge a certain fee. The fee to be paid is a
sum of money equivalent to six months' dues in the particular Lodge to which
·he applies, and the affiliation fee where such fee iii required by the By-Laws.
The fee named is not paid a.s dues, but as a. necessary condition which he must
comply with before he can file hie application for membership. He can pay
no dues until after he has been elected to membership in a. lodge, When l)e
has paid the required fee or fees, and has filed his application' for member-

ship, he has complied with the requirements of Sec. 8, Art. · V, part VI of
the ConMtitution.
The Constitution and General Regulations prescribe no other conditions
which a non-affiliated Mason is required to comply with, except thot in General Regulation No. 23 he is required to prove, to the satisfaction of the
Master of the Lodge to which he applies, that he is a Master Mason.
There is no section in our Constitution or General Regulations which defines the Masonic standing or prescribes the requirements of a non-affiliate
whose application for affiliation has been rejected by a Lodge within this jurisdiction. Such legislation is to be found only in the Meveral reports of the
Committee on Jurisprudence, which have been adopted by the Grand Lodge .
since the Constitution, as amended in 1883, went into effect.
Such legislation is reviewed aud carefully stated io the extended and comprehensive report of the Committee on Jurisprudence at the Annual Communication of 1893, and is found on pages 205 to and including 222 of Vol.
XXI of the printed proceedings. We respectfully refer to that report for the
interpretation which the Grand Lodge has given to the law.

Your committee have carefully considered the several portions of theGrand
Master's Address which were referred to them, and report as follows:The various special diapeueations which he has i88ued during the year were
issued in compliance with the provision• of our Constitution, and should be ·
approved.
Among the several decisions reported by him are the following:I. A brother who ha.a been refused advancement is entitled to know only
that be baa been refused, that the matter has been referred to a proper committee, that bis rights have been preserved, and that the Lodge has, by a proper
voie, refused to advance him.
A person having been elected to receive the degrees may, at the request
of the Lodge in which he was elected, receive the three degrees in another
Lod~e.

Charges may be withdrawn previous to the commencement of a trial, but
not afterward.
When a brother has received certain sums of money as charity from hie
Lodge, the money thus given him cannot be charged to his account as dues or
as money due from him to the Lodge.
An amendment to the By-Laws of a Lodge, remittin!! the dues of all members suspended for non-payment of dues, would be neither wise nor constitutional. It is the duty of every Mason to pay his dues when financially able,
but when he can no longer do so his Lodge, on a proper showing made, may
either remit them or extend the time of :payment. Having been suspended,
a member may be reinstated either by paymg all arrearagee, or hie dues may
be remitted hy the Lodge; but a By-Law, the effect of .w hich would be practically to require no dues at all from any member after a certain period of
delinquency, would not be constitutional.
To the query, "Can an Italian gentleman, ~peaking neither J?igli_ah nor
French, receive tlie three degrees of Masonry m a Lodge, workmg m the
French language, by the medium of an interpreter or dragoman? " I replied
that lie could not.
